(a) The tonic index (at least one spike in at least 80% of cycles) is also passed by a lift-coupled code whose count rises with |u|; nothing tests that count is independent of |u*|, or that spikes sit at the neutral phase when |u*| is small. (b) The circular-linear phase-versus-u* correlation is high for a plain sign-coded phasic code (135/315). (c) The inherited criterion '>= 70% of onsets within +-67.5 deg of 135/315' penalises a genuine proportional tonic code: with psi = 45 + 90*clip(u), every spike with |u*| < 0.25 (pitch below about 2.9 deg) lies more than 67.5 deg from both optima. So a working tonic code can fail G2 while a bang-bang code passes it. (d) NEAT is trained on J, which selects tonic over phasic only if tonic wins in J (law_strong test J = 6.29), not just at matched height. v1 drifted to over-pulsing under this J. The live v2 champion training fitness has wandered between -7.9 and -10.5 for 12 generations with no trend (runs/spike_steer/pilot_v2_s1/history.jsonl), and the validation champion at gen 11 is the gen-3 one. The expected tonic advantage, about 0.3 J per cm of height, is below that noise.

The 'why SNN/NEAT' mechanism contradicts the code. Graph/SpikingGraph (wingbeat_snn/networks.py:62-77, spike_steer/pilot.py:59-74) have a threshold and subtractive reset but no refractory period, so nothing caps spikes per cycle. Each 45-deg one-hot phase cell stays on for about 2.5 ticks, and tau_m is 5 ms, so a weight 'clearly above threshold' produces multi-tick bursts. A proportional phase shift of about 90 deg cannot come from one LIF's latency; it needs bin switching or population codes with graded weights. That is exactly the fine weight tuning NEAT failed at (lesson 2).

As written, G1(a) is likely to return a spurious 'drop' (fixable gate-design flaw). In timing_authority.json the burst-end vertical-velocity difference at the same phase varies 2.8-3.4x across the 4 cases (90-deg window at 135 deg: 0.043-0.118 m/s; 180-deg window: 0.057-0.192), a CV of about 45%. A single tick gives about 1/5 of that signal. With a 17.9-deg window, each 0.1 s burst (2.49 cycles) gets 2 or 3 ticks depending on the start phase, and the last tick lands 0-40 ms before the 20 ms end-of-burst difference. The '+-25% lift spread across four phases' criterion would therefore pass or fail at random.
fixes: Before any run, agree with the user on whether a G1-only (classical PPM) outcome is acceptable. The request is for an SNN/NEAT application, and G1-pass/G2-fail, the most likely path, is not one.

Give the tonic arms (B3, B4, SNN) a lowered motor feedforward, p['motor'] - 31.4*n, so the clipped integral is not saturated. Drop n=2, which does not fit under LOW in about half the stress cases. Log integral saturation and LOW-pinned time. Stratify or balance the tuning and test cases by motor_gain, which can be recovered from the seed like pilot.pulse_sign (it is the RNG draw just before the signs), and report results per stratum.

Redesign G1(a). Use a once-per-crank-cycle trigger instead of a 17.9-deg window. Use bursts of at least 0.3-0.5 s (8-12 cycles). Normalise by the actual tick count. Estimate pitch and vertical effects as mean accelerations by regressing the paired difference over complete cycles, not from a 20 ms endpoint difference. Use at least 8 cases and state the lift-spread test as a confidence interval.

Make G2 test the hypothesis. Add: count independence (Spearman correlation between per-cycle spike count and |u*| near 0, plus a low count CV); neutral-phase firing when |u*| is small; and a graded within-sign phase shift (slope of phase against |u*|). Replace the inherited '>= 70% within +-67.5 deg' rule with a PRC-weighted signed moment per cycle regressed on u*.

Train NEAT on the objective used for selection: height-constrained, e.g. J plus a steep penalty above 9 cm height RMSE, or a larger height weight. Otherwise selection pushes toward additive pulsing as in v1. Consider 8 cases per genome, or common random numbers across generations, to reduce the batch noise seen in v2.

Either add a refractory period to the output neurons and state that it is a design choice, or admit that the one-spike-per-cycle constraint is hand-imposed. In both cases, run the thresholded non-spiking (ANN/perceptron) arm on the same inputs with the same NEAT budget inside the gate, not only in the paper, because that is the lesson-2 test.

Gate G2 on v2's outcome. If balanced batches plus 2 motor neurons in v2 do not learn both push directions, the harder tonic plus both-direction plus phase-coding target is very unlikely at 20 generations. Skip G2 or seed a tonic motif from the start and claim only search and representation, not discovery.

Unify the runners. B2's dip exists only in timing.closed_loop and not in pilot.Steer, so implement B1-B4 and the SNN in one run() with identical metrics and per-tick crank/spike/u* logging. Note that pilot.run must be copied and extended for the per-cycle diagnostics.
critiques.reasoning:
Verdict: weak, 3/10. The topic stays inside the interface and the gate is affordable. But the SNN/NEAT part is unnecessary by design, its physics premise collides with the same LOW floor as lesson 5, and G2's metrics cannot detect the code it claims.

**Interface: compliant.** It uses ResearchEnv(mode='direct'), takes the PID command or HIGH each 2 ms tick, then the unchanged clip, 8.2 ms smoothing and motor path. Inputs are only the reading and features derived from it: PLL phase, notched gyro, PID margin. Ground truth is used only for metrics and for the open-loop phase-response measurement, which is labelled an upper bound. The PHASE_OFFSET calibration is reused, as in the existing IMU law. No sub-tick drive.

**Cost: affordable.**
- G1: about 156 grid points x 8 cases x 6 s, about 1250 episodes, about 39 min at 18 workers. Add about 4 min for the phase-response curve and about 4 min for test, plus about 13 min if B2 gets its own grid.
- G2: 32 x 20 x 4 = 2560 episodes, about 80 min.
- Total about 2.3-2.6 h.
- Code reuse is realistic. Overriding pilot's module globals works with fork-based pools (Python 3.11 on Linux). pilot.run needs copying for per-cycle logs, and B2's dip lives only in timing.closed_loop.

**Physics.** Extrapolating timing_authority.json linearly, one tick per cycle at the optimal phase gives about 0.55-0.6 rad/s:
- the 90-deg window is about 12.5 ticks per burst and gives 2.58 rad/s;
- one tick per cycle is about 2.5 ticks per burst, scaled up slightly because a single tick sits at the optimum;
- that is about 0.7x the gimbal step (0.778 rad/s), so the G1(a) timing bar of 0.5x probably passes.

The phase dependence of lift in the 90-deg data is mild (0.070/0.075/0.072/0.080 m/s at 45/135/225/315 deg). But:
- n=1 gives about 1/3 of B1's per-cycle authority during events (60-deg window, about 3.3 ticks per cycle).
- n=2 does not fit under LOW once motor_gain and the integral clip (+-40 rad/s, about 12 already used) are counted; see fatal issue 2.
- The G1(c) bar is demanding. On the same 16 test cases (artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json), law_moderate gives 4.38 deg at 8.89 cm and law_strong gives 3.03 deg at 10.86 cm. B3/B4 would need about 3.5 deg or less at 9.5 cm or less, close to law_strong's pitch with at least 1.4 cm less height.
- The oracle law grid (timing_law_grid.json) has a steep knee: about 5.0 deg at 8.2 cm against 3.7 deg at 9.8 cm.

My prior for G1 passing is about 20-25%, not 40%.

**SNN/NEAT.** B3 is the solution and G2 only asks for parity, so lessons 1-2 recur. The discovery claim is weak because:
- the network is handed the phase (PLL one-hot cells) and a spike-to-HIGH actuator;
- J does not favour the tonic over the phasic code;
- live v2 shows NEAT stagnating under batch noise of about 1 J;
- the code has no refractory period, so 'one spike per cycle' and graded phase shifts need fine weight tuning, NEAT's measured weakness (lesson 2);
- G2's tonic, phase-coding and direction criteria either do not discriminate or contradict a proportional tonic code.

My conditional prior for G2 is about 10-15%, so Go overall is a few percent. Even a Go would be 'NEAT matched a 15-line law'.

**Novelty.** The classical half is low-novelty. Constant-period in-cycle velocity-profile shaping is established: split-cycle (Doman/Oppenheimer), the patents US8700233 and US9428269, and four-segment split-cycle with DC motors (par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10463489).

**What survives.** G1 is a cheap, honest classical experiment on the lift-steering trade-off. It is worth running only if the user accepts a classical result, and only after the feedforward, n=1, motor-gain stratification and G1(a) measurement fixes.

**Key files** (under /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/):
- experiments/algorithms/snn_pid_compare/environment.py (TeacherPID integral clip, motor_gain applied after the clip)
- artifacts/pid_airborne_20261008/selected_pid.json (motor 3190, height_gains 900/500/80)
- experiments/algorithms/wingbeat_snn/networks.py and experiments/algorithms/spike_steer/pilot.py (no refractory period)
- artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_authority.json (per-case vertical-velocity spread)
- artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_law_grid.json and artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json (B1 Pareto points)
- runs/spike_steer/pilot_v2_s1/history.jsonl (v2 stagnation)

fatal_issues: SNN and NEAT are not central. The actuator is a binary 2 ms HIGH tick, and the phase is computed by the classical PLL feeding 45-deg one-hot cells. The network therefore only implements a lookup table plus a once-per-cycle latch. The 10-line B3 law, a thresholded MLP or GRU, an RL Bernoulli policy or a surrogate-gradient SNN can all represent the same thing, and v3 already measured SNN roughly equal to ANN. The gate's own target is parity (J <= 1.05x B3/B4), so reviewers will call SNN/NEAT incidental.

The classical part is split-cycle constant-period (PWM wingbeat-timing) control under another name: Doman/Oppenheimer/Sigthorsson (patent US8700233), Schenato-Campolo-Sastry CDC 2003 (PWM duty/timing per wingbeat, with a controllability-lift trade-off), RoboBee iso-lift split-cycle torque (Steinmeyer et al., RA-L 2019), and AirPulse STAR (arXiv 2602.06811, 2026: pitch from stroke-timing asymmetry that preserves mean frequency, in free flight). Only the platform-specific realisation is new: a single-motor crank, single-tick PPM, under asymmetric speed bounds.

The fallback claim that 'NEAT discovers the code' is scaffolded and not specific to SNN/NEAT. TWITCH_TICKS=1, the PLL phase cells, the PID-margin input and a height-penalised J together define a problem whose optimum is this count/phase code, so any optimiser of a binary per-tick policy should converge to it. Prior work already covers emergent temporal codes in evolved spiking agents (Floreano & Mattiussi 2001; Saggie-Wexler, Keinan & Ruppin 2004) and evolved neuromorphic split-cycle oscillators (Boddhu & Gallagher 2010; Gallagher, Doman & Oppenheimer, TEVC 2012).

The margin arithmetic rules out the antagonistic pair, which is the centrepiece of the 'SNN-native' story. Each standing HIGH tick per roughly 20-tick wingbeat adds about (3807.5-3178)/20 = 31 rad/s to the mean speed command; the lift data in timing_authority.json follow this linear estimate at about 85-90%. With n=2 the spikes take about 63 rad/s, the whole downward margin: hover would need the PID command at about 3108, below LOW = 3115, so the skip rule would fire continually. Only n=1 is viable. My first-harmonic estimate gives it about 0.7x the gimbal-step authority, against 4.1x for additive pulses, and it still halves the PID's own downward room.
fixes: Before spending compute, ask the user whether a classical-only outcome (PPM split-cycle on this platform) is an acceptable paper. If it is not, do not run this as an SNN/NEAT topic.

State the classical claim precisely and cite Doman/Oppenheimer split-cycle (US8700233), Schenato et al. CDC 2003, Steinmeyer et al. RA-L 2019 (iso-lift, which also documents the harmonic-filtering risk) and AirPulse STAR 2026. Describe the delta as quantised single-tick PPM under asymmetric bounds on a single-motor crank flapper.

Drop the standing n=2 pair. Use n=1, or one spike every k cycles. Add a margin check to G1: the distribution of the PID baseline above LOW and the fraction of post-handover cycles skipped, with a stop rule (for example, skips > 20%).

Put the centrality test in the gate itself, not only in the paper. Run two extra arms: (a) the same NEAT budget with a non-spiking thresholded-output network plus a 1-bit latch; (b) B3 tuned by CMA-ES with the same episode budget. Pre-register that an SNN/NEAT claim requires beating the non-spiking ablation in at least 12/16 paired cases, not just matching B3.

If the discovery claim is kept, remove the scaffolding: do not fix TWITCH_TICKS=1 (let spike count or bursts set the duration), replace the 45-deg one-hot cells with a continuous phase ramp or sin/cos, and run at least 3 seeds. Otherwise report the result honestly as 'recovers the hand-designed optimum'.

Make the NEAT rationale hold on the actual substrate. networks.py LIF has no refractory period (subtractive reset only, tau_m 5 ms) and delays stop at 20 ms, half the 40 ms cycle. Either add refractoriness or adaptation, or seed a tonic motif and evolve delays and topology only (weights frozen), then compare against CMA-ES on B3's continuous phase parameters.

If the SNN must be central, use it where the classical stack is weak: phase-locking from the raw pitch gyro jointly with spike timing, replacing PLL + notch. Train it with surrogate gradients and learnable delays (that approach reached 2.4 deg phase error, vs NEAT's 10 deg) and compare against PLL + B3.

Correct the bio framing. b1 phase changes stroke amplitude, so it affects both lift and yaw, and fly power muscles are asynchronous rather than phase-coded. Say 'inspired by', not 'analogue of', a count=lift / phase=moment code.
critiques.reasoning:
VERDICT: weak, 3/10. The gate is cheap and honest. Seen through novelty and centrality, though: the classical idea is split-cycle / PWM timing control, SNN and NEAT are incidental to it, and the fallback 'emergence' claim would not survive review.

NOVELTY
- The rule 'mean drive/period sets lift, in-cycle timing sets the moment' is the split-cycle constant-period concept: Doman/Oppenheimer/Sigthorsson and patent US8700233.
- Schenato, Campolo and Sastry (CDC 2003) already set duty cycle and timing per wingbeat under PWM drive and reported a controllability-lift trade-off.
- The RoboBee 'iso-lift' split-cycle work (Steinmeyer et al., RA-L 2019) produces torque at constant lift. It also documents this topic's main physical risk: actuator and transmission dynamics filter out the timing harmonics.
- AirPulse STAR (2026, two servos, PID) gets pitch from timing asymmetry that preserves mean frequency, in free flight.
- My brief searches found no single-motor crank flapper that does intra-cycle speed PPM, so the classical delta is platform-specific.
- On the neural side, prior work exists on:
  - evolved neuromorphic split-cycle controllers (Boddhu & Gallagher 2010; Gallagher et al., TEVC 2012);
  - evolved SNN delays (Wiklendt);
  - analyses of whether evolved spiking agents use spike timing (Floreano & Mattiussi 2001; Saggie-Wexler et al. 2004);
  - spike-driven (PFM) motor control (Sensors 2012).
- 'First count+phase multiplexed actuator code' is therefore a narrow first, not a strong one.

CENTRALITY
- The spike is just the actuator's binary tick, and the PLL does the phase arithmetic.
- An ANN or GRU with a 1-bit latch, an RL Bernoulli policy, a surrogate-gradient SNN, or B3 itself all represent the same code.
- The 'weights only need to be above or below threshold' premise fails on this substrate:
  - The phase cells are pulses of about 5 ms, so graded latency only covers about 20-30 deg of phase.
  - Larger shifts mean switching bins, and keeping the count constant through the switch needs matched excitation and inhibition thresholds, or a cycle-long latch the LIF does not have (no refractory period, delays up to 20 ms against a 40 ms cycle).
  - That is the fine-weight regime where NEAT was measured to be weak.
- The interim v2 run (runs/spike_steer/pilot_v2_s1/history.jsonl) has best validation J 8.59 so far (generations 3 and 11), vs v1's 7.57. NEAT is already struggling with the simpler additive code.

PHYSICS, FOR FAIRNESS
- The 90-deg-window phase-response curve in timing_authority.json is roughly sinusoidal: -0.30 / +2.70 / +0.36 / -2.46 rad/s at 45 / 135 / 225 / 315 deg.
- Lift is nearly flat across those phases: vz 0.070 / 0.074 / 0.072 / 0.080 m/s.
- Scaling to one tick by the first harmonic (sin 9 / sin 45 = 0.22) gives about 0.57 rad/s, or 0.7x the 0.78 rad/s gimbal step, so G1(a) may pass.
- But the margin arithmetic (fatal issue 4) allows only n=1. The additive laws in timing_law_grid.json run at 0.3-3% duty; n=1 is a 5% standing duty. Under the 9 cm height cap the additive law already reaches about 5.0 deg (tuning set) and 4.4 deg (law_moderate on test), so G1(c) needs about 3.5-4 deg from a channel about 6x weaker.

PUBLISHABILITY IF THE CLASSICAL LAW MATCHES
- This is the most likely case, and CMA-ES at equal budget will make B3 stronger still. What remains is a modest, simulation-only PPM/split-cycle result for one platform, not an SNN/NEAT paper.
- The emergence claim becomes meaningful only if a matched non-spiking NEAT network and CMA-ES-tuned B3 fail where the SNN succeeds. That contradicts the v3 lesson that SNN and ANN performed the same.
- By the proposal's own priors, P(Go) = 0.4 x 0.35 = 0.14. I would put it at about 0.05-0.10.

topic.title: Learning when to twitch: evolved three-factor plasticity that self-calibrates wingbeat-timed steering in flight
topic.one_line: A NEAT-evolved spiking steering circuit learns online, by reward-modulated STDP (its own twitch × the delayed IMU outcome), at which wingbeat phase a 6 ms full-range motor twitch pushes pitch up or down. The one-motor timing channel then works without a crank encoder and after in-flight shifts such as a latency jump or wing damage. A gate runs first: it measures whether those shifts exceed what a fixed law tolerates, and whether a tuned IMU-only RLS calibrator still leaves headroom.
topic.problem:
Inside the original v3 interface, the single-motor IST robot has only one fast pitch channel: timing. One-sided full-range motor twitches at a specific crank phase give 4.1x the gimbal-residual pitch authority. The IMU-only event-triggered pulse law cuts stress pitch RMS from 7.35 to 3.03 deg, at a height cost of 8.0 -> 10.9 cm.

The benefit depends entirely on the phase map 'PLL phase -> twitch onset that pushes up / down'. Today that map is one constant, PHASE_OFFSET = 84.14 deg (wingbeat_snn/plant.py), bench-calibrated in P0-E4 against the TRUE crank angle. A real robot without an encoder has no such angle. The offset is also the quantity least likely to transfer from simulation to the real robot, because it depends on sensor-filter group delay, latency, motor/driver lag and wing compliance.

The map can also move in flight:
- The gate-4 'delay_jump' (2 -> 10 ms) shifts it by about 72 deg at 24.9 Hz.
- Wing damage, servo weakening (x0.4), +2 g payload or thrust loss may shift its phase or change its amplitude. None of these has been measured. Thrust loss (speed gain x0.9) also shrinks twitch amplitude: about 629 -> 248 rad/s actual.

In the other (sub-tick) interface, the tuned law tolerated only about +-45 deg and failed beyond +-75 deg. At 180 deg a twitch pushes the wrong way, and every misplaced twitch still adds lift.

Gate 4 found that the optimal PID gains did not change for 4 of the 5 in-flight changes. This map is different: it has adaptation room whenever it moves beyond the tolerance. The problem is to learn and track the map online, from the IMU alone, while rejecting gusts and without ground truth.
topic.why_snn:
The control variable here is literally a spike:
- In this interface, the most effective actuation is a one-sided, full-range ~6 ms twitch. Its information is its timing within the wingbeat, not an amplitude (pulse 4.1x versus sinusoid 2.7x). Insect power and steering muscles work the same way: their spike phase carries the control (Sponberg & Daniel 2012).

Learning the map is a spike-timing credit-assignment problem:
- The question is which phase-locked presynaptic event coincided with a motor spike that produced a good pitch-rate change 20-100 ms later, before the lightly damped 4-5 Hz two-body oscillation swings the IMU response back.
- Three-factor STDP (pre/post coincidence -> eligibility trace -> delayed modulator) is the standard mechanism for this distal-reward problem (Izhikevich 2007).
- Eligibility only arises at synapses active during a twitch, so learning is as sparse as the actuation (~1-2 twitches/s, duty ~1%).

Spiking dynamics also provide, structurally:
- built-in exploration: a stochastic threshold crossing jitters the firing phase, which is the perturbation that gradient-free learning needs (as in songbird variability plus dopamine);
- refractoriness: at most one twitch per window, which limits wasted lift;
- synaptic delays and trace time constants that represent absolute lags (latency, actuator). These should transfer across wingbeat-frequency changes better than a phase look-up table, which is a falsifiable claim.

Honest caveat: a rate-coded three-factor rule on the same phase basis may be computationally equivalent. The full study includes that non-spiking plastic ablation. No energy argument is made.
topic.interface_check:
**Sensors.** Only the 11-D reading at 500 Hz is used. The circuit and all baselines read AHRS pitch (reading[1]) and the pitch gyro (reading[4]) through the existing WingbeatPhase PLL and its adaptive notch. Height is used only by the unchanged PID. The true crank angle, the de-rocked oracle pitch (gates.Oracle) and the hidden offset are used only to create scenarios, to score, and to analyse spike phases. No controller ever receives them.

**Actuators.** Every 2 ms, the v3 TeacherPID retuned to kp x1.5 commands gimbal alpha/beta within +-0.3 rad and the motor. A twitch sets the motor speed command to HIGH = 3807.5 rad/s for 3 ticks (6 ms). The command then passes through the same clip, 8.2 ms smoothing, servo (kp 1.045 N.m/rad, 0.02 N.m limit) and motor model (4.2 V, 6 A). There are no dips below the PID command, no sub-tick modulation (unlike the wingbeat_snn C++ phase drive) and no new actuator.

**Rates.** Control runs at 500 Hz; the SNN takes 2 x 1 ms substeps per tick, exactly as in pilot.py.

**Scenarios added (the only changes).**
- Controller-side phase miscalibration: a hidden offset, standing in for the reality gap.
- delay_steps 1 -> 5 at t = 4 s (the existing 'delay_jump').
- Servo x0.4, payload +2 g and thrust loss, all via the existing apply_change.
- One-wing damage: in-place scaling of that wing's blade-element strip areas (env.sim.backend.arrays[2k+1]). native_step.cpp reads wing.areas[i] through a pointer on every substep. HoverEnv.reset does not restore the areas, so the helper must.
- v3 stress disturbances unchanged.

Sensors, actuators, update rates and limits are unchanged.
topic.classical_baseline:
**Main baseline: an IMU-only self-calibrating pulse law with the same information.** It uses the PLL phase, notched pitch rate, AHRS pitch and its own efference copy.
- For each of its own twitches k at seen phase phi_k, it measures r_k = q(t_k+L2) - q(t_k+L1) on the low-passed notched rate.
- It runs recursive least squares with forgetting on r = a cos(phi) + b sin(phi) + c. The term c absorbs phase-independent lift, PID and disturbance effects; a 2nd harmonic is optional.
- Up phase = atan2(b, a); down phase = up + 180 deg, or a separate RLS per direction.
- While its confidence |(a,b)|/sigma is low, it fires probe twitches at uniformly random phases whenever |u| exceeds a lower threshold. Once confident, it jitters around the estimate. This instrumental-variable logic counters closed-loop confounding.
- Everything else is the tuned IMU pulse law (k_theta, k_q, threshold, width from the spike_steer v2 108-point grid; law_strong if that is unavailable).

**Secondary:** extremum seeking on psi, using a dither and the demodulated pitch-error energy.

**References:**
- retuned PID (kp x1.5);
- fixed law with the nominal calibration;
- robust-tuned fixed law: the single best psi and gains over the offset distribution;
- oracle-recalibrated law that knows the shift (upper bound).

**Same budget.** Every learner's free parameters get the same number of training episodes on the same balanced four-sign training cases. In the gate this means 24-48 configurations x 8 cases each. In the full study, the RLS calibrator is tuned by CMA-ES with as many episodes as the NEAT run.

gate.what:
Three stages, one seed, all tested on the 16-case stress test split shared with spike_steer v1/v2 (pilot.SPLITS['test']).

**S1 Room.**
- (a) PLL-referenced open-loop twitch-phase scan: 8 phases + one no-burst reference x 4 cases, 0.1 s burst at 3 s. Conditions: nominal, latency +4 and +8 ms, left-wing area -30%, left-wing outer 30% of span lost, servo x0.4, payload +2 g, thrust loss. A sinusoid fit gives each condition's phase shift dpsi*(c) and authority A(c).
- (b) For every condition with |dpsi*| >= 30 deg or |dA| >= 30%: 16 stress cases x 10 s, change at 4 s, comparing the retuned PID, the fixed law (nominal calibration) and the oracle-recalibrated law.

**S2 Learnability and classical headroom.** The RLS calibrator gets a 24-point grid (readout window x forgetting factor x probe threshold x jitter) on 8 balanced training cases with hidden offset ~U(0, 360 deg). It is tested on 16 cold-start cases (8 s) and 16 latency-jump cases (10 s; calibrated at the start, jump at 4 s).

**S3 Plastic-SNN viability and structure sensitivity.**
- Hand-built circuit: 8 or 16 PLL phase cells feed need-gated, noisy up/down LIF motor neurons. Each spike is a 3-tick twitch.
- Eligibility = twitch x phase-cell activity. The modulator is the direction-signed change in notched rate within a readout window, minus a running baseline. Weights are normalised.
- 48-point grid: rule constants (eta x noise) x structure (immediate vs delayed readout, mirrored vs independent up/down maps, one-hot vs von Mises phase code).
- The best configuration and three ablations (plasticity frozen, immediate readout, no mirror) run on the S2 test sets.
gate.code_reuse:
Repository: /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms.

**Reused:**
- spike_steer/pilot.py: the Steer/run loop (phase from WingbeatPhase.crank, twitch = 3 ticks at HIGH, J, onset logging with true crank phase and true need sign), balanced_cases, SPLITS, the SpikingGraph LIF semantics, and the tune_law grid.
- neuro_gates/timing.py: the run/measure authority scan and the closed_loop law. Replacing d.qpos[crank] with estimator.crank() plus an offset makes the scan PLL-referenced; PULSE_PHASE is reused.
- neuro_gates/gates.py: cases; apply_change (delay_jump, servo_weak, payload, thrust_loss); Oracle('derocked'), used for scoring only; HANDOVER_T; paired and summarize.
- wingbeat_feasibility/preliminary.py: WingbeatPhase.
- wingbeat_snn/plant.py: PHASE_OFFSET.
- The ProcessPoolExecutor worker pattern, 18 workers.

**New code, about 250 lines:**
- hooks for the hidden offset and in-flight changes;
- a wing-damage helper that scales and restores env.sim.backend.arrays[2k+1], identifying left/right through sim.fluid.elements[k][0].body;
- the RLS calibrator class;
- the R-STDP circuit class;
- a stage driver.

**Budget:** about 1,100 episode-equivalents, roughly 50 min at 24 episodes/min, plus margin. That is about 25 core-hours, run only after the current v2 job finishes.

topic.novelty_notes:
**Closest prior work (brief searches, abstracts only):**
- Adaptive SNN control of insect-scale flapping robots. Clawson, Ferrari, Fuller & Wood, CDC 2016, reportedly used reward-modulated Hebbian plasticity. Clawson, Stewart, Eliasmith & Ferrari, SSCI 2017, adapted online to wing asymmetries in simulation (compneuro.uwaterloo.ca/publications/clawson2017.html). Both are rate-coded attitude control, not timing within the wingbeat.
- Evolved plastic SNN neurocontrollers that adapt online to model changes after training on small UAVs: Qiu, Garratt, Howard & Anavatti, GECCO 2020 (arXiv 2002.09854). They compared only against a non-plastic counterpart, with no classical adaptive baseline.
- Evolvable-hardware oscillators that adapt split-cycle wing gaits to wing damage in flight: Gallagher & Oppenheimer 2011-2014 (doi 10.1007/s11390-012-1277-1), and Greenwood/Podhradsky et al. 2015. This is online search over waveform parameters on two-actuator FW-MAV models; it uses neither plasticity nor IMU-phase calibration.
- Evolved Hebbian rules that adapt to unseen morphological damage: Najarro & Risi, NeurIPS 2020 (arXiv 2007.02686).
- Three-factor rules for robot motor adaptation: arXiv 2306.01906.
- Onboard SNN control of a butterfly-like flapper: arXiv 2605.19430 (imitation learning, two servos, no plasticity).
- Biology: spike-phase control in hawkmoth flight muscles (Sponberg & Daniel 2012). Fruit flies compensate for unilateral wing damage partly by changing wing-rotation timing (Muijres et al. 2017, Interface Focus).

**What looks new.** I found no work that combines:
- online self-calibration of a single-motor timing channel within the wingbeat;
- using the IMU only, with no ground truth;
- where the actuation unit is itself the spike and plasticity acts on its phase;
- evaluated against a same-information classical calibrator, after a gate that first measures the room.

**Caveat.** Full texts were not checked, especially Clawson 2016's learning rule and the submitted Yang et al. 'Adaptive full-envelope SNN control of FW-MAVs'. Do this before claiming novelty.
risks: The room may rest only on latency. Plant changes (damage, servo, payload, thrust) may shift the map by less than 45 deg, and real latency is usually measurable from timestamps. The topic would then reduce to one-time cold-start calibration, which a short classical calibration flight solves; continual plasticity would add nothing.

The tuned RLS calibrator estimates only 2-3 parameters near-optimally and may recover most of the gap within 1-2 s. Then even a perfect SNN cannot win, and the most likely full-study outcome is 'the evolved plastic SNN matches RLS', which makes a modest paper.

Closed-loop confounding. Twitches fire while disturbances act, so measured outcomes mix disturbance, PID and twitch effects. Without random-phase exploration, both learners can settle on a biased map. Exploration costs lift that the lower motor bound (only 63 rad/s below hover) cannot cancel, so J may rise while learning.
Safety during cold start. With up to 180 deg of error, some twitches push the wrong way; without conservative gating the robot may crash while learning, which fails the 16/16 requirement.

SNN vs ANN. Three-factor STDP on a phase basis is close to REINFORCE/LMS, so a rate-coded plastic network may perform the same, as already happened in v3 and in phase estimation. The spiking-specific claim may not survive.
NEAT may again add about zero over a hand-built structure (G4). It then becomes an expensive way to tune 3-5 constants and should be replaced by CMA-ES.

Model realism. The quasi-steady blade-element model has no wing compliance and no change in passive rotation, so phase shifts caused by damage may be under- or overestimated. The hidden offset is a controller-side device that reviewers may call artificial unless it is tied to measured physical causes.

Implementation traps: blade-element areas persist across episodes unless restored; delay_jump freezes the reading for 8 ms at the switch; the PLL may need to relock after large changes; one seed and 16 cases make the thresholds coarse.
Metric artifact. Over 8-10 s episodes, 'headroom' depends on episode length. Time to calibrate and recovery time after a shift are the more meaningful measures and must be reported alongside J.
topic.lessons_addressed:
(1) **Classical comparison.** Every comparison includes the retuned PID, a robust-tuned fixed law, the oracle law and a same-budget tuned RLS calibrator, with extremum seeking added in the full study. G2b asks whether the classical adaptive baseline leaves any headroom before any SNN claim is made.

(2) **SNN, ANN, NEAT and energy.**
- No energy argument is made.
- SNN vs ANN is an explicit ablation, not an assumption.
- NEAT never tunes the map weights: plasticity does, from a uniform start, with the offset redrawn every episode.
- G4 tests whether structure matters before NEAT is used at all.

(3) **PID and fast attitude.** The PID and its 0.13 s attitude are untouched; the PID never receives a fast signal. The fast path is the already working twitch law on the notched gyro, and the fast outcome signals only drive plasticity.

(4) **Gate 4's lack of gain-adaptation room.** The adaptation target is the timing map, not the gains. S1 checks the same changes gate 4 used (delay, servo, payload, thrust) to see whether the map moves, so the result is informative either way.

(5) **Lift cost.** Twitches only go up, and J includes height, so probe twitches and misplaced twitches pay their lift cost.

(6) **v1 learned only one direction.** The fixes:
- balanced batches covering all four disturbance-sign combinations;
- two motor neurons, with optional mirror coupling;
- a pass criterion checked separately for each direction.

**H5.** The non-plastic networks there had no output feedback. Here, learning uses fast synaptic change plus the efference copy. The offsets go beyond the robust tolerance, so a fixed network cannot score well, and a frozen-plasticity ablation confirms that any adaptation comes from plasticity.

fatal_issues: A same-information classical calibrator is close to optimal by construction. I fitted the 180-deg-window phase scan in /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_authority.json: the phase-to-pitch-rate map is almost a pure sinusoid (amplitude 3.16 rad/s, peak about 152 deg, residual RMS 0.23 rad/s, so about 99% of the variance is the fundamental). Calibration is therefore a 3-parameter linear regression, and RLS is the efficient estimator for it. R-STDP over 8-16 phase cells is a higher-variance LMS/REINFORCE estimator with more parameters, so in expectation it cannot calibrate faster or better than RLS. G3 explicitly accepts J <= 1.15 x J_RLS. The only GO path is parity or inferiority, which repeats measured failure modes 1-2 (v3, P1).

G2b cannot discriminate. It counts the unavoidable cost of acquiring information as 'headroom', because the oracle law knows the offset. Learning only starts at HANDOVER_T = 1.5 s and needs about 2 s of twitches, so even an optimal learner leaves at least 25% of the fixed-to-oracle gap unrecovered over 2-8 s. G2b therefore passes even when RLS is optimal, and can produce a misleading GO.

Room most likely rests only on latency or on the artificial offset; the scenarios that would earn the 'strong' label are physically unlikely to qualify. On this single-motor robot, thrust loss, payload and wing damage push the hover motor command toward HIGH, so they mainly shrink the one-sided twitch amplitude rather than move its phase. Thrust loss takes it from 629 to about 248 rad/s; I estimate payload at about -33% and one-wing area -30% at about -40%. The outer-30%-span loss may use up the roughly 1.43x lift headroom entirely, so the robot may not hover at all. In adapt.json, height RMSE is already 26 cm (thrust loss) and 19 cm (payload) with the base PID. With crank-prescribed stroke and quasi-steady blade elements, damage scales force magnitude, not timing. Only latency moves the map, and by a predictable 360*f*dtau (72 deg for +8 ms), which can be measured from timestamps on hardware: this is the topic's own 'weak' case. The U(0,360 deg) hidden offset creates room through the choice of prior; a constant offset is fixed by a one-off calibration scan before flight.

The only scenario likely to pass G1 (delay_jump, delay_steps 1->5) is confounded by the base PID. In the /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/neuro_gates/adapt.json tuning grid, the 'untouched' retuned PID (kp x1.5, kd x1) has 15.8 deg post-change tilt RMS, against 8.6 deg without the jump (kd x1.2: 22.7 deg). The condition-optimal PID crashed 2/16 on evaluation. J, crashes and the twitch-response signal will be dominated by the nearly unstable two-body loop (failure mode 3), and a classical PID gain switch is the obvious remedy. The switch also freezes the reading for 4 ticks: reading_queue grows from 2 to 6 entries with no popleft (topology_hover/environment.py:124), which is trivially detectable.

NEAT is not needed as specified. The structural choices (modulator signal, readout delay, trace tau, mirrored or independent maps, gating, phase code) form a small categorical space, which the gate's own 48-point grid enumerates. G4 ('best structure beats the naive one') does not show that topology evolution is needed. DelayGenome (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms/wingbeat_snn/evolve.py) has no plastic or modulatory genes, so the full study needs a new genome type. Project history predicts about zero gain: v3 topology effect ~0, NEAT from scratch failed in P1, NEAT phase SNN 9.3 deg vs 2.4 deg for the gradient SNN.

This is essentially H5 run again. /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/wingbeat_snn_h5/H5_report.md asked 'unknown actuator phase lag: can learning adapt?' and found the networks no better than a robust-tuned fixed law (tolerant to about +-30-45 deg). Plasticity plus an efference copy addresses H5's suspected cause, but the comparison target is now a tuned RLS calibrator, which is stronger than H5's robust law. The expected outcome is again parity at best, and the user's stated aim (SNN and NEAT that add something) is not served.
fixes: Run S1a alone first (about 120 episode-equivalents, about 5 min) and gate everything else on it. Use real 3-tick twitches, not 180-deg bursts. Use stress-like cases with delay_steps=1: PHASE_OFFSET 84.14 deg was calibrated on nominal cases with delay 0, so stress cases already sit about 18 deg off. For each change, report both dpsi* and the remaining twitch headroom (HIGH minus the hover command). Stop if no plant change gives |dpsi*| >= 45-60 deg. Treat latency as a known shift and add psi += 2*pi*f*dtau as a classical reference.

Replace G2b with an information-matched test: compare the SNN with the tuned RLS on time to 45 deg and on recovery time after a shift. For any SNN claim, require the SNN to beat RLS by >= 2 paired SEM; otherwise agree in advance with the user that the claim is parity only.

Replace the frozen-plasticity ablation. Uniform frozen weights just give random-phase twitches, which is a straw man. Use instead: the fixed nominal law, a robust fixed law with a wider window, RLS, and a rate-coded (non-spiking) plastic network with the same rule. Move the SNN-vs-ANN ablation into the gate.
Latency scenario: run it with a PID that stays stable at 10 ms delay (gate-4 kp x1, kd x0.85, or a robust choice), or report it separately. Mask the 8 ms frozen-reading artifact at the switch.

Replace the U(0,360 deg) hidden offset with a justified prior, for example +-45-90 deg from realistic IMU filter, latency and driver-lag uncertainty. Add a classical pre-flight calibration as a baseline: a 1-2 s open-loop twitch-phase scan after takeoff.

Drop NEAT from the gate. Keep NEAT only if NEAT-found structures beat the best grid structure on held-out cases. Budget the new plastic/modulatory genome code explicitly; the '~250 lines' covers only the hand-built gate.

Check the information budget before writing learners. v1 logs show about 2 natural twitches/s (219 onsets over 16 episodes). Stress pulses come at t%2 in [0.6, 0.8) with a fixed sign per episode, so only one pulse (2.6-2.8 s) falls between the 1.5 s handover and the 4 s checkpoint. Estimate the single-twitch dq SNR on the low-passed notched gyro, in calm and disturbed periods; I estimate roughly 0.4 rad/s per twitch from the burst scan. Size the probe rate and its height cost from that, and consider episodes of 16 s or more for calibration claims.

Wing-damage helper: scale and restore both env.sim.backend.arrays[2k+1] and the Wing.rotational_area in env.sim.backend.wings[k], which is stored by value, not through a pointer. Restoring is necessary because SensorBackend persists across resets. Identify wings by fluid.elements[k][1] (body id) or [0].body (name). Check hover feasibility first: the outer-30%-span loss likely exceeds the motor headroom.

Define the oracle onset phase for a 3-tick twitch from its own scan: the burst-scan fit peaks near 152 deg, PULSE_PHASE uses 135 deg, and v1 need-down spikes centred at 338 deg. Measure 'time to 45 deg' from the 1.5 s handover.
critiques.reasoning:
Interface and implementability: the topic stays inside the v3 interface. It uses a controller-side offset; twitches are 3 ticks at HIGH through the unchanged clip, smoothing and motor path; changes go through the existing apply_change; damage is a scenario. The gate can be built from existing code: pilot.Steer/run, timing.run/measure, gates.apply_change/Oracle and WingbeatPhase. I verified that native_step.cpp, which sensor_step.cpp includes, reads wing.areas[i] through a pointer on every substep. BladeElement sets MuJoCo's option density to 0, so scaling the blade-element areas is the complete aerodynamic damage. Servo parameters are restored on reset by pid_airborne/core.py, but the area arrays are not. The budget is about 1,100-1,300 episode-equivalents, roughly 1 h on 18 workers, which is affordable.

The weakness is scientific, not mechanical:
1. The calibration target is about 99% a single sinusoid. A tuned RLS calibrator is close to the efficient estimator for it, so the plastic SNN can at best match RLS, and G3 is written to accept that.
2. G2b passes trivially because of the learning transient. It cannot tell 'RLS leaves room' apart from 'information acquisition costs something'.
3. On this one-motor robot, plant faults mostly consume twitch headroom (the hover command rises toward HIGH) rather than shift the phase. Only latency shifts it, by a known amount.
4. The latency jump drives the topic's own base PID close to instability: 15.8 deg vs 8.6 deg tilt.
5. NEAT's structural space can be enumerated by the gate's own grid.
6. H5 already returned a negative result on almost the same question.

The topic is honest and its gate is cheap, so it is not formally refuted; it could yield a modest 'SNN matches RLS' result. But it very likely repeats measured failure modes 1, 2 and 4, plus H5, and would end with NEAT dropped. Hence weak, 3/10.

Novelty check: a brief web search confirmed close prior work. Clawson et al., CDC 2016, used reward-modulated Hebbian SNN control in flight on RoboBee. The Portland State group (Gallagher, Greenwood et al.) learned split-cycle gaits online after wing damage.

Sources: https://compneuro.uwaterloo.ca/publications/clawson2017.html ; https://unpaywall.org/10.1109%2FCDC.2016.7798778 ; https://pdxscholar.library.pdx.edu/open_access_etds/3308 ; https://cps-vo.org/sites/cps-vo.org/files/cpsvo_file_nodes/Methodologies_for_Engineering_with_Plug-and-Learn_Components-_Synthesis_and_Analysis_Across_Abstraction_Layers.pdf

fatal_issues: The thing to be learned is a 2- or 3-parameter sinusoid, so a correctly specified classical estimator is near-optimal and the SNN can at best tie. The project's own authority scan (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_authority.json) gives the pitch-rate effect at 8 onset phases. For the 180 deg window it is -2.45, -1.01, +1.53, +3.32, +2.60, +1.20, -1.39, -3.13 rad/s. A single first harmonic plus offset fits this with about 99% variance explained (amplitude 3.16, peak about 152 deg, residual RMS 0.19). The 90 deg window is the same (2.84, about 146 deg, 0.21). RLS on [cos, sin, 1] is therefore the right-model estimator. A plastic net over 8-16 phase bins has more parameters than the problem needs, so it cannot calibrate faster. The proposal itself predicts 'matches RLS', and G3 passes at J <= 1.15 x J_RLS. A GO would therefore still contain no SNN advantage.

The SNN is nominal. Its phase cells are one-hot bins of the classical PLL phase, and eligibility = twitch x phase activity, so R-STDP reduces to w[bin] += eta*(outcome - baseline). That is a tabular LMS/REINFORCE contextual bandit. Each claimed SNN property has a one-line classical equivalent: stochastic threshold = dither, refractoriness = minimum gap between twitches, delays and traces = one lag parameter. The proposal concedes that a rate-coded rule may be equivalent. Project history points the same way: SNN = ANN in v3, and on the related phase-estimation task GRU 0.8 deg vs gradient SNN 2.4 deg vs NEAT SNN 9.3 deg (docs/wingbeat_paper/HANDOFF.md). Reviewers will say a GRU, an RL^2-style memory network or an RLS calibrator does the same job.

NEAT is incidental by construction. The 'credit-assignment structure' amounts to about 5 coarse choices. The gate's own S3 grid already enumerates them (2 x 2 x 2 structures x 6 rule constants = 48), and each has a first-principles answer. The modulator should be the notched pitch rate. The readout window comes from the measured twitch impulse response. Mirrored maps are exact, because down = up + 180 deg for a first harmonic. G4 therefore cannot justify NEAT: if structure matters, the grid has already found it. Prior evidence in this project agrees: topology effect about 0, NEAT poor at fine weight tuning, and H5 showed no adaptation (artifacts/wingbeat_snn_h5/H5_report.md). Gradient meta-learned three-factor rules (Schmidgall & Hays 2023, arXiv 2306.01906 and Meta-SpikePropamine) are the obvious alternative reviewers will demand.

The only novelty is the combination, and it is partly pre-empted (abstracts only checked). Method level: Clawson, Ferrari, Fuller & Wood (CDC 2016) adapt a LIF SNN in flight on RoboBee by reward-modulated Hebbian plasticity. Clawson et al. (SSCI 2017) adapt an SNN to unknown parameter variations and wing asymmetry. Yang (Cornell PhD 2023) adapts an SNN online by policy gradient to parameter variation and actuator failure. Qiu et al. (GECCO 2020) evolve plastic SNNs for UAVs. Soltoggio et al. 2008 and Risi & Stanley evolve neuromodulated plastic topologies. Task level: Gallagher & Oppenheimer (2011-2016) adapt split-cycle wingbeat waveforms to wing damage in flight. Fleming et al. (PLoS Comput Biol 2023) track a drifting optimal stimulation phase online for phase-locked pulses; a 2024 TMS paper (Humaidan, Ziemann, Kirchhoff) adds a sinusoid prior, which is exactly the proposed RLS baseline. Swashplateless rotors and monocopters already use one-motor, phase-timed actuation with a calibrated phase lead.

The need for adaptation is probably artificial. The U(0, 360 deg) hidden offset is a device inside the controller. In this rigid-wing, quasi-steady blade-element model the wingbeat (25 Hz) is far above the 4-5 Hz two-body mode, so the plant changes mostly scale amplitude rather than shift phase. thrust_loss is motor_gain x 0.9 (amplitude), area loss scales force, and payload and servo act in the mass-dominated regime. That leaves the 2 -> 10 ms delay jump, about 72 deg, which the proposal itself labels 'weak'; real latency is fixed and timestamped. A physical one-time offset is solved by a 1-2 s PLL-referenced phase sweep (S1a itself), so continual plasticity has nothing to do.

There is no standalone publishable claim if the classical baseline matches. What remains is a tie on a toy estimation problem with 2-3 parameters, plus a classical encoder-free calibrator. That calibrator overlaps the wingbeat paper's C1/C2 (IMU-only phase-locked split-cycle, timing tolerance) and is a section of that paper, not a new SNN+NEAT paper. H5 already reported 'no adaptation' on the same unknown-phase question, and robust tuning matched the networks.
fixes: Remove the SNN-advantage and NEAT claims from this topic. If anything is kept, keep only S1 (does the map really shift?) and S2 (the IMU-only RLS calibrator) as a robustness section of the existing wingbeat paper. Skip S3.

Before running any learner, measure how observable a single twitch is on the IMU: the SNR of the notched pitch-rate response to one 6 ms twitch during stress flight. Also add the classical baselines that are likely to dominate: a 1-2 s PLL-referenced phase sweep at takeoff for cold start, IV-RLS or Bayesian optimisation with a sinusoid prior, and extremum seeking.
Replace the U(0, 360 deg) offset with the distribution of shifts that S1 actually measures from physical causes. If only the delay jump qualifies, stop the topic.

If any SNN claim survives, tighten the pass rules. G3 should require the SNN to beat the tuned RLS/BO/ES baseline by at least 2 paired SEM on time to calibrate or on J; the current rule allows the SNN to be 15% worse. Add same-budget ablations: a GRU meta-trained across offsets with the efference copy as input, and a rate-coded plastic network. G4 should compare NEAT against the S3 grid or CMA-ES over the same structural options, not against the naive structure.

For a replacement topic where SNN/NEAT could be central, choose a policy that a few Fourier coefficients cannot describe. Example: twitch sequences timed jointly to the wingbeat and to the lightly damped 4-5 Hz two-body mode, which needs coincidence detection across two rhythms, a natural job for evolved delays. First check with an oracle sweep that such sequences beat the single-twitch law. Pre-register a 2-D Fourier RLS and an MPC baseline before evolving anything.

Read the full texts of Clawson 2016 and 2017, Yang 2023, Gallagher & Oppenheimer 2012-2016, Schmidgall & Hays 2023 and Fleming 2023 before making any novelty claim. Position the work as an application of known evolved or three-factor plasticity methods. Drop the insect-learning analogy: as far as I know, fly steering-muscle phase is set by haltere and wing mechanosensory feedback, not learned in flight.
critiques.reasoning:
Verdict through the novelty and centrality lens: refuted as an SNN+NEAT paper. No simulations were run; the evidence comes from repo artifacts and abstract-level web searches.

Centrality, SNN: The authority scan that motivates the topic shows the phase map is about 99% a pure first harmonic for both 90 and 180 deg windows (my fit to /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_authority.json). Calibrating it therefore means estimating 2-3 numbers, the up phase plus amplitude and offset, with down = up + 180 deg. A correctly specified RLS or BO with a sinusoid prior is the efficient estimator, so a spiking learner with 8-16 bins can only tie or lose on time to calibrate.

Caveat: those are oracle, true-crank measurements from 0.1 s bursts, not IMU responses to single twitches. However, the actuator path (8.2 ms smoothing plus the motor loop) low-passes a 6 ms twitch, so a low-order map is still expected.

With PLL one-hot phase cells, the proposed R-STDP is algebraically a tabular LMS/REINFORCE bandit. Exploration noise, refractoriness and delays all have trivial classical counterparts. The proposal itself expects 'matches RLS', concedes that a rate-coded rule may be equivalent, and sets G3 so that an SNN up to 15% worse than RLS still passes. A GRU or meta-RL network with the efference copy could do the same job; in this project GRUs already beat SNNs on phase estimation by about 3x.

Centrality, NEAT: The 'structure' NEAT is meant to find is a handful of choices that the gate's own 48-point S3 grid enumerates, and each has a first-principles answer. G4 cannot distinguish NEAT from grid search or CMA-ES. Project history (topology effect about 0, NEAT SNN phase error 9.3 deg, H5 with no adaptation) makes a NEAT-central result unlikely. Gradient meta-learned three-factor rules (Schmidgall & Hays 2023) are the standard alternative.

Novelty: The exact combination (single-motor flapper, IMU-only PLL, twitch-as-spike, R-STDP on phase, NEAT-evolved credit structure) appears unpublished, but every ingredient is established.
- SNNs with reward-modulated Hebbian plasticity already adapt in flight on RoboBee (Clawson 2016), and adaptive SNNs have been applied to wing asymmetry (Clawson 2017) and to actuator failures with online policy gradient (Yang 2023).
- Evolved plastic SNNs already exist for UAVs (Qiu 2020), and evolved neuromodulated topologies date to Soltoggio 2008.
- In-flight adaptation of within-wingbeat timing after wing damage was done by Gallagher & Oppenheimer.
- Online tracking of the best phase for phase-locked pulses has classical/ML solutions: Fleming 2023 (time-varying Bayesian optimisation) and a 2024 TMS phase-optimisation paper with a sinusoid prior.

Reviewers will see this as combination novelty on a toy estimation problem.

Room and motivation: The hidden U(0, 360 deg) offset is synthetic. In this rigid-wing quasi-steady model the plant changes mostly scale amplitude rather than shift phase (thrust_loss = motor_gain x 0.9; area scaling scales force; payload and servo act in the mass-dominated regime at 25 Hz). The likely surviving trigger is the delay jump (8 ms, about 72 deg), which the proposal itself calls 'weak'. A physical one-time offset is fixed by a short calibration sweep.

Publishable claim if the classical baseline matches: only a tie in a 2-3 parameter estimation, or a classical calibrator that belongs inside the existing wingbeat paper (its C1/C2). H5 (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/wingbeat_snn_h5/H5_report.md) already answered the unknown-phase question negatively for NEAT networks.

The score of 2 rather than 0 reflects that the gate is cheap and honestly designed, and that S1/S2 could give a useful classical robustness section. Neither rescues SNN/NEAT centrality.

topic.title: Lift-neutral spike steering: one motor pulse train carrying lift in its rate and pitch torque in its phase
topic.one_line: Today the controller adds a full-range pulse whenever pitch needs correcting, and every pulse costs height. Instead, run one pulse per wingbeat drawn from a shared lift budget and steer by moving each pulse to a different wingbeat phase. The pulse scheduler is a NEAT-evolved delay-LIF circuit (spike = pulse, rate = lift, phase-of-firing = torque). The mechanism is first gated in a classical version, then the SNN is compared with a same-information classical multiplexer tuned with the same episode budget.
topic.problem:
Inside the original interface, the only control authority beyond the PID is the wingbeat-timed full-range motor pulse (4.1x the gimbal residual in pitch). Every pulse adds lift, and the hover command sits only about 63 rad/s above LOW, so pitch steering is paid for in height.

The existing data show that this trade-off, not sensing, limits the timing channel:
- On the 8-case law grid (timing_law_grid.json), each 1% of pulse duty buys about 2-3 deg of pitch RMS and costs about 1-2 cm of height RMSE. The PID alone gets 7.1 deg / 7.5 cm; the aggressive laws get 1.9-2.4 deg / 13.2-13.5 cm.
- Giving the law perfect information (true de-rocked state and true crank phase) does not improve J: the best fully-flown oracle law scores 6.25 against 5.82 for the IMU-only law on the same cases.
- In the v1 test, the classical law's J is 6.29, and 3.26 of that is the height term.

If steering were lift-neutral at the pitch the aggressive laws reach, J would fall to about 4.2-4.7 (roughly 20-30% lower), and the single motor would become a two-axis actuator (pitch plus height).

Seen as an event-based problem, this is a coding question:
- The robot can only emit sparse full-range pulses. Each pulse has two free variables: whether it fires, and at which wingbeat phase.
- The plant reads these two variables separately. Lift follows pulse count: +0.054 to +0.092 m/s per pi/2 burst, at all 8 phases tested. Pitch follows phase: +2.7 rad/s at 135 deg, -2.5 rad/s at 315 deg, and about zero near 50-65 deg.
- Lowering the continuous motor command by Delta and replacing that lift with one pulse per wingbeat at the neutral phase creates the missing downward lift authority. A steering correction then moves a pulse that would have fired anyway, instead of adding one.
topic.why_snn:
On this interface the useful motor command is effectively binary (baseline or full-range pulse). The controller therefore has to emit a sparse event train, and the plant reads two things from it: pulse count gives lift, pulse phase gives pitch torque. A spike train is exactly that object: spike = pulse, rate = lift, phase-of-firing = torque. Fly steering motor neurons use the same code: b1 fires once per wingbeat, and mechanosensory input advances its firing phase.

Spiking dynamics provide the needed pieces natively:
- A neuron driven by a phase-locked input plus a demand current crosses threshold at a phase that moves with the demand. That is phase-of-firing.
- Subtractive reset and refractoriness allow at most one pulse per window and carry the residual forward, like sigma-delta modulation.
- Inhibition from steering spikes onto the lift pathway, through the shared budget, makes a steering spike use up a lift spike. This is corollary discharge.

A rate-coded ANN, or the current threshold law (which has a deadband and fires in every window while |u| is above threshold), would need an external quantizer, accumulator and scheduler added on.

The SNN claim is about representation, not energy. The gate tests it by ablating each mechanism in the evolved network: all delays set to zero, budget input removed, and reset-to-zero instead of subtractive reset.
topic.interface_check:
The controller uses ResearchEnv(mode='direct') exactly as spike_steer/pilot.py does.

Commands, every 2 ms:
- Gimbal alpha/beta come from the retuned PID (kp x1.5), unchanged.
- Motor = max(LOW, PID motor demand - Delta), except during a pulse, when it is HIGH (3807.5 rad/s) for 2-3 ticks.
- Everything then goes through the unchanged path: clip to [LOW, HIGH], 8.2 ms first-order smoothing, servo (1.045 N.m/rad, 0.02 N.m limit) and the motor speed loop (4.2 V, 6 A).
- Delta ramps in after the 1.5 s handover, so takeoff is identical to v3.

Controller inputs come only from the 11-D reading at 500 Hz, with each case's delay_steps:
- lagged AHRS pitch, reading[1];
- pitch gyro, reading[4], through the existing WingbeatPhase PLL and notch;
- height error and vertical speed, reading[9:11], used only through the PID's motor demand that feeds the budget.

The PLL gyro-to-crank offset is recalibrated once with the pulse train on, in the same way as the one-time bench calibration in P0-E4.

Truth (de-rocked pitch, crank angle) is used only for metrics and spike-phase analysis (gates.Oracle). No sensor, actuator, update rate or limit is changed. Scenarios are the v3 stress cases: direction-balanced for training, the v2 test split for testing.
topic.classical_baseline:
All baselines get the same inputs (the 11-D reading through the same PLL and notch, and the PID's motor demand), the same shared lift-budget accumulator, and the same tuning budget.

(a) Tuned IMU pulse law: v2's 108-point grid over k_theta, k_q, threshold and window.

(b) Law plus efference-copy lift payback: every pulse tick adds (HIGH - c) to a lift debt, which is repaid by lowering the continuous motor command toward LOW. This is the obvious classical fix for the height cost, and it can only repay at about 63 rad/s.

(c) Classical multiplexer:
- continuous command c = max(LOW, m_PID - Delta);
- a first-order sigma-delta accumulator converts (m_PID - c) into at most one 2-3-tick pulse per wingbeat, scheduled at a neutral phase psi0 (about 50-65 deg);
- when |u| = |k_theta*theta + k_q*q| exceeds a threshold, the pulse is moved to 135 or 315 deg (or shifted by k_psi*u, saturated at +-90 deg);
- extra steering pulses borrow from the accumulator, so lift stays neutral over a few wingbeats.

Tuning:
- G0: a 24-point grid for (c) and 4 settings for (b).
- G1: random search or CMA over the 7 parameters of (c) (Delta, psi0, width, threshold, k_theta, k_q, k_psi), using exactly the NEAT episode budget (1920 six-second episodes).

Recommended upgrade for the full study: a shared 4-harmonic notch for all arms (see risks).

gate.what:
G0, classical mechanism (about 0.2 h):
- Recalibrate the PLL offset with the pulse train on (3 short flights; true crank used only for this one-time calibration).
- On 8 direction-balanced v3-stress tuning cases (6 s each), grid the classical multiplexer: Delta in {35, 60} rad/s x psi0 in {40, 55, 70} deg x steering threshold in {0.4, 0.6} x pulse width in {2, 3} ticks = 24 settings. Also run the law plus lift payback (4 settings). v2's tuned law is the reference.
- Test the best setting of each family on the 16-case v2 test split (8 s each).

G1, spiking scheduler (about 2.1 h), only if G0 passes:
- NEAT with delay genes and speciation: population 32, 15 generations, 4 balanced cases per generation.
- Seed: a hand-wired circuit equal to the classical multiplexer. Its 13 inputs are 8 PLL phase cells, rectified pitch and rate demand (4), and the budget level (1). Coincidence neurons at psi0, 135 and 315 deg are gated by the budget and the pitch demand, with inhibition between the steering and lift pathways.
- The classical multiplexer is random-searched or CMA-tuned on the same 1920 episodes.
- Shared 16-case test of: tuned law, law plus payback, classical multiplexer, evolved SNN, and three post-hoc ablations of the evolved SNN (delays set to 0, budget input removed, reset-to-zero).

Reused:
- spike_steer/pilot.py: run loop, Steer (WingbeatPhase PLL, 8 phase cells, notch), SpikingGraph, balanced_cases/cases, summarize, make_config + neat_template.ini, initialize/export (extended to 13 inputs and a seeded topology), the train/tune_law/test drivers, onset logging.
- wingbeat_snn/evolve.py: DelayGenome (delay genes, connection rules).
- wingbeat_snn/networks.py: Graph (delay LIF, 1 ms substeps).

topic.novelty_notes:
Brief searches on 2026-10-13 found the following related work:
- SNN control of flapping robots: Clawson et al. 2016/2017 (RoboBee, rate-coded adaptive SNN); El Filali et al., arXiv 2605.19430 (2026), a butterfly flapping-wing robot using SNN state estimation plus CPG modulation, trained by imitation and compared only with an ANN on latency and power.
- Neuromorphic quadrotor attitude estimation and control: Stroobants, de Croon et al., 2022-2025.
- NEAT with synaptic delays: tau-NEAT, Caamano et al. 2016. The method itself is not new.
- Multiplexing forces and moments in the wingbeat waveform: split-cycle constant-period frequency modulation (Doman/Oppenheimer, AFRL). It uses two actuators, one per wing: collective period for lift, split-cycle for moments. The multiplexing principle is therefore known.
- Fly steering motor neuron b1: its firing phase is set by convergent wing and haltere mechanosensory input, and haltere input advances the phase during reflexes (Fayyazuddin & Dickinson 1996, 1999). The halteres are described as an adjustable clock.

I found no work where a single one-sided motor's pulse train multiplexes lift (rate) and pitch (phase) under an explicit event budget. I also found none where an evolved or spiking controller uses within-wingbeat spike timing as the actuation variable on a flapping robot. The novelty rests on the budgeted rate/phase event code inside a fixed 2 ms, one-sided command interface, and on its spiking implementation with evolved delays.

Other topics within this angle that I considered and rejected, with the data behind each:
- Latency reflex. Perfect sensing does not improve J (oracle 6.25 vs IMU 5.82). The accelerometer is useless for fast onset detection: in recorded wingbeat-line flights, acc_x carries about 32 m/s^2 of wingbeat content, and 3.4 m/s^2 remains after removing 4 harmonics, against a v3 force step of about 0.4-0.75 m/s^2. Onset detection on the gyro is a classical notch-plus-CUSUM problem.
- PLL-free event clock, or robustness to IMU dropouts. In the v1 test, 97% of the law's pulse onsets fell within +-67.5 deg of the needed phase (2.9% at the opposite phase), so there is no timing headroom. Lock time matters only at takeoff. Dropouts would be a sensor change and would need the user's approval.
- Asynchronous sensing. The interface is synchronous at 500 Hz.

No simulations were run for this proposal: I only read existing JSON files and ran a numpy pass of a few seconds over one recorded file.
risks: Most likely outcome: the classical multiplexer captures the gain and the SNN ties (lessons 1-2). My priors: P(G0 passes) is about 0.35; P(SNN <= 1.00x classical, given G0) about 0.35; P(SNN <= 0.95x, given G0) about 0.1-0.15. So P(SNN-centred paper) is about 5%, while P(a useful classical result for the project) is about 0.35.

This is a new operating point: one pulse per wingbeat (about 10-15% duty), against at most 3% tested so far. Its effects on rocking amplitude, the PLL offset, AHRS ripple reaching the PID, and motor current near the 6 A limit are unknown. G0 is designed to expose these in about 10 minutes.

Fore-aft drift is invisible to J. In timing_authority.json, pulse bursts at every phase produced a backward velocity change (pi windows: -0.04 to -0.20 m/s per 0.1 s, mean -0.12). A steady pulse train may therefore add a constant backward force. The gate guards this with the xy offset, and the fix may need a calibrated gimbal-trim feedforward.

Lift per pulse varies by about +-25% with phase (pi/2 bursts: +0.054 to +0.092 m/s), so moving a pulse is only approximately lift-neutral. The PID height integral (about +-40 rad/s) has to absorb the rest.

Sigma-delta can produce irregular pulse patterns, which put sub-harmonic forcing (for example 12.5 Hz) into the IMU that the 2-harmonic notch does not remove. Mitigation: keep exactly one pulse per wingbeat and put the remainder in pulse width or the continuous command.

With the continuous command near LOW, fast downward height corrections rely on skipping pulses, which is quantized to one decision per wingbeat. For some Delta values this may make height control worse.
NEAT may not improve on the hand-wired seed within 15 generations. In that case the gate effectively compares the seed with a tuned classical multiplexer.

The classical baselines can get stronger. In my offline check on recorded flights (wingbeat-line data, true crank, 0.2 s windows), the pitch-gyro residual is 0.86 rad/s after removing 2 wingbeat harmonics and 0.19 rad/s after removing 4. v2's law and SNN both use the 2-harmonic notch. A 4-harmonic notch may cut ripple-triggered pulses in every arm and shrink this topic's headroom, so it should be in any final comparison.
The multiplexing principle itself is known (split-cycle constant-period frequency modulation), so novelty depends on the single-motor, one-sided, budgeted event code and its spiking implementation.

The benefit here comes from the event code, not from a sensing-side neuromorphic property. If the orchestrator needs latency, noise or dropout benefits specifically, none of those variants survived my data checks (see novelty notes).
topic.lessons_addressed:
1. Every claim is made against same-information classical controllers: the tuned IMU pulse law, the law plus lift payback on the continuous command, and a classical multiplexer tuned with exactly the NEAT episode budget. G0 is purely classical, so the topic dies early if the mechanism cannot beat them.

2. There is no energy argument. The SNN claims are about representation and are tested by ablating delays, the budget pathway and subtractive reset. NEAT starts from a hand-wired seed and only has to change wiring, delays and coarse weights; it never has to regress a continuous phase, which is where it stalled at about 10 deg. The SNN-vs-ANN and topology-vs-weights arms come later, and only if G1 passes.

3. The gimbal and attitude loop stays the retuned PID with its 0.13 s attitude. Nothing faster is fed to it.

4. No online adaptation is claimed; all controllers are fixed.

5. The topic builds on the timing channel and attacks its measured weakness, the lift cost of steering (about 1-2 cm of height RMSE per 1% of duty). Oracle sensing does not move that trade-off, so this is not a sensing problem.

6. Both directions are wired into the seed, and cases are direction-balanced. Every wingbeat carries a pulse, so steering means moving a pulse rather than a rare event. The onset-phase test requires at least 20 onsets per direction.

fatal_issues: The premise is contradicted by a per-case reading of the existing data. The pulse law's height cost is not a per-pulse lift cost. It sits in the stress cases with high motor gain, where the hover command is only about 16-35 rad/s above LOW. (ControlEnv multiplies the clipped command by motor_gain = 1 + U(+-1.5%), so hover is about 3178/g and the headroom ranges from 16 to 111 rad/s.) In the v1 test (artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json), 91% of law_strong's +2.90 cm mean height excess comes from 4 of 16 cases with g = 1.0108-1.0148 (+4.6, +6.5, +11.3, +19.8 cm). The 10 cases with g <= 1.005 average +0.12 cm at the same duty (0.9-1.1%), and corr(g, height excess) = 0.68. On the 8 tuning cases (timing_law_grid.json, timing_imu_law.json), the single g = 1.0137 case carries +30.4 cm for the oracle law and +11.7 cm for the IMU law, while every case with g <= 0.9994 stays within +-0.75 cm for every law. 'About 1-2 cm per 1% duty' is the average of a bimodal distribution. Where the cost exists, the multiplexer's c = max(LOW, m - Delta) is pinned at LOW and there is almost no base lift to reallocate. Where headroom exists, there is no height cost to recover. The ideal ceiling (law pitch plus PID height) is J = 5.42, 13.8% below 6.29, but nearly all of that gap sits in cases that no allocation can neutralise, so the G0 bar (at least 10% below min(law, payback)) is essentially unreachable.

Multiplexing creates no downward authority. For any allocation, the mean motor command is at least LOW + steering duty x (HIGH - LOW). The multiplexer's lift-neutral steering capacity is Delta_eff / pulse_worth, with Delta_eff <= m - LOW. That is equal to the capacity of law + efference-copy payback (b), and smaller for Delta = 35. To first order the multiplexer is baseline (b) plus a persistent pulse train, which brings only side effects. The proposal's statement that it 'creates the missing downward lift authority' is false.

The proposed operating point has already been tested and fails. One 2-3-tick pulse per wingbeat means 10-15% duty, which exceeds the lift-neutral duty ceiling (m - LOW)/(HIGH - LOW): about 9% at nominal gain, about 2.3% at g = 1.015, about 16% at g = 0.985. timing_closed_loop.json already contains laws at 10-22.6% duty: 23 of 24 runs ended in height_escape, and the survivor had 39.7 cm height RMSE. This contradicts the claim that at most 3% duty has been tested. A real sigma-delta will therefore fire irregular trains below one pulse per wingbeat (0.2-0.9 pulses per wingbeat depending on headroom). That puts sub-harmonic forcing in the 2-8 Hz band around the lightly damped 4-5 Hz two-body mode, the fragility behind lesson 3.

SNN and NEAT are unnecessary by construction. G0 is purely classical, and the G1 seed is functionally the classical multiplexer. The lift budget enters the network as a classical accumulator input. Graph has one global tau_m (5 ms in pilot SPEC), so the membrane residual decays by about e^-8 per wingbeat, and 'subtractive reset = sigma-delta' cannot carry lift debt across wingbeats. The 'budget input removed' ablation would pass trivially, because it deletes the classical signal. 'J_snn <= 1.00 x multiplexer' passes about half the time under a pure tie. NEAT against a CMA-tuned 7-parameter law on 480 noisy 4-case evaluations repeats lessons 1-2, and the proposer's own estimate of P(SNN-centred result) is about 5%.

The obvious same-information classical fix for the real failure mode is missing, and G0 is biased. Pulse aggressiveness can be gated or scaled by the PID's own motor headroom (m_PID - LOW), or pulses suppressed while the PID is pushing toward LOW. That is 1-2 parameters and attacks exactly the cases that carry the cost. Meanwhile G0 gives the multiplexer 24 settings plus a deadband-free phase term (k_psi), but gives law + payback only 4 settings and no such term. A multiplexer 'win' would therefore confound the budget, proportional steering and the multiplexing mechanism.
fixes: Reframe the problem as headroom-limited steering before building anything. Report J stratified by motor gain (g > 1.008 versus g <= 1.008); the numbers above came from a few-second numpy pass over the existing JSONs, with no new simulation. Then run the trivial classical baseline first: a headroom-gated pulse law (threshold or width scaled by max(0, m_PID - LOW)/63, or pulses vetoed when m_PID - LOW < X), on a 12-24-point grid over 8 balanced tuning cases (about 0.1 h). Any lift-allocation scheme has to beat it.

If a multiplexer is still tested: drop 'one pulse per wingbeat' and cap total pulse duty per case at (m_PID - LOW)/(HIGH - LOW). Give law + payback the same grid size and the same deadband-free phase term. Add the headroom-gated law as baseline (d). Require the win to hold in both gain strata, not only in the mean.

Measure the neutral phase and the PLL jitter before running the grid. The zero crossing is the steepest point of the phase-response curve (about 0.043 rad/s per degree per 0.1 s pi/2 train; zero near 52 deg for pi/2 windows, near 63 deg for pi windows, unknown for 2-3-tick pulses). In v1 the IMU law's onsets fell about 28 deg after the intended centre, with about 11 deg spread. Calibrate the PLL offset for each pulse configuration, and check whether the offset drifts with case headroom (base rate); if it does, a single calibration is not valid and per-case truth calibration would break the interface.

Guard against fore-aft drift explicitly. Averaged over the 8 phases, a pi/2 burst gives about -0.052 m/s of forward velocity per 0.1 s, so a persistent pulse train implies a steady backward force with no xy loop to correct it. pilot.run() does not return xy_offset_m (the metric exists in HoverEnv.metrics), so add it, and abort if the xy offset exceeds 2x the law's.

Do not proceed to G1 on this topic. If an SNN arm is ever run: exclude the classical budget input from the ablation criterion; back any accumulator claim with per-neuron long time constants (a new class); and require paired statistics for 'continue' (for example at least 11/16 wins plus a bootstrap CI), not a mean ratio of 1.00 or below.

For the next topic search, look for a computation the same-information classical law cannot express structurally, not one it merely has not been tuned for. Across this project, the only SNN-positive result so far is the surrogate-gradient phase estimator; NEAT has not beaten a same-budget classical baseline in P1, H5, Step 2 or spike_steer v1.
critiques.reasoning:
Verdict: the topic is refuted on feasibility. The interface and compute parts hold up. The mechanism's premise is contradicted by the project's own data, the mechanism is first-order equivalent to a trivial classical baseline, and the SNN arm cannot add anything a classical law with the same information lacks.

What holds:
- Interface: the topic stays inside the original interface. It runs ResearchEnv in direct mode, clips commands to [LOW, HIGH], and keeps the 8.2 ms smoothing, the servo and the motor loop unchanged. Truth is used only for metrics and for a one-time PLL offset calibration, which follows the P0-E4 precedent.
- Compute: G0 is about 280 episodes (about 12 min); G1 is about 4000 episodes (about 2 h).
- Code reuse: pilot.py's Steer, run, balanced_cases and export can be reused. Two small gaps: pilot.run() does not return xy_offset_m (HoverEnv.metrics has it), and TWITCH_TICKS is a module constant.

Why it fails:
1. Wrong premise (data, read-only numpy pass).
   - The stress motor_gain U(+-1.5%) multiplies the command after clipping (snn_pid_compare/environment.py, lines 97-100), so hover headroom above LOW spans about 16-111 rad/s.
   - The law's height cost lives almost entirely in the low-headroom cases. In the v1 test, 4 of 16 cases with g = 1.011-1.015 carry 91% of the +2.90 cm excess; the 10 cases with g <= 1.005 average +0.12 cm at the same duty; corr = 0.68.
   - On the 8 tuning cases, the single g = 1.0137 case carries +30.4 cm (oracle law) or +11.7 cm (IMU law); every case with g <= 0.9994 stays within +-0.75 cm for every law.
   - This also explains why the oracle law does not beat the IMU law on J: it fires more in the floor-bound case.
   - Where the cost exists, c = max(LOW, m - Delta) is pinned at LOW and there is almost no base lift to reallocate. Where headroom exists, there is no cost to remove.
2. No new downward authority. Mean command >= LOW + steering duty x (HIGH - LOW) for every allocation, so the multiplexer's lift-neutral capacity (Delta_eff / pulse_worth) equals law + payback's (smaller with Delta = 35). 'Creates the missing downward authority' is false.
3. The operating point exceeds the lift-neutral duty ceiling (about 9% at nominal gain), and it has already been tested. timing_closed_loop.json has 10-22.6% duty runs: 23 of 24 height escapes. A real sigma-delta will produce irregular trains with sub-harmonic forcing near the 4-5 Hz two-body mode (lesson 3).
4. Side effects on top of zero first-order gain.
   - The neutral phase (zero crossing near 52-63 deg) is the steepest point of the pitch-response curve (about 0.043 rad/s per degree per 0.1 s train). The v1 IMU law's onset spread was about 11 deg with a +28 deg bias, so continuous base pulses inject pitch noise and bias.
   - The common-mode backward effect is about -0.052 m/s per 0.1 s pi/2 burst, which implies xy drift; the xy guard is likely to trip.
5. SNN and NEAT are unnecessary by construction.
   - The classical multiplexer is the G1 seed, and the lift budget is a classical input.
   - The global tau_m of 5 ms cannot hold lift debt across 40 ms wingbeats.
   - The 'budget removed' ablation passes trivially, and the 'J_snn <= 1.00x' criterion passes about half the time on a tie.
   - NEAT against a CMA-tuned 7-parameter law is exactly lessons 1-2 again; the proposer's own P(SNN-centred result) is about 5%.
6. Missing baseline. The same-information classical fix for the real failure mode, a pulse law gated by the PID's own headroom m_PID - LOW, is absent. G0 also gives the multiplexer 24 settings plus a proportional phase term against 4 for law + payback.

The proposer's prior of P(G0 passes) about 0.35 should be well under 0.1.
