- artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json
- artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_law_grid.json
- artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_imu_law.json
- artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_closed_loop.json
- artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_authority.json
- experiments/algorithms/snn_pid_compare/environment.py
- experiments/algorithms/topology_hover/environment.py
- experiments/algorithms/wingbeat_snn/networks.py
- experiments/algorithms/wingbeat_snn/evolve.py
- experiments/algorithms/spike_steer/pilot.py

fatal_issues: The premise is mostly a saturation effect in a few cases, not a structural lift-for-pitch trade-off. Each stress case draws motor_gain = 1 ± 1.5%, applied AFTER the [LOW, HIGH] clip (experiments/algorithms/snn_pid_compare/environment.py:97-100; topology_hover/environment.py:65). The downward headroom (about 3178/g - 3115 rad/s) therefore ranges from 16 to 108 rad/s per case. I replayed only the RNG draws (no simulation). The pulse law's excess height follows this headroom almost monotonically. IMU law on the 8-case set (artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_imu_law.json): case 4 (about 20 rad/s) +11.8 cm and case 6 (about 33 rad/s) +2.2 cm make up 95% of the excess; the other 6 cases are each within +0.6 cm. v1 test, law_strong (artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json): cases 7, 6, 4 and 10 (headroom 16, 21, 24, 29 rad/s) carry +19.8, +11.3, +6.5 and +4.6 cm, which is 91% of the excess; the 10 cases with at least 47 rad/s of headroom add about +1.4 cm combined. The '1-2 cm of height per 1% duty' figure is an average over this mixture.

The multiplexer cannot 'create the missing downward lift authority'. Total lift reduction is bounded by m_PID - LOW whether lift is removed by lowering c, by skipping pulses, or by payback (b). In the cases where the cost actually occurs, that budget is 16-36 rad/s. One 1-tick HIGH pulse per wingbeat already needs about 35 rad/s, and the proposed 2-3-tick pulse about 69-104. So the neutral-phase baseline train, and the 'exactly one pulse per wingbeat' mitigation, cannot exist there, and the scheme reduces to law + payback or rationing with the same budget. Where the budget is large, the law's height cost is already about 0. There the 10-15% duty train only adds risk: rocking, PLL offset, and a backward force of about -0.04 m/s per 0.1 s pi/2 burst near the 45-65 deg neutral phase (timing_authority.json).

The gain bound is overstated, and G0 is nearly unpassable as written. The '4.2-4.7 J (20-30% lower)' estimate uses oracle-law pitch (1.9-2.4 deg). With the deployable IMU law, perfect lift neutrality at unchanged pitch gives J 5.82 -> 5.25 (-9.5%, 8-case grid) and 6.29 -> 5.42 (-13.8%, v1 test), before any side effects. G0 asks for <= 0.90x the better of the tuned law and law + payback, plus at least 12/16 paired wins. At least 10 of the 16 test cases have essentially no excess height to recover.

Novelty: the core principle is published for single-actuator aircraft. One actuator, with the force level over several cycles setting altitude and pulses at specific phases within each cycle setting attitude or lateral motion, is described for the SAM/F-SAM single-actuator monocopters (AIM 2020; Win et al., Bioinspiration & Biomimetics 2021: 'altitude control by regulating the force ... throughout multiple rotations. Lateral control is achieved by pulsing the thrust unit at specific instances during each cycle of rotation'). SUTD patents define square-wave cyclic thrust as an offset plus an amplitude whenever sin(azimuth + direction) exceeds a threshold, with offset, amplitude and duty as the tuned parameters; that is essentially classical multiplexer (c). Paulos and Yim (ICRA 2015, JGCD 2018) modulate one motor's torque in phase once per revolution to get thrust plus roll and pitch. Split-cycle modulation (Doman/Oppenheimer) and Vejdani et al. 2022 (a continuously rotating crank with variable-time segments per wingbeat) cover intra-wingbeat timing. Spikes driving motors directly as pulse-frequency modulation: Jimenez-Fernandez et al., Sensors 2012. That an integrate-and-fire neuron is a first-order sigma-delta modulator is textbook. What remains is an adaptation to a crank-driven flapper with a one-sided command bound, in simulation only.

SNN and NEAT are not central, by construction. The seed is 'functionally equal to the classical multiplexer': the subtractive-reset LIF is the sigma-delta accumulator, refractoriness gives one pulse per window, the coincidence cells are the phase gate, and the delays restate psi0 and k_psi. Each proposed ablation has a classical twin, so it tests the mechanism, not spiking. There is no ANN/GRU arm with the same thresholded, refractory output, and no fixed-topology CMA arm on the seed's weights and delays (the project's lesson 2: topology-evolution effect about 0). So even a G1 win could not be credited to SNN or NEAT, and any structure NEAT found could be distilled back into the classical law. The claim that a rate-coded ANN 'would need an external quantizer, accumulator and scheduler' is a strawman, since any recurrent policy with a thresholded output can implement these. The proposer's own estimate of P(SNN-centred paper) is about 5%.

If the classical baseline matches, there is no publishable core. The mechanism is prior art, and the effect is confined to the 4-6 simulated cases where the motor-gain draw leaves little headroom. The obvious classical fix is missing from the baselines and would probably capture whatever gain exists: schedule the law's aggressiveness, or a token-bucket duty limit, on m_PID - LOW, which the controller can compute from the 11-D reading.
fixes: Stratify every J, height and pitch result by per-case headroom (the replayed motor_gain draw, or the PID's settled motor command). Test any lift-neutrality claim only inside the low-headroom stratum, where the effect actually exists.

Before any SNN work, add the cheapest classical competitors: (i) the IMU law with threshold and width scheduled on m_PID - LOW, and on height error and vertical speed; (ii) a token-bucket duty limiter fed by m_PID - LOW; (iii) law + payback. G0 must beat the best of these, not the plain law.

Restate the mechanism honestly: it redistributes the fixed m_PID - LOW budget in time and phase and creates no new authority. Recompute the bound with IMU-law pitch, which gives at most about 10-14% before side effects. Make the G0 ratio and the 12/16 paired-win rule consistent with the roughly 6 of 16 test cases that have anything to recover.

Add a centrality gate with an identical output quantizer and refractory rule and the same episode budget: NEAT-SNN vs CMA-ES on the seed's weights and delays (fixed topology) vs a GRU/MLP policy with thresholded output. Claim SNN or NEAT only if the SNN beats both and its gain cannot be distilled into the classical multiplexer. Otherwise present the SNN as an equal implementation from the start.

Position the work against SAM/F-SAM monocopters, Paulos and Yim, split-cycle modulation, Vejdani 2022, Jimenez-Fernandez 2012 and the integrate-and-fire / sigma-delta equivalence. The one unclaimed hook I found, a robot implementation of a b1-style phase-advance motor neuron, is a framing, not a result.

Note for the orchestrator: the claim that 'oracle sensing does not improve J' (6.25 vs 5.82), which was used to reject the sensing-side topics, has the same confound. In the 5 grid cases with at least 65 rad/s of headroom, the oracle law beats the IMU law by about 0.6 deg of pitch (J about 4.38 vs 4.91, -11%) at no height cost. Re-check the rejected topics on stratified data, keeping in mind that any sensing gain still needs a classical comparison such as a 4-harmonic notch.
critiques.reasoning:
Verdict: refuted on all three counts: novelty, SNN/NEAT centrality, and the fallback classical claim. The project data also undercut the premise.

1) The premise. I split the existing results by case. The height cost of pulse steering is not a general rate of 1-2 cm per 1% duty. It comes almost entirely from the cases where the random motor gain, applied after the command clip, leaves the hover command only 16-36 rad/s above LOW. I checked this by replaying only the RNG draws, in milliseconds with no simulation.
- 8-case IMU law: 95% of the excess height is in 2 of the 8 cases.
- v1 test: 91% is in 4 of the 16 cases, and the 10 cases with at least 47 rad/s of headroom have about zero excess.
- In exactly those cases the multiplexer's lift budget, m_PID - LOW, is smaller than one pulse per wingbeat. Lift that is moved still has to come from the same bounded headroom as law + payback. Where headroom is large, there is nothing to recover.
- The 20-30% gain estimate uses oracle-law pitch. With the IMU law, perfect neutrality at unchanged pitch gives only -9.5% (grid) to -13.8% (v1 test), before side effects. That is at or below G0's own 10% bar, and the 12/16 paired-win rule cannot be met when about 10/16 cases have nothing to recover.

2) Novelty. The core principle is published for single-actuator aircraft:
- SAM/F-SAM monocopters: altitude from the thrust level over several rotations, lateral control from pulses at specific phases of each rotation. Their patents describe square-wave cyclic thrust (offset plus amplitude while a phase condition holds, with a tunable duty), which is essentially classical multiplexer (c).
- Paulos and Yim: one motor's torque, modulated in phase once per revolution, gives thrust plus roll and pitch.
- Split-cycle modulation and Vejdani 2022 cover intra-wingbeat timing.
- Jimenez-Fernandez 2012 drives motors directly with spike trains (pulse-frequency modulation), and integrate-and-fire is equivalent to sigma-delta.
What remains new is a simulation-only adaptation to a crank-driven flapper with a one-sided bound.

3) Centrality. The SNN is seeded to equal the classical multiplexer: integrate-and-fire = sigma-delta, refractoriness = one pulse per window, coincidence = phase gate, delays = phase offsets. Each ablation has a classical twin. There is no ANN/GRU arm and no fixed-topology CMA arm, so even a win could not be credited to spiking or to NEAT. The project's lessons (SNN vs ANN tie, topology effect about 0, NEAT weak at fine-tuning weights) and the proposer's own roughly 5% estimate both point the same way.

4) Fallback. If the classical version ties, the result is a prior-art mechanism confined to a few saturated simulated cases. A trivial headroom-scheduled law, missing from the baselines, would likely capture any gain.

There is one useful side finding. The same confound affects the earlier rejection of sensing-side topics: in high-headroom cases, oracle sensing improves J by about 11%. Those topics deserve a stratified re-check, against classical estimators.

topic.title: Spiking righting reflexes: NEAT-evolved event sequencers for large-upset recovery of the single-motor flapping robot
topic.one_line: Keep the slow PID, which is the only stable continuous loop on this two-body plant. Add a NEAT-evolved delay-LIF circuit that detects large upsets from the IMU and fires a multi-phase program: saturated gimbal twitches plus wingbeat-phase-locked motor twitches to counter, brake, top up lift and hand back. Test it against a classical recovery automaton tuned by CEM with the same budget, the same signals and the same twitch primitives.
topic.problem:
The earlier gates were small-signal: v3 stress gives about 7 deg pitch RMS, and retuning the PID captured nearly everything. A single-loop controller is structurally weakest against a large upset: a bump or strong gust that spins the 15 g robot (7 g thrust unit on a gimbal above an 8 g lower body) at 3-6 rad/s toward 30-70 deg tilt. Flies correct rolls of up to about 100 deg within about 30 ms; small perturbations fit a linear PI, large ones show nonlinear, hierarchical control (Beatus 2015).

On this plant the PID's attitude and its D-term both come from the 0.13 s AHRS. At 4 rad/s, a first-order 0.13 s lag gives only about 32% of the true rate after 50 ms, so the PID reacts late. Its gimbal stays mostly unsaturated, and the lightly damped 4-5 Hz two-body mode rings. Above 45.6 deg tilt the range finder gives no samples (cos > 0.7 check), so the height observer coasts. Above 80 deg tilt the episode terminates.

Inside the interface, the actuators are strong when used early and at saturation (timing_authority.json):
- a +0.035 rad gimbal step for 0.1 s gives 0.78 rad/s pitch rate, after an inverse response of -0.6 deg;
- a 180 deg one-sided motor-pulse window centred on 135 deg crank phase gives about 3.2 rad/s and about +11 deg in 0.1 s;
- roll has only the gimbal.

A recovery is inherently multi-phase:
1. Detect the upset, although the pitch gyro carries about +-12 rad/s of wingbeat rocking.
2. Counter-rotate with saturated actuators.
3. Brake before the slow AHRS even registers the reversal (an input-shaping-like second burst near half the two-body period).
4. Top up lift while tilted. Pulse lift is normally a cost; here it helps.
5. Hand back to the PID.

The right order and timing depend on axis, direction, magnitude, wingbeat phase and whether a second hit arrives. With the inverse response and the ringing mode, this is hard to design by hand.

It matters because the survival envelope against bumps and gusts, not 1 deg of hover tilt, limits a 15 g robot outside the lab. It also tests behaviour-level structure (when, which primitive, how long).

The other listed behaviours are weak inside this interface:
- Ground takeoff and landing would need new physics: the model has no contact (collision masks off; clearance is geometric only).
- Velocity authority is tiny: about 0.14 m/s per rad of pitch reference.
- Launch from rest is the natural second scenario for the full study, through tilted releases (case['degrees']). Every episode already starts this way: release at 0.8 m, motor off, 0.1 s ramp. In the archived trace of the selected PID, the robot drops about 16 cm and swings about +-13 deg in pitch in the first 0.3 s.
topic.why_snn:
1. Bang-bang structure. The actuators saturate and are slew-limited: servo torque limit 0.02 N.m, 8.2 ms smoothing, motor clipped at HIGH. A near-time-optimal recovery is therefore a short sequence of saturated bursts with a few switch times, and a spike train of twitch events encodes exactly that. Refractoriness gives dwell time and hysteresis against chattering; an FSM must add these by hand.
2. Event detection. An LIF unit integrates rectified notched-gyro and lag-inverted attitude evidence up to a threshold. That makes it a leaky sequential detector: it fires on sustained body rotation and can ignore the +-12 rad/s wingbeat rocking. False triggers are penalised in hover.
3. Timing from structure. Counter-to-brake intervals of about 50-150 ms (near half the 4-5 Hz two-body period) are far longer than tau_m = 5 ms and the 0-20 ms synaptic delays (MAX_DELAY = 20). The program must therefore be carried by delay chains through hidden units, or by recurrent latches. The time structure lives in topology and integer delays, which lesion tests can check.
4. Phase locking. Motor twitches act through crank phase (135/315 deg optimum). spike_steer v1 has already shown this can be learned (resultant length 0.90).
5. Stability. The reflex is open-loop between events, and the slow PID stays the only continuous loop. So it does not recreate the fast continuous attitude loop that destabilises this plant.

Energy is not claimed.
topic.interface_check:
Sensors: only env.last_reading (11-D at 500 Hz, including the case's delay_steps): AHRS roll/pitch (0.13 s), gyro x/y and range-finder vz. IMU-only signals derived inside the controller:
- the WingbeatPhase PLL on gyro y, with the fixed PHASE_OFFSET calibration, giving crank phase and a notched pitch rate;
- a moving average of gyro x over one PLL wingbeat period;
- a lag-inverted attitude, AHRS + 0.13 s x rate. This uses the AHRS time constant, which is a sensor specification.

Actuators: on every 2 ms tick the command is the retuned TeacherPID command (kp x1.5, as in pilot.run). Active twitches override:
- alpha and/or beta with +-0.3 rad (the existing limit);
- and/or omega with HIGH = 3807.5 rad/s.

The command then goes through np.clip(LOW, HIGH) and env.step((cmd - CENTER)/HALF) in direct mode. The unchanged 8.2 ms smoothing, servo kp 1.045 N.m/rad with its 0.02 N.m limit, and the motor speed loop (4.2 V, 6 A) all apply. Twitch dwell is 20 ms for the gimbal and 6 ms for the motor. Freezing the PID integrator while an axis is overridden is controller-internal TeacherPID state.

Rates: 2 ms control ticks. The network's two 1 ms neural substeps are internal computation.

Limits: none changed.

Truth (env.samples, gates.Oracle, true crank angle) is used only for metrics and spike-phase diagnostics.

The only new element is a test scenario: a 20 ms external torque on base_link through sim.external_body_forces. That is the same channel and the same body as the v3 stress pulses. It is injected by wrapping env.air.advance for the episode, and the v3 periodic pulses are switched off in upset cases. The environment code is not modified.
topic.classical_baseline:
Three classical controllers, all IMU-only and tuned on the same training upsets, plus one conditional upper bound:

1. Retuned PID: the 25-point kp/kd grid from gates.GRID.
2. PID plus the IMU phase-locked pulse law (timing.py / spike_steer law family): a 36-point grid over k_theta, k_q, threshold and window width.
3. Designer hybrid recovery automaton (the main baseline). It uses exactly the same features and the same twitch primitives as the SNN:
   - rate estimates: notched pitch rate from the PLL, and roll rate from a wingbeat moving average of gyro x;
   - lag-inverted attitude theta_hat;
   - states and transitions:
     - HOVER to COUNTER when |rate| > w_on or |theta_hat| > theta_on; the direction comes from sign(rate + k x theta_hat). COUNTER holds saturated gimbal twitches. For pitch it also fires motor-up twitches inside a +-w/2 PLL window around 135/315 deg.
     - COUNTER to BRAKE when the rate falls below w_brk or after T_c. BRAKE fires opposite saturated twitches for T_b.
     - BRAKE to HANDBACK to the PID (the integrator was frozen during overrides).
     - A refractory period T_r follows, but the automaton can re-trigger on a new hit in another direction.
   - an optional lift top-up: motor-up while |theta_hat| > theta_lift.

   That gives 10 parameters, tuned by CEM: 24 candidates x 8 iterations x 8 training upsets (all 8 directions) = 1536 episodes. This equals each NEAT arm's training budget.
4. Conditional privileged upper bound, used only if the automaton fails to beat the single-mode controllers: a per-case open-loop twitch schedule on top of the PID, optimised by CEM (24 x 10) on 4 cases, with known onset and direction. It distinguishes "no headroom" from "weak automaton".

All controllers are compared on one shared, paired, held-out test set.

gate.what:
Run after spike_steer v2 has finished. Use the unchanged ResearchEnv in direct mode, with stress-type sensor cases (biases, motor gain +-1.5%, delay_steps=1, noise) and the v3 periodic pulses off. The upset is a 20 ms torque about a horizontal axis in the heading frame, at t0 = 2.40 s + U(0, 40 ms) so the crank phase is random. There are 8 directions (+-pitch, +-roll and the 4 diagonals). Half the cases get a second hit 80-200 ms later. Episodes last t0 + 1.5 s, about 4 s.

Stage A, about 45 min (headroom):
- A0: calibrate 6 magnitudes x 8 directions with the retuned PID and pick 4 levels where it survives about 80/60/40/20%.
- Tune the retuned-PID grid (25 x 8 cases) and the PID+pulse-law grid (36 x 8).
- Tune the designer automaton by CEM (1536 episodes).
- Test all of them on 32 held-out paired cases: 8 directions x 4 levels, half with a double hit, seeds disjoint from training and validation.
- If the automaton does not beat the best single-mode controller, stop. Optionally run the privileged per-case bound (about 17 min).

Stage B, about 70 min (spiking sequencer):
- NEAT delay-LIF arm.
  - 18 inputs: 8 PLL phase cells; rectified lag-inverted pitch and roll attitude (+-); notched pitch rate and roll rate (+-); range-finder vz (+-).
  - 8 hidden LIF units (tau_m 5 ms, tau_s 2.5 ms).
  - 5 spiking outputs: alpha+, alpha-, beta+, beta-, motor-up twitch.
  - Genome 0 is silent, so it equals the PID.
  - Population 24 x 16 generations x 4 direction-balanced cases (+-pitch, +-roll) = 1536 episodes, plus 4 validations of 16 cases.
- NEAT ANN arm with the same budget: recurrent tanh units via Graph.ann_step; an output above 0.5 fires the same twitch.
- Evaluate both on the same 32 test cases.
- Two lesion tests on the SNN champion: all delays set to 0, and hidden-to-hidden edges removed.
- Onset sign and crank-phase histograms (truth used only here).
gate.pass_criterion:
GO requires A and B1-B4 together.
- A (headroom): the automaton beats the best single-mode controller (the better of the retuned PID and PID+pulse law, each selected on training upsets). It must either survive at least 6 more of the 32 cases, or have mean J <= 0.8x with at least 22/32 paired wins. If A fails, it is NO-GO: multi-phase logic has no leverage on this plant (the privileged bound then shows whether a better automaton could exist).
- B1: SNN survivals >= automaton - 2, and mean J <= 1.05x the automaton. J <= 0.90x the automaton is a strong GO.
- B2 (structure is used): setting all delays to 0, and separately removing hidden-to-hidden edges, each raise the SNN's J by at least 20%. In at least 50% of recoveries, the SNN must also emit a brake (opposite-direction) or motor twitch 30-200 ms after its first counter twitch.
- B3 (spiking premise): J_SNN <= J_ANN. If J_ANN <= 0.95 x J_SNN, the spiking premise is rejected.
- B4 (both directions): at least 20 correcting onsets for each of +-pitch and +-roll, at least 70% of them with the correct sign against the true upset. False triggers before t0 must not exceed the automaton's.

If A passes but B fails, only the classical reflex automaton gets written up, and the SNN/NEAT topic is NO-GO.

topic.novelty_notes:
The searches were brief; a full literature review is needed before writing.

The closest flapping-robot work uses RL or MPC, not SNN/NEAT:
- Tu, Fei & Deng (Purdue): RL-learned hummingbird escape maneuvers and flips. The learned policy assists or takes over the stabiliser ([TR21](https://friends.cs.purdue.edu/pubs/TR21_BioInspiredLearning.pdf), [thesis](https://hammer.purdue.edu/articles/thesis/Reinforcement_Learning_enabled_hummingbird-like_extreme_maneuvers_of_a_dual-motor_at-scale_flapping_wing_robot/9937085)).
- Xue et al. 2023: DRL for large-perturbation hovering, in simulation; they note that linear PD controllers fail there ([Biomimetics](https://www.mdpi.com/2313-7673/8/3/295)).
- Hsiao et al. 2025 (MIT): deep-learned robust tube MPC for aerobatics on a 750 mg robot ([arXiv 2508.03043](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.03043)).

SNNs on flapping robots:
- Clawson, Ferrari et al. 2016/2017: adaptive LIF/Hebbian hover and trajectory control of RoboBee, in simulation ([clawson2017](https://compneuro.uwaterloo.ca/publications/clawson2017.html)).
- A 2026 butterfly robot with imitation-learned SNNs driving a CPG for pitch and heading tracking ([arXiv 2605.19430](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.19430)).
- Neither addresses large upsets or evolved event sequencing.

Evolved SNNs for micro air vehicles are single-phase:
- divergence-based landing ([Hagenaars 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03118); Dupeyroux on Loihi, [mavlab](https://mavlab.tudelft.nl/?p=2628));
- NEAT for SNN control on benchmark tasks ([Qiu 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.01180)).

The mechanisms exist, but not for flight control:
- evolved SNN finite-state machines for pattern recognition (Wróbel et al., GReaNs; [PMC4699019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4699019/));
- tau-NEAT, NEAT with evolvable synaptic delays for time series ([Caamaño, NPL](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11063-015-9426-5)).

Recovery from arbitrary attitude has been done for quadrotors with model-based control: single-throw recovery with INDI ([Blaha 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.11723)) and rotor-failure recovery (Sun 2020). Hybrid automata with a recovery mode exist but are hand-designed (Casau et al., [IJ054](https://isr.tecnico.ulisboa.pt/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/3273_IJ054.pdf)).

Biology:
- Ristroph 2010 PNAS: magnetic-pulse "stumbles" reveal an autostabiliser ([PMC2841947](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2841947)).
- Beatus 2015 JRSI: roll corrections of up to 100 deg within about 30 ms; PI for small perturbations, nonlinear and hierarchical control for large ones ([PDF](https://cohengroup.lassp.cornell.edu/userfiles/pubs/Beatus%20et%20al_Interface_2015.pdf)).

Not found anywhere:
- NEAT evolution of topology plus integer delays for a spiking event sequencer that recovers a flapping robot from large upsets;
- a comparison of such a sequencer with a same-budget tuned hybrid recovery automaton inside a fixed low-rate actuator/sensor interface;
- use of wingbeat-phase-locked motor twitches as one primitive of such a sequence.

The novelty lies in this combination and in the honest comparison; the individual pieces exist.
risks: The designer automaton may capture all of the headroom, leaving the SNN at best equal. This A-pass/B-fail outcome is fairly likely; the gate is built to reveal it within about 2 h.

NEAT may not grow structure in 16 generations: the v1 champion stayed at 7 nodes and 78 edges. Timing may then be carried by weights and biases, the lesions would show no use of delays, and the 'why SNN/NEAT' argument would fail.

False triggers in hover: a detector fed by a gyro with +-12 rad/s wingbeat rocking may fire saturated bursts in normal flight. J includes the pre-upset hover, but any later claim also needs long quiet-hover runs (8 s nominal and stress).

The PLL may slip during fast body rotations, because body rate then dominates the pitch gyro. Motor twitches would be mistimed, so the phase error against the true crank angle must be logged during recoveries.

Physical limits may dominate: the 0.02 N.m servo torque limit, 8.2 ms smoothing, the inverse response and the ringing two-body mode could make all event programs perform alike. Stage A tests this, and the privileged bound tells 'no headroom' from 'weak design'.

Scenario conventions shape the results: an idealised torque impulse on the lower body, blade-element aerodynamics at large tilt, range-finder dropout above 45.6 deg, the 80 deg termination and the 0.68 m altitude margin. Report upsets in induced-rate units, and add aerodynamic gust trains (backend.wind) and tilted-release launches in the full study.
Design bias: both arms share a primitive library (saturated twitches, 20 ms and 6 ms dwell) and features chosen by us. A different library could favour one side; keep it fixed and report it.
A single-seed gate is noisy. A pass must be replicated with at least 5 NEAT seeds, matched CEM restarts and fresh test seeds before writing.

Direction bias (lesson 6) could recur over 4 output directions. The fallback is a bilateral mirror genome, with phase cells shifted by 180 deg for pitch; the v2 outcome shows whether balanced batches are enough.
Compute contention: the machine is busy until v2 finishes. At the conservative 24 episodes per minute for 8 s episodes, the gate takes about 2.2 h of wall time, including the conditional bound.
topic.lessons_addressed:
1. Same-budget classical comparison. The baselines are the retuned PID (kp/kd grid), the tuned PID plus IMU pulse law, and a CEM-tuned designer recovery automaton. The automaton gets exactly the NEAT budget (1536 episodes), the same features, the same twitch primitives and the same paired held-out test. GO requires parity with the automaton, not with the PID, and Stage A stops the topic if multi-phase logic has no leverage.

2. SNN vs ANN, topology effect about zero, weak weight tuning, energy. The gate includes an ANN-NEAT arm with the same budget, and B3 rejects the spiking premise if the ANN is at least 5% better. Two lesions (delays set to 0, hidden-to-hidden edges removed) must each cost at least 20%, so topology and delays must do measurable work. NEAT chooses only discrete structure over saturated primitives; no fine amplitudes are learned, and fine continuous control stays in the PID. Energy is never claimed.

3. Fast attitude destabilises the PID. The reflex is event-triggered and open-loop between events. The slow PID remains the only continuous loop, with its integrator frozen during overrides. Fast signals (notched gyro, lag-inverted attitude) feed event decisions only, never a continuous loop. The brake phase explicitly targets the 4-5 Hz two-body mode.

4. No room for in-flight adaptation. The topic does not rely on adaptation. It targets a new disturbance class (large upsets and double hits) that the earlier small-signal gates never probed, and it measures headroom before any learning.

5. Timing channel and the strong classical pulse law. Phase-locked motor twitches are only one primitive (the 135/315 deg optimum is known), and the tuned IMU pulse law is a baseline. Any gain must come from sequencing beyond the timing channel. Its lift side-effect, a cost in hover, becomes useful while tilted.

6. One-direction learning. Training covers 8 upset directions, and every NEAT batch contains +-pitch and +-roll. Each direction has its own output neuron. B4 requires at least 20 correct-sign onsets per direction, with at least 70% correct sign. The fallback is a bilateral mirror genome.

fatal_issues: The claimed mechanism, timing carried by network structure, does not exist in the reused code at this budget. A counter-to-brake gap of 50-150 ms has to be carried by the network itself. But the neurons are fast (tau_m 5 ms, tau_s 2.5 ms; spike_steer/pilot.py:51), and a synapse can delay at most 20 ms (MAX_DELAY; wingbeat_snn/networks.py:19). In neat-python 2.0.0, an add-node mutation disables the original edge, gives the new node bias 0.0, and creates both replacement edges with delay 0 (DelayConnectionGene starts at mean 0, stdev 0; evolve.py:36-38). So add-node shortens or cuts a timed path instead of lengthening it. Delays only drift by Gaussian steps of 3 ms at rate 0.3 per edge per offspring, not in 1 ms steps. The measured growth agrees: the v1 champion went from 7 nodes/78 edges to 8/68 over 20 generations, always 1 species. The v2 run in progress (runs/spike_steer/pilot_v2_s1/history.jsonl) is at 8-9 nodes/81-84 edges after 11 generations, against 8/84 at the start. A chain of 4 or more hops at about 20 ms each will not appear with 24 genomes x 16 generations. The brake can then only be timed by seeing the rate reverse, which the automaton already does explicitly (w_brk). 'Why SNN' #3 and the 'why NEAT' mapping are unsupported.

GO only requires a tie (B1: J <= 1.05x the automaton), and a tie cannot show SNN/NEAT is needed. The topic itself frames recovery as a short bang-bang sequence of saturated primitives with a few switch times. That is exactly its 10-parameter designer automaton, with the same features, primitives and 1536-episode budget, and it is also what textbook minimum-time switching plus input shaping at the known 4-5 Hz mode gives. A full GO would only show NEAT matching an automaton written in one paragraph at equal cost (lesson 1). Only the strong GO (<= 0.90x) would mean something, and that contradicts measured data. In v1 the SNN was 1.30x the classical law (J 8.17 vs 6.29), on an easier task: one output, one primitive, and a larger 32x20 search. The authors already call A-pass/B-fail 'fairly likely'.

B1 and B2 pull against each other, and B2 cannot detect sequencing.
- If the useful program is a one-shot reflex (fire a saturated counter twitch early from the notched rate), NEAT might reach a tie, but no internal timing is needed. If real sequencing is needed, the previous issue rules it out at this budget.
- Zeroing all delays also removes the 0-8 ms input and phase-cell delays (roughly 0-75 deg of crank phase). That shifts motor-twitch phase and reaction latency, so J can rise without any sequencing.
- Removing hidden-to-hidden edges also removes the thresholding relay that an add-node split creates. A bias-0, weight-1 LIF on a rate input fires only when the input is above about 1, so it acts as an upset detector, not a timer.
- 'A brake OR motor twitch 30-200 ms after the first counter twitch' is met by any network that keeps twitching (v1 duty 1-5%).
A B2 pass would therefore not support the central claim.

The objective is decided mostly by survival, at a boundary that behaves almost randomly.
- A crash scores J = 60-100; a survivor scores roughly 20-30. Selection therefore runs on nearly binary outcomes.
- The PID's survival region is large and not monotonic in upset size. In artifacts/snn_hover_20261009/development/pid_envelope.json (original PID, tilted releases) it survived 45 deg in 3 of 4 directions but crashed at 30 deg/270 and 45 deg/90.
- With 4 cases per genome, 8 per CEM candidate and 32 paired test cases, the spread of the paired survival difference is about 3-4 cases. That puts criterion A (>= 6 more survivals) and B1 (>= automaton - 2) only about 1-2 standard deviations from noise.
- The 6x8 A0 calibration has 8 episodes per magnitude, pooled over axes, and roll has only the gimbal. It will produce levels split by axis, not graded levels.
fixes:
Run Stage A alone first (about 45 min), and add two cheaper classical baselines that use the same information:
(a) a gain-scheduled PID whose D-term switches to the PLL-notched gyro rate above a rate threshold (2-3 parameters);
(b) a one-shot reflex: one saturated counter twitch plus integrator freeze, no brake (3-4 parameters).
Tune both by CEM or grid on the same upsets. If either captures >= 80% of the automaton's gain, multi-phase logic has no leverage, so drop Stage B. Reason: the PID's D-term (kd 0.127 pitch / 0.115 roll on the AHRS-derived rate; selected_pid.json) already saturates the 0.3 rad gimbal once the lagged rate passes about 2.4-2.6 rad/s. That happens about 35-115 ms into a 4-10 rad/s upset, so the gimbal is not 'mostly unsaturated', and the headroom is mainly earlier onset plus overshoot handling.

Before choosing primitives, measure what a single twitch actually does: a 20 ms ±0.3 rad gimbal twitch and a 6 ms motor twitch, open loop, in hover and at about 40 deg / 5 rad/s. Measure the lower body (base_link), the thrust unit and whole-body angular momentum separately.
From the MJCF, the system centre of mass is within about 1-3 mm of the gimbal pivots. Whole-body moment therefore comes only from shifting the 8 g lower body: a rough estimate is 0.6 mN.m, about 45 rad/s^2, at full deflection.
Scaling the measured -2.3/+3.7 deg split (lower-body vs joint rotation), a full counter twitch first turns base_link about 8-10 deg the wrong way. Both the termination check (tilt > 1.4 rad) and J are computed on base_link. Add a thrust-unit or whole-body tilt metric so that changes in internal posture are not counted as recovery.

Set GO at the strong level: J <= 0.90x the automaton, or >= 3 more survivals over >= 96 cases. Alternatively, name an advantage that the automaton's parameters cannot express, and check it against the privileged per-case bound.
Use the PID retuned on upsets (the gates.GRID winner) as the base controller of every arm, instead of the fixed kp x1.5 from pilot.run, so that base gains do not confound the comparison.

Wait for the v2 result before committing to 5 outputs. If v2 (balanced batches, 2 motor neurons) misses its both-directions criterion, start directly from the bilateral mirror genome.
Also initialise readout weights near zero or with a negative output bias. Otherwise ±0.3 rad false triggers in hover dominate the early population, and the search simply collapses back to the silent genome 0.

Log the range-finder height bias during upsets. sensors.py:81 converts range to height using the 0.13 s-lagged AHRS attitude, so during fast tilts the height loop under-commands lift. This changes what 'lift top-up' does. Compute J's altitude term from truth only.
critiques.reasoning:
Verdict: weak, 3/10. The gate is cheap, stays inside the interface and can be built from existing code, but its SNN/NEAT half is very likely to end NO-GO, and a GO at a tie would not show SNN/NEAT is needed. Not refuted, because all the fixes are controller-internal and Stage A is new, useful information.

What checks out:
- Interface. ControlEnv.step zeroes sim.external_body_forces every tick and then calls air.advance (snn_pid_compare/environment.py:103-107). So adding a torque inside a wrapper of air.advance uses the same channel and body (air.env.body = base_link) as the v3 pulses. There is direct precedent in snn_hover/environment.py:50-56 (advance_instrumented). Setting pulse_force and pulse_torque to 0 turns the v3 pulses off without changing the random-number order. Confirmed in code: the range finder only samples when cos(tilt) > 0.7, i.e. below 45.6 deg (sensors.py:76); the tilt > 1.4 rad termination; the clearance check is geometric ground clearance only. Using sensor_tau = 0.1305 s for lag inversion is a sensor specification. Twitches at ±0.3 rad and at HIGH are within LOW/HIGH.
- Code reuse. Every named piece exists: pilot SpikingGraph, Steer, initialize, export, make_config, balanced_cases, tune_law and test; gates GRID, SPLITS, HANDOVER_T and Oracle; Graph.ann_step; WingbeatPhase; PHASE_OFFSET.
- Compute. v1 measured about 150 s per generation for 96 six-second episodes on 18 workers, about 3.8 simulated seconds per wall second. The planned ~6,500 four-second episodes therefore take about 1.9-2.2 h.
- The upset regime is genuinely untested. The snn_hover recovery protocol used 16-64 uN.m pulses and was never run formally. In its development PID envelope, the peak tilt came from the release transient, not the pulse.

Where it is weak:
1. Headroom over the PID is real but narrow. The PID's D-term saturates 35-115 ms into a large upset, so what is left is mostly earlier onset and handling overshoot. That is classical territory.
2. The mechanism the topic relies on is not available. The neurons are fast (tau 5/2.5 ms), delays are capped at 20 ms, and neat-python's add-node resets the new edges' delays to 0. Neither v1 nor v2 grew any structure. Any brake timing will come from seeing the rate reverse, which the automaton already does.
3. It repeats measured failure modes. Lesson 1: the topic's own same-budget automaton is the natural answer. Lesson 2: topology had no effect, the v1 champion barely changed, and v2 validation J went 9.96 → 8.59 → 9.39 by generation 7. Lesson 6: one-direction learning, now multiplied across four directions plus the motor output.
4. GO is set at a tie. A tie with a one-paragraph automaton tuned at the same cost does not show SNN/NEAT is needed.
5. B2's lesions are confounded by twitch phase alignment and by thresholding relays, so passing B2 would not demonstrate sequencing.
6. Survival-dominated J at a calibrated boundary that behaves almost randomly makes 32 test cases underpowered.
7. Plant physics: the centre of mass is within about 1-3 mm of the pivots, and a full counter twitch first turns base_link roughly 8-10 deg the wrong way. Both the 80 deg check and J are measured on base_link, so twitches can raise measured tilt before helping. This should be characterised before choosing primitives.

Likely outcomes are therefore A-fail (stop) or A-pass/B-fail (only the classical automaton gets written up).

fatal_issues: The SNN is not central by construction. Every 'why SNN' mechanism is supplied by shared classical parts or is equally open to an ANN or the automaton. (a) Dwell and hysteresis come from the twitch decoder (TWITCH_TICKS in spike_steer/pilot.py Steer.step), not from the neuron: the Graph LIF uses subtractive reset with no refractory period (wingbeat_snn/networks.py snn_substep; pilot.SpikingGraph). (b) Rejecting the +-12 rad/s rocking is done before the network sees the signal, by the PLL notch and the one-wingbeat moving average. tau_m = 5 ms cannot average a 40 ms wingbeat anyway. (c) Phase locking is supplied by the one-hot PLL phase cells, so the network only has to AND a phase cell with a need signal. (d) The argument 'open loop between events, PID stays the only continuous loop' holds identically for the automaton and for any ANN.

The 50-150 ms counter-to-brake timing has no native carrier in this SNN. With tau_m 5 ms, tau_s 2.5 ms and MAX_DELAY 20 ms, NEAT would have to grow 3-8-hop delay chains, and it has not grown structure here. The v1 champion has 8 nodes (one added) and only 3 hidden-to-hidden edges with 3-5 ms delays (artifacts/spike_steer/v1/best_policy.json). The v2 champion has 8-9 nodes at generation 8 (runs/spike_steer/pilot_v2_s1/history.jsonl). A recurrent tanh unit with one near-unity self-loop gives a 100 ms timer, so on this point the SNN is at a disadvantage. Any program that emerges will most likely be reactive (gyro threshold crossings). That is a static switching function, which the 10-parameter automaton or any ANN represents equally well.

B3 (the spiking premise) is confounded. The ANN arm uses Graph.ann_step, which ignores delays, has no leak and updates once per 2 ms tick (networks.py line 12, lines 79-84). The SNN has 0-20 ms delays and two leaky 1 ms substeps per tick. An SNN win therefore could not be attributed to spiking. With one seed and 32 cases, J_SNN <= J_ANN is a coin flip at a tie. There is also no recurrent policy trained by RL (PPO/SAC GRU) over the same primitives, which is the standard modern comparator for learned recovery: recurrent asymmetric actor-critic fall recovery (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.16513), multitask SAC flip recovery (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.08259), SAC for large-perturbation flapping-wing hover (https://www.mdpi.com/2313-7673/8/3/295). 1536 episodes of 4 s is about 3M steps, a normal PPO budget, so reviewers will ask for this arm.

B2 cannot show sequencing, or that NEAT is needed. (1) Lesioning a trained network shows dependence, not necessity. A network evolved with delays breaks when they are zeroed even if a delay-free network trained from scratch would do as well. (2) Input delays of 3-5 ms shift motor-twitch phase by about 27-45 deg. The wingbeat line found that a systematic error of about 30 deg (~3 ms) is fatal at critical disturbances, so zeroing delays can raise J by >=20% through lost phase alignment alone. (3) The clause 'brake or motor twitch 30-200 ms after the first counter twitch' is met trivially by repeated same-direction motor twitches, one per 40 ms wingbeat. (4) The gate has no fixed-topology arm, so the value of topology search is untested, and the earlier finding was 'topology effect ~0'.

There is no publishable SNN/NEAT claim if the classical baseline matches. The topic itself says B-fail means a classical-only write-up. At B1 parity (<=1.05x), the result reads: 'a NEAT-evolved network with dozens of weights and delays matches a 10-parameter CEM-tuned automaton built on the same features, primitives, PID, integrator freeze and phase reference'. Reviewers will see SNN/NEAT as incidental. The substantive contribution would be the classical counter-brake-lift-handback mechanism, which is a modest, simulation-only controls result.

Prior evidence predicts that B1 fails. In v1 the SNN's J was 8.17 against 6.29 for the classical law (1.30x) on a simpler single-output task (artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json). v2 validation J is 8.59 at generation 3 and 9.39 at generation 7, no better than v1's 7.57. The group's own wingbeat paper records NEAT residuals as no better than retuned hand laws, and a NEAT-SNN phase estimator at 9.3 deg against 2.4 deg for the gradient SNN and 0.8 deg for the GRU (docs/wingbeat_paper/HANDOFF.md; paper_outline.md, C3). The proposed gate is strictly harder (18 inputs, 5 outputs, 8 directions, double hits) on a smaller budget: 1536 episodes of 4 s against v1's 1920 of 6 s.

Novelty is only in the combination, and the novelty notes miss the closest conceptual prior art. Neuromorphic event-based control already frames 'spike = impulsive actuation event, with an automaton generating the event sequence and a regulator tuning its timing': Schmetterling, Forni, Franci & Sepulchre 2024 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05339) and the hybrid-systems analysis by Petri et al. 2025 (https://arxiv.org/html/2504.06046v1). Both are designed and analysed, not evolved, which also undercuts 'hard to design by hand'. Further prior work: NEAT-SNN control explicitly aimed at flapping-wing MAVs (Qiu 2019, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.01180); an evolved SNN control layer in flight (Paredes-Valles 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08778); a detector-triggered switch to a recovery controller on an insect-scale robot (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.03043); a switch to a flip-recovery policy (PolyU 2026). The phase-locked motor-twitch primitive also overlaps the group's own forthcoming split-cycle wingbeat paper.
fixes: Make B3 a real test of spiking with a matched non-spiking arm: the same Graph with identical integer delays, two 1 ms substeps and leaky rate units with a smooth nonlinearity, so that only threshold and reset differ. Add a PPO- or SAC-trained GRU over the same 6 discrete primitives with the same episode budget. Claim a spiking benefit only if the SNN beats both over >=5 seeds with a paired sign test.

Replace lesion-based B2 with equal-budget retrained ablations: the SNN with delays frozen at 0, the SNN with no hidden-to-hidden edges, and a fixed dense recurrent SNN with CMA-ES on weights and delays. Define 'sequencing' as an opposite-sign gimbal brake event 30-200 ms after counter onset in >=50% of recoveries, not counting repeated same-direction motor twitches. Log the PLL phase error so that lost phase alignment is not credited as lost sequencing.

Either give the SNN a mechanism that can hold 50-150 ms intervals (adaptive-threshold/ALIF units, a slow-tau unit class, MAX_DELAY >= 100 ms, or seeded delay chains), or drop 'timing from structure' and state that switching is reactive.

Remove claims the implementation does not support: refractoriness (none in the Graph LIF; dwell lives in the decoder), wingbeat-robust event detection (done by the notch and moving average), and phase locking (supplied by the PLL phase cells). Argue SNN centrality only from what the network itself contributes.

In Stage A, add a single-mode nonlinear baseline, e.g. the PID plus a dead-zoned notched-rate term that saturates the gimbal early on large rates. Without it, 'multi-phase leverage' is inferred only against a linear PID and the pulse law.

Pre-register a fallback framing in which NEAT could be central: NEAT as a structure-discovery tool. Any phase or rule the champion uses that the automaton lacks is transplanted back into an automaton v2 with the same CEM budget, and the paper reports whether the gap closes. Otherwise plan the write-up as the classical recovery-automaton result, with SNN/NEAT as a reported negative control.
Gate Stage B on v2: if v2 misses its own criteria (J_snn > 1.05x the tuned law, or one direction not learned), run Stage A only. Stage B is a strictly harder version of the same learning problem.

Expand the related work and state the claim as the controlled comparison, not 'first SNN for flapping-robot recovery'. Position against: Sepulchre-group neuromorphic event control (2024-25), Qiu 2019, Paredes-Valles 2024, Stroobants 2024 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.13945), recurrent-RL fall recovery (arXiv 2606.16513, 2503.08259), MIT tube-MPC recovery switching (arXiv 2508.03043), Xue 2023, the Purdue hummingbird-robot RL maneuvers, and the group's own wingbeat paper.
critiques.reasoning:
Verdict: weak, 3/10. The topic is new only as a combination, SNN/NEAT would look incidental to reviewers, and its own criteria cannot show they are central.

Novelty: brief searches found no work that evolves delay-LIF event sequencers for upset recovery of a flapping robot. Every ingredient exists, though:
- event-based spiking control with sequencing automata (Schmetterling et al. 2024 https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05339; Petri et al. 2025 https://arxiv.org/html/2504.06046v1), which the novelty notes miss;
- NEAT-SNN control aimed at flapping-wing MAVs (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.01180);
- an evolved SNN control layer flown in hardware (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08778);
- learned upset and fall recovery with recurrent RL policies (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.16513, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.08259), DRL for large perturbations of flapping-wing flight (https://www.mdpi.com/2313-7673/8/3/295), and detector-triggered recovery switching (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.03043).

Centrality: code inspection undercuts each 'why SNN' point.
- The twitch dwell and hysteresis live in the decoder: TWITCH_TICKS in /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms/spike_steer/pilot.py.
- The LIF has no refractory period (subtractive reset): /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms/wingbeat_snn/networks.py.
- Wingbeat rejection and phase are supplied by the classical PLL, notch and phase cells.
- The stability argument applies equally to the automaton and to any ANN.
- The 50-150 ms brake timing exceeds tau_m 5 ms and MAX_DELAY 20 ms. NEAT has not grown the needed chains: the v1 champion has 8 nodes and 3 hidden-to-hidden edges at 3-5 ms (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/spike_steer/v1/best_policy.json); v2 has 8-9 nodes at generation 8 (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/runs/spike_steer/pilot_v2_s1/history.jsonl). A tanh self-loop can hold such an interval trivially.

The tests cannot settle centrality:
- B3's ANN arm (Graph.ann_step) has no delays, no leak and one update per tick, so an SNN win cannot be credited to spiking.
- There is no RL-trained GRU arm, the obvious reviewer request.
- B2 lesions can pass through lost phase alignment, and its 'motor twitch 30-200 ms later' clause is met trivially by repeated counter twitches.
- The gate has no fixed-topology arm, so the value of NEAT's topology search is untested.

If the classical automaton matches, there is no SNN/NEAT claim; the topic itself concedes a classical-only write-up. Parity would read as a large evolved network matching a 10-parameter automaton on identical features and primitives.

The prior strongly predicts the A-pass/B-fail outcome:
- v1: J 8.17 against 6.29 for the tuned law (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json).
- v2 so far: validation J 8.6-9.4.
- The wingbeat line's negative NEAT results (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/docs/wingbeat_paper/HANDOFF.md, paper_outline.md C3).
- Stage B is harder on a smaller budget.

What is sound: the interface claims check out against the code. The range finder drops out at cos <= 0.7 (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms/topology_hover/sensors.py). Tilt > 1.4 rad terminates the episode, and external_body_forces is cleared before each advance, so an advance wrapper can inject the upset without editing the environment (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms/snn_pid_compare/environment.py). The authority numbers match timing_authority.json. Stage A is a cheap, honest headroom test.

The topic is therefore worth Stage A as a controls question. As an SNN/NEAT paper it needs the matched-ANN and RL-GRU controls, retrained ablations, and a mechanism that can hold long intervals before any centrality claim survives review.

topic.title: Lift-neutral phase coding and an emergent b1/b2-like tonic/phasic division of labor in NEAT-evolved spiking steering units of the single-motor flapper
topic.one_line: The robot's measured split-cycle physics, where a pulse's lift does not depend on wingbeat phase but its pitch effect reverses with phase, is used for two tests. First, is the Drosophila pitch allocation optimal for a flapping body? In flies a tonic unit firing once per stroke and coding by phase carries displacement (b1, integral term), and a phasic burst unit carries velocity (b2, proportional term). Second, do NEAT-evolved spiking circuits given one small and one large motor unit find this split on their own?
topic.problem:
Inside the original interface, the strongest pitch channel is motor pulses timed to the wingbeat (4.1x the gimbal-residual authority). Event-triggered pulses, however, trade height for pitch. On the 16 test cases the IMU-only event law gives 3.03 deg / 10.9 cm (strong) or 4.38 deg / 8.9 cm (moderate), against 7.35 deg / 8.0 cm for the retuned PID. The oracle-law grid shows the same monotone trade-off: 2.4 deg / 13.2 cm at 1.9% duty, 3.8 / 9.8, 5.3 / 8.2. The cause is that every pulse adds lift, and the lower bound leaves only about 63 rad/s to remove it (about 16-111 rad/s once the +-1.5% motor gain is included).

The authority scan (artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_authority.json) shows how a different code could escape this. For a 180-deg pulse, the vertical-velocity effect barely depends on phase (0.129-0.151 m/s over 8 phases), while the pitch-rate effect changes sign (-3.1 to +3.3 rad/s). For 90-deg pulses the neutral phases are about 52 and 233 deg. A train at constant rate (tonic) whose phase is shifted around a neutral phase therefore steers both ways at nearly constant lift. Phasic events instead accumulate lift.

Flies use exactly two kinds of steering motor units:
- b1 is tonic: it fires once per stroke and steers by phase advance; haltere afferents set its phase (Tu & Dickinson 1996; Fayyazuddin & Dickinson 1996/1999).
- b2 is phasic: it fires in bursts during maneuvers (Lindsay et al. 2017).
- In pitch, b1 carries the integral (displacement) term and b2 the proportional (velocity) term (Whitehead et al. 2022). That paper gives only a functional framing, not a mechanistic one, and notes that b1 phase cannot be manipulated in free flight.

The topic has two parts:
- (i) Test whether side-effect accumulation makes the fly allocation optimal on a physically faithful flapper: persistent displacement goes to the tonic phase code, transient velocity goes to phasic bursts. This is the opposite of the usual coarse/fine dual-stage allocation in engineering, which sends low frequencies to the large actuator.
- (ii) Test whether NEAT+SNN finds this allocation without being told.

This matters for biology, because it would give a mechanistic explanation and a model in which b1 phase can be manipulated. It matters for the robot, because it targets the pitch-height trade-off of the event law.
topic.why_snn:
The plant's best authority comes as discrete, phase-specific events (at most one useful twitch per wingbeat). The controller's output is therefore a spike train, and the hypotheses are properties of spike trains: tonic versus phasic firing, and spike phase as the code. These can be compared directly with b1/b2 recordings (b1 fires once per stroke and steers by phase advance; b2 bursts).

Tonic phase coding is a built-in regime of an LIF unit that phase afferents entrain once per cycle. Here the PLL phase cells play the role of haltere campaniform fields firing at their preferred phases. Excitatory drive advances the spike and inhibition delays it (a latency code), which is how descending input shifts mnb1 phase. No explicit phase arithmetic is needed, and the regime holds over a wide range of weights (an Arnold tongue).

Threshold integration plus the twitch dead time gives all-or-none recruitment for the phasic unit and limits it to about one event per cycle. Integer synaptic delays set phase offsets.

Not claimed: better performance than an ANN (v3 found no SNN-ANN difference) or energy savings. An ANN with thresholded event outputs is a control in the full study, so that what is specific to spiking is stated honestly.
topic.why_neat:
The hypothesis is about wiring. It concerns which motor unit receives the displacement afferents (lagged pitch +/-) and which the velocity afferents (notched rate +/-), with which sign (advance or retard), and which phase afferent or delay entrains the unit. The fly-like and swapped allocations differ only in topology. NEAT's add/remove-connection mutations and integer delay genes search exactly these deciding variables.

Weights only need the right order of magnitude, because entrainment and threshold recruitment tolerate a wide range of weights. The fine-tuning weakness that stopped the NEAT phase estimator at about 10 deg (a continuous regression) does not apply here.

Starting from a minimal network and adding structure gives sparse circuits that can be read like a connectome (per unit, which paths come from displacement and which from velocity) and lesioned unit by unit, the same toolkit neurophysiology uses.

Speciation (6-8 species in v2) keeps rival organizations alive, for example tonic-displacement against phasic-only. Convergence to one organization across seeds is then an argument from convergent evolution. A fixed-topology SNN control (evolve.py `snn_fixed`, weights and delays only) tests in the full study whether the structural search itself matters.
topic.interface_check:
Every 2 ms tick, the retuned PID (kp x1.5, kd x1) computes gimbal alpha/beta and the motor speed from the 11-D reading, exactly as in every baseline. The motor units only replace the motor command after a spike:
- Unit S (small): 1 tick at min(PID + 300 rad/s, HIGH).
- Unit L (large): 3 ticks at HIGH, as in v1.

The command then passes through the unchanged path: clip to [3115.2, 3807.5] rad/s, the +-1.5% motor gain, 8.2 ms smoothing, and the servo and motor models. Gimbal limits are not touched. The sub-tick C++ phase drive in wingbeat_snn/plant.py is not used.

Inputs are IMU-only:
- PLL phase and notched rate from the pitch gyro (reading[4]), with the same one-time offset calibration (PHASE_OFFSET).
- Lagged AHRS pitch (reading[1]).
- The stress-case 2 ms reading delay is kept.
- No truth, no new sensor, no rate change.

The disturbance is the v3 stress pulse with signs balanced across cases, which is an allowed test scenario. The true crank angle and the de-rocked oracle are used only for metrics and spike-phase analysis.

A once-per-stroke S train adds at most 15 rad/s to the mean command. That fits inside the nominal 63 rad/s room. The room is logged per case, because the +-1.5% motor gain can shrink it to about 16 rad/s.
topic.classical_baseline:
The baseline is the hand-designed version of the hypothesis plus its rivals, all using the same IMU information and all tuned on the same 16 balanced 6 s training cases (`balanced_cases('train', 16, 6., offset=900_000)`, the cases v2's `tune_law` uses):
- **F, fly-like two-tier.** The tonic unit fires one S-sized pulse per PLL wingbeat at phase psi0 + s*clip(g*u_theta, +-90 deg), around the measured neutral phase (psi0 in {52, 233} deg; s = +1 / -1 respectively); u_theta comes from lagged pitch. The phasic unit is the event law (window at HIGH centered on 135 or 315 deg) driven by notched rate.
- **S-swap.** The tonic unit is driven by rate and the phasic unit by displacement.
- **P.** The existing event law (k_theta, k_q, threshold, width) taken from v2's 108-point `tune_law`.
- **V.** The event law with k_theta = 0, which isolates the gain from simply removing displacement-driven pulses.
- **T.** Tonic unit only.
- The retuned PID.

Gate grids:
- F: 24 points (neutral phase 2 x tonic gain 2 x pulse size 2 x phasic k_q 3).
- S-swap, T and V: 12 points each.

That is 960 episodes, plus the 1728 episodes of P from v2. In the full study each family is tuned by CEM with the same episode budget as one evolution run (about 2.6k episodes per seed), and the comparison is repeated for every seed.

gate.what:
Two stages, seed 1 only, about 2 h on the 18-worker machine.

Stage A, classical physics (about 35 min):
- Add a TwoTier law in one new module.
- Grid-tune F, S-swap, T and V on the 16 balanced training cases.
- Evaluate the best of each family, v2's tuned P and the retuned PID on the shared 16 test cases (8 s, `pilot.cases('test')`).

Stage B, emergence (about 75 min):
- NEAT-SNN set up as pilot v2: 12 IMU inputs (8 PLL phase cells plus rectified lagged pitch and notched rate), 6 hidden delay-LIF units, compatibility 3, balanced 4-case batches, population 32 x 20 generations.
- The one change: two motor units of different size (S: 1 tick at PID+300; L: 3-tick twitch at HIGH).
- Test the champion on the same 16 cases three ways: intact, S silenced, L silenced.
- Log per tick the true crank phase, lagged pitch, notched rate and spikes per unit.
gate.metric:
J = pitch RMS (deg, de-rocked truth, t >= 2 s) + 0.3 x height RMSE (cm), as in the pilot. Also height RMSE and per-case paired differences.

For each motor unit:
- Tonic index: fraction of wingbeats (true crank cycles) with at least one spike.
- Spikes per active cycle.
- Displacement share D = |b_theta| / (|b_theta| + |b_q|), from a standardized regression of per-cycle signed effort E = sum(size x a(psi at pulse center)) on cycle-mean lagged pitch and notched rate. Here a(psi) is the authority curve measured in timing_authority.json. D is the per-unit counterpart of Whitehead's Ki/Kp attribution.
- Mean spike phase in need-up versus need-down cycles.
- Change in J when the unit is silenced.
gate.pass_criterion:
GO only if both A and B hold.

A (physics):
- J_F <= 0.95 x min(J_P, J_V).
- Height RMSE_F <= height RMSE_P - 1.0 cm, with pitch RMS_F <= pitch RMS_P + 0.5 deg.
- J_F < J_S-swap in at least 12 of 16 paired cases.

B (emergence):
- The SNN flies 16/16 with J_SNN <= 1.10 x J_F.
- Unit S: tonic index >= 0.5, D >= 0.6, R^2 >= 0.1, and both need signs represented (at least 20 cycles each, mean phases on opposite sides of the neutral phase).
- Unit L: tonic index <= 0.2 and D <= 0.4.
- Silencing either unit raises J in at least 11 of 16 cases.

If A fails: NO-GO. The embodiment explanation does not hold on this platform, and that is reported as a negative result.
If A passes and B fails: the physics holds but evolution did not find the split with this budget. This is not yet a NEAT/SNN paper; ask the user before a 3-seed x 40-generation run.
gate.code_reuse:
Reused:
- spike_steer/pilot.py: SpikingGraph, balanced_cases/pulse_sign, cases, make_config + neat_template.ini, initialize, export, pool, summarize. Set pilot.OUTPUTS = 2 and subclass Steer for per-unit decoders. Use v2's tune_law JSON as P.
- neuro_gates/timing.py (PULSE_PHASE) and artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_authority.json (a(psi) and the neutral phases).
- neuro_gates/gates.py: Oracle for metrics only, HANDOVER_T.
- wingbeat_feasibility/preliminary.py: WingbeatPhase PLL and notch.
- wingbeat_snn: networks.py (Graph), evolve.py (DelayGenome, plain_tanh), plant.py (PHASE_OFFSET only).

New: one module, spike_steer/division.py, about 300 lines: the TwoTier law, the per-unit decoder, extended logging and the regression and ablation analysis. No existing file is modified.

If v2's tune_law output is missing, rerun it (about 50 min, which brings the gate to about 2.8 h).

topic.novelty_notes:
Searches (Oct 2026) found the biological facts this topic relies on, but no work that explains them physically or shows them emerging in evolved spiking circuits:
- Whitehead et al. 2022, Sci Adv (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9750141/): in pitch, b1 maps to the integral (Ki) term and b2 to the proportional (Kp) term. The paper offers only a functional framing and lists b1 firing phase and the upstream circuit as open questions.
- Lindsay, Sustar & Dickinson 2017, Curr Biol (https://core.ac.uk/works/62711956): every sclerite has small tonic muscles for fine adjustment and large phasic muscles for big changes.
- Tu & Dickinson 1996 (https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:20181116-091112744): b1 fires once per stroke and its phase advance raises amplitude; b2 fires intermittently or in bursts.
- Fayyazuddin & Dickinson 1996 (https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:20181116-073005324): haltere afferents drive mnb1 electrotonically.
- A 2025 eLife reviewed preprint extends b1/b2 tests to roll (https://elifesciences.org/reviewed-preprints/112125; not read in full).
- Sponberg/Putney (hawkmoth): spike timing carries the information across the flight motor program.

Robotics:
- Split-cycle constant-period frequency modulation (Doman/Oppenheimer patents, e.g. https://patents.google.com/patent/US8700233).
- Single-motor intra-stroke timing, including the 2026 AirPulse STAR generator (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06811v1). These are hand-designed, with no neural organization and no lift-side-effect allocation argument.
- Spiking control of flapping robots: Clawson et al. 2016/2017 adaptive SNN for RoboBee hover (https://compneuro.uwaterloo.ca/publications/clawson2017.html); not evolved, no comparison with biology.
- NEAT-evolved SNN control (Qiu et al. 2019, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.01180) only names flapping MAVs as future work.
- Evolved CTRNNs for simulated flapping animats exist, but without spiking units or comparison with muscles.

What is new here:
- A quantitative allocation principle (side effects that accumulate favor tonic phase coding for persistent errors), measured on a physically faithful flapper and opposite to the usual coarse/fine dual-stage allocation.
- Its emergence in NEAT-evolved spiking motor units.
- A robot on which "b1 phase" can be manipulated and lesioned.

Paper-level predictions beyond the gate:
- More tonic use when height weighs more or the lift reserve is larger (+2 g payload or a thrust-loss scenario).
- More phasic recruitment under stress2x.
- Whitehead-style PI fits after ablation: silencing S lowers Ki, silencing L lowers Kp.

Follow-up: replace the PLL phase cells with rectified raw-gyro afferents (a haltere-like metronome) to test whether the b1-like unit can be timed directly by the robot's own wingbeat vibration.
risks: The tonic channel may be too weak. 1-2-tick pulses of +300 rad/s, after 8.2 ms smoothing and the motor speed loop, may give only about 0.3-0.7x the gimbal-residual authority. F would then match V and A fails; the honest conclusion would be that the lift room near the lower bound (about 63 rad/s, 16-111 across stress cases) leaves no affordable tonic channel on this robot.
The retuned PID's attitude loop already supplies the displacement (integral-like) correction, so a tonic displacement unit may be redundant even if it is lift-neutral.

The allocation may not matter, or the robot may prefer the swapped assignment (S-swap >= F). That would refute the embodiment explanation of b1/b2 on this platform; it is informative, but kills the biology paper.

Lift is only roughly phase-independent: +-8% for 180-deg windows and up to about +-25% for 90-deg windows. Tonic phase shifts can leak into height. The constant pulse train may also change the gyro waveform and bias the PLL's calibrated phase offset (closed-loop PLL error is already about 5-6 deg).

A single seed with 20 generations can miss the organization (v1 settled on a one-direction phasic solution), so a negative B is only weakly informative. The full study needs at least 5 seeds x 40 generations and equal-budget CEM for the classical laws.

Defining a small and a large unit in advance shapes the solution space, and reviewers may say the split is imposed. Controls are needed: two identical units or an evolvable unit size, a fixed-topology SNN, and an ANN with thresholded event outputs.

The fly analogy is partial. Fly steering muscles act on the wing hinge, not on the power drive. What transfers is the side-effect-accumulation allocation principle, and it must be presented as a hypothesis the robot supports, not as proof about flies.

Displacement and velocity are correlated in closed loop, so the per-unit share D can be ambiguous. Mitigations: standardized multiple regression, per-unit path attribution from the inputs, and ablations.
If the small unit fires several times per cycle (rate-coded rather than phase-coded), the tonic index can be high without phase coding. 'Spikes per active cycle' and R^2 are logged to catch this.
Schedule: the gate depends on v2's tune_law output for P and can only start after v2 frees the machine.
topic.lessons_addressed:
1. Same-budget classical comparison. Every claim is checked against classical laws using the same IMU information, all retuned on the same balanced cases: P (v2's 108-point grid), V, T, the hand-designed hypothesis F, its rival S-swap, and the retuned PID. Stage A tests the physics without any learning. The SNN only has to match F (J within 10%); the scientific claim is about organization, not about beating the classical laws.

2. No SNN-ANN, topology or energy claims. There is no claim that SNN beats ANN, that topology improves performance, or that energy is saved. NEAT is used where structure is the hypothesis itself: assigning displacement and velocity to units, the advance/retard sign, and the entraining phase afferent or delay. Entrainment and threshold recruitment tolerate a wide range of weights, unlike the phase regression where NEAT stalled at about 10 deg.

3. Slow attitude only for the PID. The PID keeps its 0.13 s attitude and its retuned gains, and no PID is ever given a faster attitude. Corrections go through the motor-timing channel, which avoids the two-body inverse response of gimbal pulses.

4. No adaptation claim. Nothing relies on in-flight adaptation. Plant changes (payload, thrust loss) appear only later, as scenarios that vary the lift reserve to test predictions.

5. Builds on the timing channel. The strong IMU-only pulse law is reused as baseline P. The new element, tonic phase coding, targets the measured pitch-height trade-off of event coding, using the measured fact that pulse lift barely depends on phase.

6. Both directions. A tonic phase-coded unit steers both ways by construction (advance versus retard around one neutral phase). The v2 fixes are kept (balanced batches covering all four pulse-sign combinations, speciation). Gate B explicitly requires both need signs, on opposite sides of the neutral phase.

fatal_issues: The project's own data contradict the core premise. The event law's height cost does not come from phasic pulses piling up lift. It comes from the lift reserve of each case: reserve ≈ 3178/g − LOW, where g is the ±1.5 % motor gain drawn as in pilot.pulse_sign, and environment.py line 100 multiplies the clipped command by it. On the 16 v1 test cases (artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json), law_strong cuts pitch from 7.3 to 3.0 deg in every case. In the 10 cases with reserve ≥ 47 rad/s it costs only +0.13 cm of height over the retuned PID (6.5 vs 6.4 cm). In the 6 cases with reserve ≤ 36 rad/s it costs +7.5 cm (+1.1, +1.8, +4.6, +6.5, +11.3, +19.8 cm), which is the whole average cost. The oracle law grid and the IMU-law runs show the same pattern on their 8 tuning cases (timing_law_grid.json, timing_imu_law.json). Even the 2.2–2.4 deg laws stay within +0.2 cm of the PID in the 5 cases with reserve ≥ 65 rad/s. All of the cost, +1.6 to +14.7 cm, sits in the 3 cases with reserve ≤ 40 rad/s, and the lift-shedding 'dip' variant changes nothing there (24.2 vs 24.1 cm). Where reserve exists, a lift-neutral code has no height cost to remove. Where it does not, the limit is the fixed LOW bound, not how pulses are coded.

The tonic unit makes the reserve-limited cases worse, by simple arithmetic. S = min(PID+300, HIGH) adds about 300 rad/s × 2 ms × 26 Hz ≈ 15.6 rad/s of constant mean command, which is about +0.8–1 % of hover lift. That is roughly twice the event law's mean extra command (duty 1.0–1.2 % × about 630 rad/s ≈ 6–8 rad/s), and it is added even when the PID sits at LOW. In the worst test case (g = 1.0148, reserve ≈ 16 rad/s), the lowest achievable mean lift then roughly equals the weight, so the robot can no longer descend. Gate A's 'height_F ≤ height_P − 1.0 cm' cannot be met: averaged over 16 cases it would need about −2.7 cm in the reserve-poor cases, while F adds more mean lift there than P does. NO-GO is predictable without running anything.

SNN/NEAT are unnecessary by construction. F is a hand-written classical law, and the SNN only has to come within 10 % of it. The problem that actually exists, height control limited by reserve, has an obvious classical fix that uses information the controller already has: schedule the event law's threshold, width or pulse budget on the PID's own motor command distance to LOW, or on its height-integrator state.

Stage B cannot support the emergence claim and will very likely fail. (a) S and L are given different pulse sizes in advance, so under a height-penalised J any optimiser uses the cheap unit often and the expensive one rarely. The tonic-index criteria follow from that, not from emergent organisation, and the needed controls (identical units, fixed-topology SNN, ANN) are deferred to the full study. (b) pilot.initialize() connects all 12 inputs to all 6 hidden units and every hidden unit to every output (84 edges with 2 outputs), and champions stay dense (v1 78→64 edges; v2 generation-11 champion 83). The 'allocation' is therefore a weight pattern, not the topology NEAT is claimed to search, which repeats lesson 2. (c) J_SNN ≤ 1.10 × J_F is out of reach: v1 reached 8.17 vs 6.29 (1.30×), and v2's validated champion has not improved since generation 3 (8.59 at generations 3 and 11). The proposal already calls a B failure 'weakly informative', so the gate cannot reject the SNN/NEAT half.

'Lift barely depends on phase' holds only for 180° windows, because a half-cycle box window cancels the 2nd harmonic of lift versus phase. The 90° data in timing_authority.json show lift from 0.054 to 0.092 m/s, with a 2nd harmonic about 19 % of the mean (maximum near 0/180°, minimum near 90/270°). Per-pulse lift changes by about +31 %/−16 % for ±45° around 52°, and +17 %/−2 % around 233°, and the change follows the steering direction. A 1-tick (about 19°) S pulse would see the unfiltered modulation, about 30 %. Its authority, neutral phase and lift curve were never measured; the 90° and 180° windows already disagree on the neutral phase (52/233° vs about 63/246°), yet F fixes ψ0 ∈ {52, 233}.
fixes: Re-scope the problem as reserve-limited height control, and test the simple classical fix first. Schedule the event law's threshold and width, or a pulse budget, on the PID's own low-passed motor command distance to LOW (or on z-integrator saturation). Tune it on the same 16 balanced training cases (balanced_cases('train', 16, 6., offset=900_000)), about 10–20 grid points and roughly 15 min. Any learned or tonic controller must then beat this reserve-aware law.
Report every comparison split by motor-gain or reserve tercile, not just as 16-case means. This can be done now from the existing JSON rows without running any simulation.

If a tonic channel is kept, budget its lift explicitly: switch it off or shrink it when the PID command is within about 40 rad/s of LOW. First measure the 1-tick S-pulse authority, lift-versus-phase curve and neutral phase: 8–16 phases, paired, 4 nominal cases, a few minutes with timing.py's pattern. Stop if the S train's mean lift is not well below the reserve wherever it is active.

For any emergence claim, use identical motor units or an evolvable pulse-size gene. Start from a sparse topology if topology is the hypothesis. Include fixed-topology SNN and thresholded-ANN controls, and run at least 3 seeds. Make Stage B conditional on v2 reaching ≤ 1.10 × J_law with one unit, because a two-unit organisation is strictly harder.

Give every family the same tuning budget inside the gate. Currently P gets 108 points, F 24, and V, S-swap and T 12 each; use equal-episode CEM instead. Use paired statistics, for example at least 12 of 16 cases plus a bootstrap CI, rather than a 5 % mean margin. The paired J SD is about 1.1–1.7, so 5 % (about 0.3) on 16 cases is only about 1 SE.

Implementation note if anything is run: pilot.run() hard-codes cmd[2]=HIGH for any spike and logs only the first firing output, and pilot.task/train are bound to pilot.run and pilot.Steer. Per-unit decoders therefore need their own run, task and train functions in the new module; subclassing Steer is not enough.
critiques.reasoning:
This is a read-only review: no simulations were run and no files were written. All numbers come from existing artifacts, recomputed in stdin Python.

Interface and compute pass:
- The S command min(PID+300, HIGH) stays within [LOW, HIGH]. It goes through the unchanged clip, motor gain, 8.2 ms smoothing and DC-motor speed loop (ControlEnv.step, Airborne.advance).
- Inputs are IMU-only, using reading[4] and reading[1] with the stress delay_steps=1.
- PHASE_OFFSET (84.14 deg) is a constant calibrated once against truth, acceptable as a bench calibration.
- Stage A is about 960 six-second episodes, roughly 30–35 min on 18 workers. Stage B runs at v2's measured rate of about 185 s per generation, roughly 65–80 min. About 2–2.5 h in total is realistic.
- Reusing the code is feasible, but run, task and train must be re-implemented, not just Steer subclassed.

The topic fails on its premise, which the existing data already settle. Two checks:
1. **Height cost splits by lift reserve.** I split the existing per-case rows by the stress case's motor gain:
   - artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json
   - artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_law_grid.json
   - artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_imu_law.json

   The event law's pitch reduction is the same in every case. Its height cost is about 0 in cases with at least 47–65 rad/s of reserve and very large in cases with at most 36–40 rad/s. Lift shedding by a 'dip' half a cycle later does not help, because there is no room below the PID command.
2. **A tonic train spends exactly the scarce resource.** Its one-sided pulses add a constant +15.6 rad/s mean command, about twice the event law's mean, on top of the PID even at LOW. It cannot help where the trade-off exists and has nothing to gain elsewhere. Gate A's height criterion is therefore essentially unreachable.

The physics citation is also weaker than stated. Phase-independent lift in the 180° data comes from the window cancelling the 2nd harmonic. The 90° data show a 2nd-harmonic lift modulation of about 19 % that moves with steering direction near the neutral phases. The S-pulse curve was never measured.

On the SNN/NEAT side:
- The classical F is the solution by construction, and the real problem has a trivial reserve-aware classical fix.
- The B test is confounded by the S/L pulse sizes fixed in advance.
- NEAT's 'topology' rationale contradicts the dense initialisation in pilot.initialize (experiments/algorithms/spike_steer/pilot.py, lines 218–239). This repeats lesson 2 (topology effect about 0; NEAT weak at fine weight tuning).
- v1 and v2 put the evolved SNN about 30 % behind the classical law. v2's validated champion has been unchanged since generation 3 (runs/spike_steer/pilot_v2_s1/history.jsonl), so J_SNN ≤ 1.10 × J_F is very unlikely.
- A B failure is pre-declared weakly informative, so the gate cannot say no to the larger follow-up.

The biology citation is accurate. Whitehead et al. 2022, Sci Adv (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9750141/; summary at https://phys.org/news/2022-12-fruit-flies-muscles-pitch-stable.html) map b1 to the integral term and b2 to the proportional term in pitch. However, the robot's pulses act on the power drive, not on hinge steering muscles, so the 'mechanistic explanation' would not transfer to flies.

Minor points:
