- The retuned PID has effectively no pitch integral (ki_pitch = −0.0104 in selected_pid.json), so a tonic train placed off its neutral phase would leave a standing pitch bias.
- Inside the gate, tuning budgets are unequal (P 108 points vs V and S-swap 12 each).

Verdict: refuted as proposed. The parts worth keeping are the cheap per-reserve analysis and a reserve-aware classical baseline. Any future SNN/NEAT topic on this platform must beat that baseline.

fatal_issues: SNN and NEAT are incidental by construction. The hand-designed law F already emits b1/b2-like tonic and phasic pulse trains, so 'the output is a spike train comparable to b1/b2 recordings' holds for the classical law too. The SNN only needs J <= 1.10 x J_F, so there is no performance claim. What remains is 'emergence', and the setup pre-structures it: S and L units of fixed different sizes, inputs already split into displacement and rate, a classical PLL supplying phase, and the PID doing everything else. Any optimizer would find the same allocation: CMA-ES on the ~6-parameter two-tier law, or an ANN/GRU with sin/cos phase inputs and thresholded event outputs. v3 already measured SNN~ANN and a topology effect of ~0. The reused NEAT setup does not search topology: pilot.initialize() wires all 12 inputs to 6 hidden units to the outputs (78 edges in v1, 84 with two outputs), and v1 champions kept 64-78 edges. It is a dense weight GA. So 'the fly-like and swapped allocations differ only in topology' and 'sparse, readable connectome' do not hold.

The gate cannot tell the claimed new mechanism from the textbook one. S and L share the same clip, 8.2 ms smoothing and motor loop, so they have identical bandwidth and differ only in size. The size principle / fine-coarse allocation (small unit for small persistent residuals, large unit for large transients; Henneman; Lindsay 2017) predicts exactly the outcomes Stage A and B test: F beats S-swap, S is tonic with high D, L is phasic with low D. 'Integral -> tonic' is also nearly tautological, since a persistent correction needs a persistently active effector. A full pass therefore would not support 'side-effect accumulation'. The 'opposite of dual-stage engineering allocation' contrast is overstated, because cost-weighted frequency-split allocation that reserves costly actuators for transients is standard (e.g., Haerkegaard 2004 dynamic control allocation).

The 'fly-like' wiring contradicts fly physiology, and the robot is not a b1 model. Wing input sets mnb1's baseline phase, while haltere (angular-velocity) input transiently shifts it during equilibrium reflexes (Fayyazuddin & Dickinson 1996, 1999). At the afferent level the fly's tonic unit is rate-driven, which is the topic's S-swap, and Gate B (S: D >= 0.6) would fail the fly's own wiring. The robot's units pulse the crank power drive, not hinge steering muscles, whereas Whitehead's PI acts on the forward stroke angle. The robot therefore cannot be 'a model in which b1 phase can be manipulated'. Biology reviewers will point to fly-faithful substrates: Whitehead's own flight simulation, and the Melis et al. 2024 Nature steering-muscle-to-wing-motion model.
fixes: Add the missing classical competitor C: a zero-mean, sub-room sinusoidal (or pulse+dip pair) phase modulation, with amplitude limited to the logged downward room and driven by lagged pitch, plus the event law for velocity; also C alone. Report the height cost of the S train alone. If C >= F, drop the 'tonic spike phase code' claim, because the lift-neutral principle would then favour an analog code.

Make the gate discriminating. Use identical-size units (or an evolvable pulse size per unit), and add a lift-cost sweep: height weight 0.3 vs 1.0, or +2 g payload / -10% thrust. Side-effect accumulation predicts the allocation shifts with lift cost; the size principle does not.

Run the centrality controls inside the gate at equal episode budget, not deferred: CMA-ES on the parametric two-tier law, a fixed-topology SNN, and an ANN/GRU with sin/cos phase inputs and thresholded event outputs. Pre-register that if all reach the same organization, the paper is a physics/optimality result with no NEAT/SNN-centrality claim.

If NEAT stays central, start minimal (direct input-to-output, no dense hidden layer) so wiring is actually searched and the circuits can be read. Use >= 5 seeds x 40 generations with common random numbers. In v1, with 3-case batches, best fitness swung between -6.2 and -9.8 across generations and validation J between 7.6 and 10.7, which is too noisy to resolve the ~0.3 J (5%) effects the gate needs.

Strengthen selection pressure. Under J = pitch + 0.3 x height, the strongest-pulse laws are already J-optimal (law_grid: J ~6.3 vs 6.7-7.7 for milder laws), so evolution has little reason to save lift. Use a height constraint or a heavier height weight.

If the biology angle is kept, redefine 'fly-like' from the real wiring: a tonic unit entrained by the wingbeat whose phase is shifted by rate (haltere-like) input. Ask how such a unit yields Whitehead's Ki-like action, e.g. through entrainment or phase dynamics; that is where spike-timing dynamics would be central. Present the robot as an illustration of a generic allocation principle, not as a b1-manipulable fly model, and check the principle on a fly-faithful actuation model before claiming a mechanism.

Narrow the novelty statement and cite the closest prior work: split-cycle / AirPulse STAR (lift-preserving intra-stroke timing); Gallagher, Doman & Oppenheimer 2012 IEEE TEC (evolved oscillators for split-cycle flappers); Hagenaars et al. 2020 RA-L (evolved SNNs on real MAVs); El Filali et al. 2026 arXiv 2605.19430 (SNN control of a flapping robot); Dideriksen & Farina 2013 (evolutionary optimization of motor-unit organization, where orderly recruitment emerged only when size was tied to excitability — a direct warning about imposed outcomes).
critiques.reasoning:
Bottom line: the exact combination (a b1/b2 allocation explanation tested by evolved SNNs on this robot) appears unpublished. But SNN and NEAT are incidental by design, and if the classical baseline matches, no NEAT/SNN-central claim survives. The biology hook is mismatched, and the 'tonic spike phase code is lift-neutral' premise is probably beaten by a known analog code. I default to weak rather than refuted only because Stage A is cheap and has not been run, and a heavily redesigned emergence study could still be an ALIFE-type paper.

NOVELTY
Open question, confirmed. Whitehead et al. 2022 map b1 to Ki and b2 to Kp in pitch, but their Discussion only 'confirms a previous hypothesis' and says 'functional stratification is a ubiquitous feature of muscle systems' (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9750141/). No mechanism is given, so the why-question is open. I found no robot or SNN work on it.

Every ingredient is already known:
- Lift-preserving intra-stroke timing for moments: Doman/Oppenheimer split-cycle (US8700233); AirPulse STAR 2026 (arXiv 2602.06811).
- Evolved controllers for split-cycle flappers: Gallagher, Doman & Oppenheimer 2012, IEEE TEC.
- Evolved SNNs flying real MAVs: Hagenaars et al. 2020, RA-L.
- SNN control of flapping robots: Clawson 2017; El Filali et al. 2026 (arXiv 2605.19430).
- Small-tonic / large-phasic organization and its evolutionary optimization: Henneman; Lindsay 2017; Dideriksen & Farina 2013.

The 'opposite of dual-stage allocation' contrast fails. S and L share one actuator path, so they have the same bandwidth, and sending large transients to the large unit is ordinary fine/coarse allocation.

CENTRALITY
The classical law F is itself a tonic-plus-phasic pulse generator. The SNN target is only 'match F', so the only SNN/NEAT-specific claim left is emergence. That emergence is pre-structured by the experimenter (pre-sized units, pre-split inputs, PLL phase, PID) and does not depend on the optimizer. The reused NEAT setup is a dense weight GA (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms/spike_steer/pilot.py, initialize(): 78-84 initial edges; v1 champions kept 64-78). v3 already showed SNN~ANN and a topology effect of ~0, so the planned controls will most likely show equivalence. The gate also cannot tell 'side-effect accumulation' apart from the size principle, because both predict every Stage A/B criterion.

BIOLOGY
Fayyazuddin & Dickinson 1999: wing input sets mnb1's baseline phase, and haltere (rate) input transiently shifts it. At the afferent level the fly is therefore 'S-swap', and Gate B would fail the fly's own wiring. The robot's units pulse the crank power drive, not hinge muscles.

PHYSICS, FROM REPO DATA
Sources: /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/neuro_gates/timing_authority.json and timing_law_grid.json.
- Lift is roughly phase-neutral for 180-deg windows (vertical velocity 0.129-0.151 m/s) but varies about +-26% for 90-deg windows (0.054-0.092).
- Per-impulse pitch authority is about 0.16 rad/s per (rad/s x s) for the 90-deg pulse, the 63 rad/s dip and the 300 rad/s sine.
- The S train (+300 rad/s x 2 ms per wingbeat) therefore gives only about 0.3-0.4x the gimbal-residual step (0.78 rad/s) at maximum phase deflection.
- The S train is not lift-neutral: it adds a constant +15 rad/s. That is 24% of the nominal 63 rad/s room and about 94% of the 16 rad/s worst case.
- A zero-mean sinusoid of about 50-63 rad/s (both halves push the same way) would give about 0.6-0.8x at roughly zero mean lift. This baseline is missing.
- The downward room is the binding constraint: the law grid's lift-shedding 'dip' variants changed height RMSE by at most 0.03 cm.
- Under J = pitch + 0.3 x height, the strongest-pulse laws are J-optimal (about 6.3 vs 6.7-7.7), so there is little selection pressure toward lift saving.
- v1 fitness noise (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/spike_steer/v1/history.jsonl: best fitness -6.2 to -9.8; validation J 7.6 to 10.7) means one seed x 20 generations cannot resolve the ~5% effects the gate requires. A failure of B would be uninformative.

IS THERE A PUBLISHABLE CLAIM IF THE CLASSICAL BASELINE MATCHES?
- Robotics: the result would be classical (F), with no need for an SNN.
- Biology: undermined by the actuator mismatch and by the haltere wiring of b1.
- Emergence: pre-structured and non-discriminating. It becomes publishable only after a redesign: identical or evolvable units, a lift-cost sweep, >= 5 seeds, and equal-budget ANN/CMA-ES controls. Even then NEAT/SNN would likely remain one method among several, not the method.

topic.title: Evolve the timing, differentiate the gain: Lamarckian NEAT with plant-kernel surrogate gradients for spike-timed wingbeat steering
topic.one_line: NEAT evolves only the discrete timing structure of a delay-LIF steering circuit: integer delays, wiring and the number of motor neurons. Each output spike is a 6 ms full-range motor twitch. The circuit's weights are trained by surrogate gradients (kernel-credit surrogate gradient, KCSG). The credit for each spike comes from the twitch's response kernel, identified on the non-differentiable MuJoCo plant and indexed by wingbeat phase, applied to the actual rollout. In effect, this is gradient-based iterative learning control (ILC) lifted from an open-loop input to the weights of a spiking feedback policy.
topic.problem:
**Control problem.** Reject the v3 stress disturbance in pitch using only the IMU, through the wingbeat-timed motor channel inside the original interface. This channel is the only one that clearly beats the retuned PID: pitch RMS falls from 7.35 to 3.03 deg, and the objective J (pitch RMS + 0.3 x height RMSE in cm) from 9.74 to 6.29.

**Method problem.** How do we train event-output controllers on a simulator that is non-differentiable and expensive (an 8 s episode costs 45 CPU-s)?
- NEAT finds the right structure but cannot tune the gains. In v1 its spikes were phase-locked (resultant length 0.90, mean 338 deg against an optimum of 315 deg) and 85% need-gated, yet J was 8.17 against 6.29, and it learned only one direction.
- Surrogate gradients tune well when the loss is differentiable (phase estimation: 2.4 deg against 9.3 deg for NEAT), but the simulator gives no gradient.

**The bridge.** One twitch is a large, repeatable and nearly linear event.
- A 0.1 s burst of 180 deg windows at 135 deg adds +3.3 rad/s of pitch rate and +0.13 m/s of climb. At 315 deg the pitch effect flips sign; the climb effect does not.
- So the plant's response to a spike can be identified once as kernels h_theta(phi,tau) and h_z(phi,tau), with a low-order Fourier basis in the crank phase phi.
- On every real rollout, the hindsight credit of a spike is g(t) = dJ/ds(t) = sum_tau [e_theta(t+tau)*h_theta(phi_t,tau)]/(N*RMS_theta) + 30*sum_tau [z(t+tau)*h_z(phi_t,tau)]/(N*RMS_z).
- This credit is backpropagated through a float64 torch twin of the SNN, re-simulated on the recorded inputs.

**Why it matters.**
- For this robot, it is the route to SNN controllers that can actually compete with the tuned classical law.
- More generally, event actuators (pulsed thrusters, motor twitches, impulsive control) on non-differentiable simulators are where SNNs fit naturally, yet there is no good training method for them.

**If the gate says GO, the paper contains:**
- a kernel-fidelity study;
- a comparison at equal total budgets of: NEAT-only, KCSG-only, Lamarckian and Baldwinian NEAT+KCSG, GRU+KCSG, and the classical law (grid, CMA-ES, and the same KCSG optimizer);
- what NEAT adds: evolved, zero or gradient-learned delays; evolved twitch length and hold-off; a PLL-free variant where raw gyro taps with evolved delays act as phase shifters;
- 5 seeds, a 32-case test, and stress2x plus randomized-onset disturbances as new test scenarios.
topic.why_snn:
**Structural reasons (not energy):**

1. **The output is a spike train.** Inside this interface the best actuation is not a continuous command but a sparse train of one-sided, all-or-none, phase-locked motor twitches (lesson 5):
   - one-sided full-range pulses give 4.1x the gimbal authority, sinusoids 2.7x;
   - downward pulses give at most 0.7x, because the lower bound is only about 63 rad/s below the hover command.

   The control information is in spike timing relative to the wingbeat, not in amplitude: a twitch at 135 deg pitches up, at 315 deg pitches down, and both add lift. A LIF neuron's threshold and reset make it an event-triggered controller by construction, and the twitch occupancy acts as a refractory period.
2. **Delays give phase selectivity.** With synaptic delays, LIF units are coincidence detectors on the periodic sensory stream. A delay is a phase shifter (1 ms is about 9 deg at 25 Hz), so phase selectivity and need-gating are the computation of one neuron.
3. **The training method is spike-native.** Each output spike has an identified plant kernel, so the plant becomes one more synaptic layer of a spike-response model. Each spike's credit is the error correlated with its kernel, exact to first order, on real (not imagined) trajectories.

**Honest limits:**
- Energy is not used as a motivation.
- An event-ANN or GRU with a thresholded output can represent the same policy. It gets the identical credit as baseline arm C.
- Parity between SNN and ANN is expected (lesson 2). The SNN claim is therefore about representational fit and the method, not raw performance, unless arm C is measurably worse.
topic.why_neat:
NEAT is used only for what gradients cannot do here, and is relieved of what it is bad at: fine weight tuning (lesson 2).

1. **The timing decisions are discrete.** The variables that decide when a twitch lands are:
   - integer synaptic delays of 0–20 ms, i.e. 0–180 deg of wingbeat;
   - which phase cells or IMU channels connect to which motor neuron;
   - the number of motor neurons;
   - in the full study, event-rule genes: twitch length (1–5 ticks) and hold-off, and delay taps that replace the PLL.

   Surrogate gradients give no signal for integer delays or Heaviside event rules, and phase alignment on a periodic signal is multimodal.
2. **NEAT has already shown it finds this structure.** From closed-loop fitness alone, v1 found phase-locked, need-gated firing near the optimal phase (338 deg against 315 deg). It failed only at the gains.
3. **Selection sees cliffs that a first-order credit cannot.** Aggressive pulsing ends in height escape (the classical law with threshold 0.2 flew 0/8). In the Lamarckian loop, selection guards the gradient.

**Division of labour.** Evolution decides where and when; the gradient decides how much. Trained weights are written back to the genome (Lamarckian); Baldwinian inheritance is an ablation.

**Caveat.** v3 measured a topology-evolution effect of about zero. The gate's criterion P3 tests directly whether a NEAT-evolved structure beats a dense random-delay network under the same gradient. If it does not, we report that NEAT is not central.
topic.interface_check:
- **Sensors.** The controller reads only `env.last_reading`: the 11-D reading at 500 Hz, including the case's delay_steps.
  - Its 12 inputs are those of `spike_steer/pilot.py`: 8 one-hot phase cells from the existing WingbeatPhase PLL on gyro y (reading[4], P0 offset), plus the rectified AHRS pitch reading[1]/0.1 and the rectified adaptive-notch rate `estimator.slow`.
  - The range finder is used only inside the unchanged PID height loop. No sensor is added.
- **Actuators.**
  - The retuned TeacherPID (kp x1.5) computes all three commands every 2 ms.
  - A spike only sets `cmd[2] = HIGH[2] = 3807.5 rad/s` for 3 ticks (6 ms).
  - The command then passes, unchanged, through ResearchEnv direct mode: the clip to [LOW, HIGH], motor_gain, the 8.2 ms first-order smoothing, the servo (kp 1.045 N.m/rad, 0.02 N.m limit) and the motor speed loop (4.2 V, 6 A).
  - Gimbal commands are untouched.
  - There is no sub-tick actuation. The C++ phase drive in `wingbeat_snn/plant.py` is NOT used.
- **Rates.** Decisions are made once per 2 ms tick. The SNN's two internal 1 ms substeps are computation, not actuation.
- **Privileged signals.** The true crank angle, the de-rocked true pitch (`gates.Oracle`) and the true height appear only in three places: the objective, the training credit, and the kernel-identification runs. They never reach the deployed controller. Identification twitches are ordinary in-range commands.
- **Scenarios.** The v3 stress cases are used unchanged: 6 mN, 8 uN.m, 200 ms every 2 s, random signs. In the full study, randomized-onset disturbances are added as new test scenarios, which the rules allow.
topic.classical_baseline:
**Same information.** The 12 SNN inputs are computed from exactly the signals the classical IMU-only pulse law uses: PLL phase from gyro y, the adaptive-notch pitch rate, and the 0.13 s-lagged AHRS pitch.

**The law.** u = -(k_theta*theta_AHRS + k_q*q_notch). While |u| > u0, the motor command goes to HIGH inside a window w centred on psi = 135 deg (u > 0) or psi + 180 deg (u < 0). An optional variant also sheds lift ("dip"). It runs on the same retuned PID (kp x1.5).

**Tuning plan:**
- **Grid:** v2's 108-point grid (k_theta in {3, 5, 8}, k_q in {0.2, 0.4, 0.8}, u0 in {0.4, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8}, w in {45, 60, 90} deg) on 8 direction-balanced cases, 864 episodes.
- **CMA-ES:** with `cmaes` 0.11.1 (installed), over (k_theta, k_q, u0, w, psi), starting from the grid best, 720 episodes. This equals the budget of each gradient arm.
- Both are selected on the same validation cases, and the better one is the reference.
- The retuned PID (kp x1.5) is reported as well.

**Full study:**
- equal TOTAL budgets, counting NEAT's episodes;
- a same-optimizer control: the law's parameters trained with the identical kernel credit through a sigmoid relaxation;
- an augmented law (hold-off, height-aware threshold u0 + c_z*z) whenever the SNN is given extra inputs.

gate.what:
The gate runs after v2 finishes. It needs `runs/spike_steer/pilot_v2_s1/best_policy.json` and `artifacts/spike_steer/v2/law_tuned.json`. Every controller sits on the retuned PID (kp x1.5) and runs with 18 workers.

**Step 1: kernel identification and fidelity (about 0.1 h).**
- Paired runs, same seed with and without a twitch, as in `timing.py`.
- 6 balanced training stress cases. One 3-tick twitch is forced at the first tick after t0 (3.0 or 3.6 s, separate episodes) whose true crank angle falls in each of 8 45-degree bins.
- That is 96 twitch runs plus 6 baselines, each run to t0 + 1.5 s.
- Fit two kernels by least squares, with a Fourier basis up to the 2nd harmonic in the crank phase: h_theta (de-rocked true pitch, tau up to 0.8 s) and h_z (true height, tau up to 1.5 s).
- **Fidelity check (a):** leave-one-case-out prediction of the local change in J (DeltaJ) for held-out single twitches.
- **Fidelity check (b):** on 8 held-out cases, replay open-loop on the PID-only flight the twitch trains recorded from the v2 champion and from the tuned law. Compare the predicted sum of kernel responses with the actual change.

**Step 2: four arms, 40 iterations x 18 direction-balanced 6 s cases = 720 episodes each (about 0.45 h each).**
- **A:** v2 NEAT champion + KCSG. Topology and delays are frozen. Zero-weight candidate edges complete the input-to-hidden-to-output pattern, so the gradient can grow a missing direction.
- **B:** dense 12-6-2 random-delay SNN from `pilot.initialize`, no evolution, + KCSG.
- **C:** GRU with 16 units and Heaviside event outputs (sigmoid straight-through) + KCSG.
- **D:** classical law tuned by CMA-ES from the grid best.
- **Each KCSG iteration:**
  - roll out;
  - record per tick: the inputs, a free-tick mask (no twitch running), the true crank angle, the de-rocked pitch and the height;
  - compute the credit g(t) from the kernels;
  - re-simulate the network in a float64 torch twin on the recorded inputs, with loss = sum of g(t)*s(t);
  - take an Adam step on weights and biases.
- Validate on 8 balanced cases every 10 iterations and keep the best. On a crash or regression, revert and halve the learning rate.

**Step 3: shared test (about 0.1 h).** v2's 16 test cases, 8 s each, with: PID retuned, law (grid), law (CMA), NEAT v2 champion, A, B and C.
gate.metric:
**Main metric.** J = pitch RMS (deg, de-rocked truth, t >= 2 s) + 0.3 x height RMSE (cm), on the shared 16-case test. Report:
- flown count;
- paired per-case differences against each reference.

**Diagnostics:**
- **Kernel fidelity:** R^2 of predicted versus actual change in pitch and in height on the replayed trains; for single twitches, sign agreement and Spearman rho between predicted and actual local DeltaJ.
- **Spike phase by need:** spike-phase histograms split by the sign of the true need, with the share within +-67.5 deg of 135 and 315 deg.
- **Learning curves:** validation J against episodes for every arm.
gate.pass_criterion:
**GO only if all four hold.**

- **P0 (the gradient source is valid):** replay R^2 >= 0.6 for the change in pitch and >= 0.5 for the change in height; single-twitch DeltaJ sign agreement >= 75% with Spearman >= 0.6. If P0 fails, stop after 0.1 h: NO-GO.
- **P1 (the gradient fixes NEAT's fine-tuning):** A flies 16/16 and J_A <= 0.95 x J of the NEAT v2 champion. The gain must also exceed what NEAT itself gained over its last ~720 episodes in the v2 history.
- **P2 (A beats the classical law with the same information):** J_A <= min(J law grid, J law CMA), with at least 10/16 paired wins. Both directions must be learned: at least 20 onsets each for need-up and need-down, and at least 70% within +-67.5 deg of 135 and 315 deg.
- **P3 (NEAT is central):** J_A <= 0.95 x J_B, or B fails to fly 16/16, or B fails to learn both directions.

**How to read other outcomes:**
- **P0–P2 pass but P3 fails:** the gradient, not NEAT, does the work. Report it; this is NO-GO for a NEAT-centred paper.
- **A is within 5% above the law:** borderline. Allow one 20-iteration extension within the 3 h cap, then decide.
- **C within 5% of A:** expected. It does not block GO, but the SNN claim then rests only on representational fit.
gate.code_reuse:
**Reused, under /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/:**
- `experiments/algorithms/spike_steer/pilot.py`: `run` loop, `Steer`, `SpikingGraph`, `features`, `balanced_cases`, `cases('test')`, `initialize`/`export` (arm B), `pool`/`task`, `summarize`, `test`.
- `experiments/algorithms/neuro_gates/gates.py`: `Oracle('derocked')`, `HANDOVER_T`.
- `experiments/algorithms/neuro_gates/timing.py`: the paired with/without methodology and `PULSE_PHASE`.
- `experiments/algorithms/wingbeat_feasibility/preliminary.py`: `WingbeatPhase` (PLL plus notch).
- `experiments/algorithms/wingbeat_snn/networks.py`: `Graph` semantics (delays, two 1 ms substeps, subtractive reset).
- `experiments/algorithms/wingbeat_snn/phase_train.py`: `TorchSNN` and the `Spike` surrogate as the template for the torch twin; `GRUPhase` and `TorchStep` for arm C.
- `tests/test_wingbeat_snn.py::test_torch_snn_exports_to_identical_numpy_graph`: template for the bitwise test between the torch twin and numpy.
- `experiments/algorithms/wingbeat_snn/evolve.py`: `DelayGenome`, for the full study's NEAT outer loop.
- `torch` 2.6.0 and `cmaes` 0.11.1 are already installed.

**New code:** one module of about 400–500 lines containing:
- a forced-twitch `Steer` and a rollout recorder;
- the kernel fit and the credit computation;
- the float64 torch twin with delays and spiking outputs;
- the KCSG loop, the CMA-ES arm, and an extended shared test.

risks: Kernel superposition may fail at realistic twitch densities. The height PID sits only about 63 rad/s above the lower bound and saturates under frequent twitches. Overlapping twitches interact through the 8.2 ms smoothing and the 6 A / 4.2 V motor limits, and twitches shift the crank phase. The credit would then under-count the height cost and drive over-firing. P0 measures this within 0.1 h.

The first-order credit ignores the policy's own reaction to its spikes and cannot see crash cliffs, so training may oscillate or step off a cliff. Mitigations: validation-gated steps with revert and learning-rate halving; in the full method, NEAT selection.

Headroom may be small. With the same information, the tuned law may already sit near the best attainable pitch–height trade-off: J is flat, about 5.8–6.8 across the better half of the earlier grid. The hybrid may only match the law, which makes a weak paper.

NEAT may not be needed (lesson 2): arm B, a dense random-delay SNN with the kernel credit, may match NEAT plus the kernel credit. The result would then be a gradient method for event SNNs, not a NEAT paper (criterion P3).
Parity between the SNN and the GRU is likely. The SNN case would then rest on representational fit and the spike-native credit, not on performance.

The gate's budgets are asymmetric. A inherits about 3200 NEAT episodes; B, C and the CMA-ES law get 720 each (the law also had the 864-episode grid). The gate is a feasibility test, and the full study must equalize total budgets.
With a single seed and 16 test cases, differences below about 5% are not conclusive; paired wins are reported.

The training signals are privileged: true crank, de-rocked pitch and true height. That is legitimate in simulation, but on hardware, identifying the kernels would need an encoder or motion capture. This sim-to-real gap must be stated.

Implementation risk: the float64 torch twin must reproduce the numpy SpikingGraph spikes exactly (delays, spiking outputs, two substeps, twitch occupancy), otherwise credit attaches to the wrong spikes. A bitwise test is required.
The gate needs v2's outputs and an idle machine (load is about 18 now). It cannot start until v2's training, law tuning and test have finished.
topic.lessons_addressed:
1. **Same-budget classical.** The classical law uses the same information. It is tuned by grid (864 episodes) and by CMA-ES (720 episodes, the same as each gradient arm). It is tested on the same 16 paired cases, alongside the retuned PID. The full study equalizes total budgets and adds a same-optimizer law.

2. **SNN about equal to ANN, topology effect about zero, NEAT weak at weights, energy invalid.**
   - The weights are tuned by gradient, not by NEAT; NEAT handles only discrete timing structure.
   - Criterion P3 tests NEAT's contribution against a dense random-delay network trained with the same gradient.
   - Arm C tests SNN against GRU with the same credit.
   - Energy is never invoked.

3. **Two-body inverse response.** The gimbal PID and its slow 0.13 s attitude are untouched, and nothing faster is fed to the gimbal. The effects of twitches, including the two-body ringing, are measured empirically in the kernels.

4. **Little room for in-flight adaptation.** No online plasticity or adaptation is claimed; all learning is offline.

5. **The timing channel and its lift cost.** The method is built on that channel. The kernels are its impulse responses, and the credit carries both the pitch benefit and the height cost of every twitch.

6. **v1 learned only one direction.**
   - The credit is negative at 135-degree ticks whenever pitch-up is needed, so the missing direction gets an explicit gradient.
   - Zero-weight candidate edges let that direction grow.
   - v2's balanced batches and two motor neurons are kept, and P2 checks both directions.

fatal_issues: Most of the J headroom comes from height-loop saturation, not from steering. I recomputed the per-case v1 test results (artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json) and replayed the case RNG to get each case's motor gain. In the 4 cases with motor gain >= 1.0108 (seeds 2020100004/06/07/10), law_strong's height RMSE is 17.2/22.2/38.0/14.7 cm against 10.7/10.9/18.2/10.1 cm for the PID. In the 10 cases with gain <= 1.005, the law costs at most 0.6 cm of height. The four high-gain cases average J 10.0 against 5.04 for the other twelve, so they carry 40% of the law's total J. Lesson 5's 'lift cost' is therefore the downward margin running out: about 3178/g - 3115 rad/s, which is only 16-29 rad/s in those cases. Three consequences follow. (a) An h_z kernel indexed by phase and fitted from single twitches on 6 random cases cannot represent a response that depends on the case, saturates and accumulates, so P0(b) height R^2 >= 0.5 is likely to fail; where it passes, the credit misprices exactly the cases that dominate J. (b) None of the SNN's 12 inputs carries height, vertical-speed or command information, so it cannot learn the one change that matters: fire less when the margin is gone. (c) A classical law gated by the PID's own motor-command margin, or by range-finder z (both inside the interface), is a one-parameter fix. I estimate it brings the law's test J from 6.29 to about 5.3-5.5.

Information is not the bottleneck, so a classical controller with the same information already sits near the attainable J. On the same 8 tuning cases, the law fed with oracle state and true crank phase scores J 6.32, worse than the IMU-only law's 5.80. Across the whole oracle grid, the better half spans 5.96-6.8. A richer policy class (SNN or GRU) has no identified physical lever beyond the law. The expected outcome repeats lesson 1: parity at best against a 4-5 parameter law tuned by grid plus CMA-ES. Against a margin-aware law it is a likely loss.

The gate is biased toward GO on P1 and P3, so it cannot show what the paper claims. In P3, A inherits about 3200 NEAT episodes plus a tuned champion, while B gets 720 KCSG episodes from scratch. P3 also passes if 'B fails to learn both directions', which is likely after only 40 steps from a random start. P3 can therefore pass for budget reasons alone, while lesson 2 predicts B ≈ A at equal budget. In P1, the comparator is NEAT itself, which is already known to be weak at weights, not a same-budget black-box tuner of the same weights (CMA-ES or ES on the champion's weights and biases). P1 cannot attribute a gain to KCSG. The method in the title, Lamarckian NEAT+KCSG, is not tested by the gate at all.
fixes: Model the height channel honestly. Condition h_z (and ideally h_theta) on the PID's downward margin at the twitch, cmd_PID[2]-LOW[2], which is a signal inside the controller and inside the interface; or stratify by motor gain. Report J and P0 separately for gain <= 1.005 and gain > 1.005.

At the gate, add to arm D a margin- or height-aware law: suppress pulses when cmd_PID[2]-LOW[2] < m0, or use the threshold u0 + c_z*z. If the law gets that input, give the SNN the same one (the margin or z). Otherwise the comparison is decided by a lever the SNN cannot see.

Make P3 budget-fair. Either give B the same total budget as A (about 3920 episodes), or compare A with A-shuffled (same champion, delays and topology randomized, same KCSG budget). Remove the one-sided 'B fails to learn both directions' clause, or apply it to A as well.

Add arm A_ES: CMA-ES or OpenAI-ES on the v2 champion's weights and biases with 720 episodes and common random numbers. Add 'NEAT continued for 720 episodes from the v2 population', tested on the same 16 cases, as P1's comparator. The noisy 8-case validation history should not serve as that comparator.

Use a finite-difference (midpoint) credit for binary events instead of the derivative at the realized trajectory, i.e. remove (s-1/2)*sum(h^2)/(N*RMS). Twitches are large: a 0.1 s burst moves pitch 11.9 deg, so one twitch moves it about 1 deg. The self-term is then a sizeable share of the signal, and it biases the gradient toward over-firing, which is exactly the height cliff. In P0(a), compare actual DeltaJ with J(e0+h_hat)-J(e0), not with the first-order formula.

Identify the kernels where the law actually fires. Use onsets sampled during and just after the gust (2.6-3.2 s and 4.6-5.2 s), including twitches while the 6 mN / 8 uN.m pulse is acting, not only at t0 = 3.0 and 3.6 s.

In the KCSG loop, use common or paired cases to accept or reject steps, or reuse a fixed case set ILC-style with separate validation. With fresh cases every iteration, the per-case J SD of about 2.6 (mostly from motor gain) makes 'regression' on training batches pure noise. Balance batches by motor gain as well as by pulse sign.

Budget realistically. The torch twin (arbitrary NEAT graph, per-edge delays, spiking outputs ORed over 2 substeps and 2 neurons, twitch occupancy, handover mask) is new code: the existing TorchSNN is dense, has zero delays and non-spiking outputs, and its test covers zero delays only. Expect about 700-1000 lines plus an equivalence test that includes delays. Run arms interleaved so the 18 workers stay busy; at about 45 s per 18-case iteration plus twin time, the gate takes about 2.2 h.

Cost the full study before committing: Lamarckian and Baldwinian NEAT+KCSG, 5 seeds, about 10 arms, delay ablations, 32-case tests and stress2x. If the inner KCSG step does not reuse the evaluation rollouts, the cost per generation multiplies by roughly 10-20x.
critiques.reasoning:
**Conclusion: weak (3/10).** The topic stays inside the original interface and the gate is affordable, but the problem it targets is mostly a height-saturation artifact. The kernel credit cannot model that artifact, the SNN cannot observe it, and a one-parameter classical gate can fix it. The gate's P1 and P3 are also biased toward GO.

**Checks that pass**

- **Interface.** `pilot.run` only overwrites `cmd[2]` with `HIGH[2]`. The command then goes through the unchanged path: direct-mode clip, `motor_gain`, the 8.2 ms smoothing in `core.advance`, and the motor speed loop. Privileged truth (true crank, de-rocked pitch, true height) is used only in the objective, the training credit and the identification runs. Training on privileged signals in simulation matches v1/v2 practice.
- **Affordability.**
  - Step 1 is about 102 short runs (about 5 min) plus the P0(b) replays (about 2 min).
  - Each arm is 40 iterations of 18 six-second episodes, about 30 min with twin time, so about 2 h for four arms.
  - Step 3 is 112 episodes (about 5 min).
  - The total, about 2.2 h, fits the 2.5 h claim.
  - cmaes 0.11.1, torch 2.6.0 and neat-python 2.0.0 are installed in the mujoco env.
  - v2 is at generation 8 of 25 (validation J 8.59 at generation 3, 9.39 at generation 7) and should finish around 02:45 including tune_law and test.
- **Code reuse** is real for `run`, `Steer`, `cases`, `Oracle`, the PLL, `Graph` and `DelayGenome`. The torch twin is new work, though: `phase_train.TorchSNN` is dense, has zero delays and non-spiking tanh outputs, and the existing equivalence test covers zero delays only.

**Main finding: the J headroom is height-loop saturation**

I recomputed per-case results from `artifacts/spike_steer/v1/pilot_test.json` and replayed each case's RNG (`SeedSequence([seed, 981])`) to get its motor gain.

- **Where the height cost comes from.** In the 4 cases with gain 1.0108-1.0148, the law's height RMSE is 14.7-38.0 cm. In the 10 cases with gain <= 1.005, the law costs at most 0.6 cm of height relative to the PID. The four high-gain cases average J 10.0 against 5.04 for the other twelve, so they carry 40% of the law's total J.
- **Why.** `command[2]` is clipped at LOW before it is multiplied by the motor gain. The downward margin is therefore about 3178/g - 3115, which is 16-29 rad/s in those cases. The 'pitch-height trade-off' of lesson 5 is this saturation, not a smooth physical trade-off.
- **Consequence for the kernel credit.** A phase-indexed h_z kernel cannot predict an accumulating, saturating response that depends on the case, so P0(b) height is likely to fail.
- **Consequence for the SNN.** None of its 12 inputs carries height, vertical-speed or command information, so it cannot learn to fire less when the margin is gone.
- **Consequence for the classical baseline.** A law gated by the PID's own command margin, or by range-finder z, is a trivial fix inside the interface.
- **Information is not the bottleneck either.** On the same 8 tuning cases (`timing_imu_law.json`), the oracle-information law scores J 6.32, worse than the IMU-only law's 5.80, and the oracle grid's better half spans 5.96-6.8. This repeats lesson 1: expect parity with the law at best.

**v1's gap was mostly one missing direction**

The v1 SNN matched the law's pitch (3.1-4.1 deg) in the 8 cases with x-force sign -1 and failed (5.5-6.4 deg) in the 8 with sign +1. v2's balanced batches target exactly this. In its good direction the SNN's J was 7.46 against the law's 6.53, and most of that gap is extra height in the high-gain cases.

**Gate design problems**

- **P3** is confounded. A carries about 3200 extra NEAT episodes plus a tuned start, and P3 has a one-sided 'B fails both directions' escape clause. P3 can therefore pass without NEAT mattering, while lesson 2 predicts B ≈ A at equal budget.
- **P1** has no same-budget black-box weight tuner as a comparator, so a gain cannot be credited to KCSG.
- **Credit bias.** The first-order derivative credit for binary spikes overprices fired spikes and underprices unfired ticks by half the self-term. Twitches are large, so this pushes the gradient toward over-firing, which leads to the height cliff.
- **Identification coverage.** Kernels are identified at 3.0 and 3.6 s, while the gust acts at 2.6-2.8 and 4.6-4.8 s, which is when the law mostly fires.
- **Noisy step acceptance.** Fresh cases every iteration, with a per-case J SD of about 2.6, make the 'revert on regression' rule noise-driven.
- **Title method untested.** The gate does not test the Lamarckian loop named in the title.

**Not refuted** because the proposal violates no interface rule, the gate is cheap and is designed to stop early at P0, and the fixes listed are concrete.

**Key files** (all under `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\home\robot\FlapSim-repo\FlapSim\`):
- `artifacts\spike_steer\v1\pilot_test.json`
- `artifacts\neuro_gates\timing_imu_law.json`
- `artifacts\neuro_gates\timing_law_grid.json`
- `artifacts\neuro_gates\timing_authority.json`
- `experiments\algorithms\snn_pid_compare\environment.py` (clip before `motor_gain`; gust at t%2 in [0.6, 0.8))
- `experiments\algorithms\topology_hover\environment.py` (motor-gain draw; `height_rmse_m` computed over the whole episode)
- `experiments\algorithms\wingbeat_snn\phase_train.py` (TorchSNN: dense, zero delays, non-spiking outputs)
- `runs\spike_steer\pilot_v2_s1\history.jsonl`

fatal_issues: SNN is not central, and the proposal itself concedes this. Arm C (a GRU with Heaviside outputs) gets the identical credit and parity is 'expected'. The 'spike' is a hand-made output wrapper (any threshold crossing becomes a 6 ms twitch), so any thresholded unit, or the 4-5 parameter classical law, produces the same twitch train. KCSG is not spike-specific either: the full study plans to train the law with it. Energy is excluded. The project's own data already show a GRU >= the gradient SNN: phase RMS 0.8 vs 2.4 deg, and equal in closed loop (docs/wingbeat_paper/HANDOFF.md lines 57-60). 'Representational fit' alone will be read as incidental.

NEAT is not central, and P3 cannot show that it is. (a) The v1 'NEAT champion' (artifacts/spike_steer/v1/best_policy.json) is the dense 12-6-1 random-delay initializer (pilot.py initialize, lines 218-239; delays drawn from 0-8 ms) after GA weight and delay noise. NEAT changed little: +1 hidden node, +4 edges (two from the node split), 14 edges disabled, 68 of 82 enabled. It acted as a weight/delay GA, not a structure finder. (b) Arm A adds zero-weight candidate edges, so A is dense too; A and B then differ only in delay values and pre-training. (c) The inputs are one-hot 45-degree PLL phase cells and actuation is quantized to 2 ms ticks (about 18 deg), so delays (about 9 deg per ms) are largely redundant with readout weights over the phase cells. (d) Exact gradients for delays exist (Meszaros, Knight and Nowotny, Nat. Commun. 2025, including recurrent delays; DelGrad; DCLS), so 'gradients give no signal for delays' is outdated. (e) The 'selection guards cliffs' role is duplicated by the KCSG loop's own validation-gated revert. (f) P3 compares A (warm-started from about 3200 NEAT episodes, plus 720) with B (720 from scratch), so a pass measures pre-training budget, not structure. (g) The prior lesson is that the topology-evolution effect is about 0.

The method's novelty is incremental, and the stated defence against the expected objection fails. Back-propagating cost through identified model Jacobians along REAL rather than imagined trajectories is the defining feature of SVG(inf)/SVG(1) (Heess et al., NeurIPS 2015). KCSG is that action-to-cost term with the state-to-policy path dropped: the recorded inputs are frozen, so the gradient ignores weights -> spike -> plant -> IMU -> later spikes, which biases it for a feedback policy. Iterative Feedback Tuning (Hjalmarsson) is the established fix for 'ILC lifted to feedback-controller parameters'. Every other component is also prior art: phase-indexed impulse responses (LTP / harmonic transfer functions; flapping-MAV LTP identification by Passaro & Lovera and Hayajnh et al. 2024; phase-response-curve, phase-locked stimulation by Cagnan et al.); SNN controllers whose control is set by output spike timing, with weights updated from plant derivatives (Kang & Banerjee 2017, arXiv 1708.02603, which the proposal cites only for its forward kernel); evolution plus gradients with Lamarckian write-back for control (ERL, CEM-RL); and evolving structure while training weights by gradient (CoDeepNEAT, SNN-NAS such as AutoSNN). Only the specific combination is new.

If the classical law matches, nothing about SNN or NEAT remains publishable, and matching is the likely outcome. The law already has the right structure (phase window AND |need| > u0) with 4-5 parameters. The SNN sees a coarsened copy of the law's inputs (8 x 45-degree cells instead of continuous phase), plus memory. gates_report section 4b shows that perfect state plus perfect phase did not improve J: the oracle law reached 2.4 deg / 13.2 cm (J about 6.36) and 3.3 deg / 10.1 cm (J about 6.33), against 3.0 deg / 9.4 cm (J about 5.82) for the IMU-only law, which Pareto-dominates the second oracle point. The frontier is therefore set by lift per twitch (both pulse phases add lift; the floor is about 63 rad/s below hover), not by information. A learned controller with the same lever and no height input can only move along that frontier. J is flat (5.8-6.8). Per-case J is driven by 3-4 height-escape cases: in v1 law_strong, case 2020100007 has a 38 cm height RMSE and J 14.1, and four cases supply about 40% of total J. With 16 cases and 1 seed, differences of 5% or less are noise, and 10/16 paired wins has p of about 0.23.

The project's own record on this line predicts the same result. P1: the learned residual matched the tuned law but had 1.8-7.2 deg larger peaks. H5: the learned network was equivalent to the robust-tuned law. The NEAT SNN phase estimator reached 9.3 deg, worse than the tuned PLL at 4.7 deg. v1 learned only one direction. The paper outline already lists NEAT as a negative result (C3).

Any methods claim lacks the baselines that decide it. There is no black-box optimizer on the same SNN weights (CMA-ES or OpenAI-ES at 720 episodes) and no REINFORCE/PPO with Bernoulli spike outputs, which is the textbook trainer for event policies on non-differentiable simulators (SNN-RL examples include Van den Berghe et al., NeurIPS 2025). The KCSG-trained law is deferred to the full study. The premise 'there is no good training method' is overstated.
fixes: Add a cheap headroom gate (about 0.2 h) before any KCSG work. CMA-tune both the oracle law (de-rocked truth plus true crank phase) and the IMU law, and plot pitch-RMS against height-RMSE Pareto fronts. If the oracle front does not beat the IMU front by a pre-registered margin (for example 10% or more in J at height weights 0.15, 0.3 and 0.6), stop: no learned controller with the same lever can win.

If continuing, give the policy a lever that targets the binding constraint, the lift cost, while staying inside the interface: 'dip' events that command LOW, and/or range-finder height and vertical-speed inputs (existing sensors). Give the augmented law exactly the same signals. Otherwise drop the performance claim.

Make P3 a real test. Equalize total episodes: either B gets about 3900 KCSG episodes, or A's weights are re-initialized on its NEAT structure. Add arms 'dense + gradient-learned delays (EventProp or DCLS style)' and 'dense + zero delays', and run at least 3 seeds and 32 test cases. Call NEAT central only if A beats every arm at equal budget by at least 5% with a sign test p < 0.05.

Move into the gate itself: CMA-ES or ES on the same SNN weights; REINFORCE/PPO with Bernoulli spike outputs; and the classical law trained by KCSG, all at equal budget. Together these decide whether KCSG contributes anything beyond black-box tuning.

Add to P0 a direct gradient-validity check: the cosine between the KCSG gradient and paired finite-difference or SPSA closed-loop gradients along a few weight directions, because KCSG drops the policy's feedback path. Consider an IFT-style correction.
Replace the single J = pitch + 0.3 x height with Pareto fronts or hypervolume, plus J at several weights. Report per-case results separately for height-escape and non-escape cases.

Reposition honestly. Either (a) a methods paper on phase-indexed impulse-response credit for event-actuated control, with the SNN as one policy class next to the GRU and the law, positioned against SVG(inf), IFT/ILC, phase-response-curve phase-locked stimulation, LTP identification and Kang & Banerjee 2017; or (b) fold this into the existing paper's C3 negative result. Use the blowfly b1 steering motor neuron (one phase-locked spike per wingbeat whose phase shift steers) as motivation for spike-timed control, not as evidence that the SNN is central.

If SNN centrality is the goal, the only place where delay-LIF coincidence detection does real computation is the PLL-free front end (raw gyro taps). It must be in the gate, trained by gradient (NEAT already failed at 9.3 deg) and compared with a GRU at equal budget. Prior data (GRU 0.8 deg vs SNN 2.4 deg) predict it will not beat the GRU, so pre-register that outcome.
critiques.reasoning:
VERDICT: refuted under the novelty and centrality lens. Neither of the topic's two named pillars is central: the proposal concedes SNN parity, and the evidence against NEAT is strong while the planned test of NEAT is confounded. The method is a combination of known pieces, and the defence the proposal prepares against the 'SVG' objection is SVG's own defining feature. If the tuned law matches, which the measured physics suggests it will, no SNN or NEAT claim survives. What remains publishable is a methods note on KCSG with the SNN incidental, or a negative result.

NOVELTY. Quick searches found no exact match for 'identified phase-indexed twitch kernels used as a differentiable layer, plus NEAT-evolved delays, for wingbeat-locked twitch control', but every component exists:
1. **Real-trajectory gradients.** SVG(inf)/SVG(1) (Heess et al. 2015) back-propagate through model Jacobians along observed trajectories specifically to limit model exploitation. KCSG is the action-to-cost term of that idea with the observation path frozen.
2. **Closed-loop tuning.** Iterative Feedback Tuning already handles 'ILC for feedback-controller parameters' and estimates the closed-loop gradient correctly. KCSG's frozen-input gradient is biased for a feedback policy.
3. **Phase-indexed impulse responses.** These are LTP models, harmonic transfer functions or phase response curves (flapping-MAV LTP identification; Cagnan et al.'s phase-locked stimulation).
4. **Spike-timed SNN control.** Kang & Banerjee 2017 control with output spike timing and update weights from plant derivatives with respect to control.
5. **Evolution plus gradients.** ERL and CEM-RL combine them with Lamarckian write-back for control; CoDeepNEAT and SNN-NAS evolve structure while gradients train weights.
6. **Delays.** tau-NEAT evolves them; DCLS, DelGrad and Meszaros/Knight/Nowotny (Nat. Commun. 2025) give exact gradients for them.

The proposal's novelty notes miss SVG, IFT, ERL/CEM-RL and the 2025 delay-gradient work. The physical channel (intra-stroke speed asymmetry, split-cycle) is also prior art; only the 'inside the v3 interface' framing is new.

SNN CENTRALITY. A GRU or event-ANN trained with the same credit represents the same policy, and the classical law is already an event-triggered, phase-locked pulse controller. With one-hot PLL phase cells as inputs, the SNN's 'computation' is a two-input AND: phase cell and need above threshold. Delays as phase shifters are redundant with weights over the cells, given the 18-degree actuation quantization. Project data: GRU >= SNN for phase estimation, and equal in closed loop.

NEAT CENTRALITY. The v1 champion is essentially pilot.initialize's dense random-delay network after GA weight and delay noise (+1 node, +4 edges, 14 disabled). Arm A is then densified with zero-weight edges. P3 compares a warm-started A (about 3900 total episodes) with a cold B (720 episodes), so even a pass would not isolate structure. The 'cliff guard' role is already provided by the validation-gated revert, and the v3 topology effect was about 0.

PUBLISHABILITY IF THE BASELINE MATCHES. The law has the optimal structure with 4-5 parameters. In gates_report section 4b, perfect state plus perfect phase did not lower J (oracle 6.36 and 6.33 against 5.82 for the IMU law), and the IMU law Pareto-dominates one oracle point. The pitch-height frontier is therefore fixed by the lift added per twitch, not by information. The SNN has no height input and no lift-shedding lever, so it can only move along that frontier. A match is the most likely outcome, and at that point the paper says only that a complex method reproduces a grid-tuned 4-parameter law. With 16 cases, 1 seed and per-case J dominated by 3-4 height escapes, the P2 criterion (J at most the law's, 10/16 wins; p about 0.23) cannot separate the two.

CREDIT. The gate is cheap (2.5 h), has an early exit at P0, and pre-states its own NEAT-negative outcome. That design is good, but under this lens the topic as framed (Lamarckian NEAT plus kernel surrogate gradients for SNNs) does not hold.

ranking.title: Spiking righting reflexes: NEAT-evolved event sequencers for large-upset recovery of the single-motor flapping robot
ranking.summary:
(behavior; critics 3/3) Best of a weak set. Its premise, large upsets, does not depend on the motor-gain headroom confound that undercuts every timing-channel topic. In a large upset the PID's 0.13 s-lagged D term saturates 35-115 ms in, and the range finder is blind above 45.6 deg. Stage A is purely classical: retuned PID, PID+pulse law, gain-scheduled PID, one-shot reflex, and a CEM-tuned multi-phase automaton. Whatever it finds answers the plant question left open in gates_report section 5.6. This is also the only topic where NEAT's structural search has a plausible job: sequencing and arbitration across axes, directions and double hits.

The SNN half fails as proposed, for four reasons:
- 5 ms LIF units with delays of at most 20 ms cannot hold 50-150 ms brake intervals, and add-node zeroes the delays.
- GO was set at parity, and the lesion tests were confounded.
- J is survival-dominated, and 32 cases are too few.
- The CoM sits about 1-3 mm from the gimbal pivots, so a counter twitch first turns base_link the wrong way.

With the fixes: P(Stage A GO) is about 30%; P(SNN/NEAT-central GO) is about 3-5%.

ranking.title: Evolve the timing, differentiate the gain: Lamarckian NEAT with plant-kernel surrogate gradients for spike-timed wingbeat steering
ranking.summary:
(method; critics 3/2.5) The first decision point (kernel fidelity plus a gradient-validity check, about 0.4 h) is a genuine unknown. The method targets NEAT's measured weakness, fine weight tuning.

Weaknesses:
- The J headroom is mostly LOW-floor saturation in the 6/16 low-headroom test cases. The 12-input SNN cannot observe this, and a margin-aware law fixes it classically at almost no cost.
- On high-headroom cases the oracle law's apparent 0.6 deg 'information' gain comes with 2x the pulse duty.
- Novelty is SVG/IFT-like, and parity with a GRU is expected.
- The v2 champion is structurally the dense initializer (8 nodes/83 edges), so the NEAT-structure test (P3) will very likely fail.

It is worth running to P2 as a methods test, with these fixes: margin inputs for all arms, midpoint credit, gust-window kernels, an SPSA check, and CMA-ES on the same weights as comparator. P(NEAT-central GO) is about 3-5%.

ranking.title: Phase-multiplexed motor spikes: lift from spike count, pitch from spike phase (tonic antagonistic code)
ranking.summary:
(temporal; critics 3/3) Interface-compliant and cheap, but a per-case replay contradicts the premise:
- law_strong's height cost is +0.12 cm in the 10 test cases with at least 47 rad/s headroom, and +7.5 cm in the 6 cases with 16-36 rad/s.
- So where there is budget there is nothing to recover, and where the cost arises there is no budget.
- One standing HIGH tick per cycle adds about 31 rad/s of mean command, which saturates the +-40 rad/s height integral; n=2 does not fit under LOW at all.
- The classical law B3 is the solution by construction, and G2's metrics cannot detect a tonic proportional code.

Keep only a redesigned 1-tick phase-response measurement (about 10 min) as a side note.

ranking.title: Learning when to twitch: evolved three-factor plasticity that self-calibrates wingbeat-timed steering in flight
ranking.summary:
(plasticity; critics 3/2) The gate is honest and cheap, but:
- The phase-to-pitch map is about 99% a first harmonic, so a tuned RLS is the efficient estimator. R-STDP on one-hot phase cells is a tabular LMS bandit and can at best tie.
- Plant changes mostly scale twitch amplitude. The only room left is latency (predictable and measurable from timestamps) or an artificial U(0,360 deg) offset.
- The delay-jump scenario destabilises the base PID itself.
- H5 already found no adaptation.
- G2b counts the learning transient as headroom.

Keep S1a (a PLL-referenced twitch-phase scan under plant changes, about 5 min) only as a robustness measurement.

ranking.title: Lift-neutral phase coding and an emergent b1/b2-like tonic/phasic division of labor in NEAT-evolved spiking steering units of the single-motor flapper
ranking.summary:
(science; critics 2/2.5) The b1/b2 framing is appealing, but the same headroom data refute the premise:
- The tonic S train adds about 15 rad/s of mean command exactly in the 16-36 rad/s cases, so Gate A's 'height -1 cm' target is unreachable.
- With fixed S/L sizes under a height-penalised J, the split is imposed rather than emergent.
- In the fly, b1's phase is shifted by haltere (rate) input, so the fly is actually the 'S-swap' arrangement.
- The robot's pulses act on the power drive, not on hinge muscles.
- The F law is classical.

Not worth running.

ranking.title: Lift-neutral spike steering: one motor pulse train carrying lift in its rate and pitch torque in its phase
ranking.summary:
(event; critics 2/2) Refuted:
- For any allocation, mean command >= LOW + duty x (HIGH-LOW). The multiplexer therefore creates no new downward authority and is, to first order, equal to the law plus payback.
- The proposed 10-15% duty has already failed: 23/24 height escapes in timing_closed_loop.json.
- The principle is published (SAM/F-SAM monocopters, Paulos & Yim, split-cycle).
- The SNN seed equals the classical multiplexer.

Its useful by-products, the headroom stratification and the missing margin-gated baseline, are folded into Step 0 of both plans.

top.title: Spiking righting reflexes: NEAT-evolved event sequencers for large-upset recovery of the single-motor flapping robot
gate_steps:
Step 0, prerequisites (no simulation; about 10 min after v2 frees the machine, about 02:45 JST):
(a) In /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/artifacts/spike_steer/v2/test.json, record whether v2 learned both need directions (at least 20 onsets each, at least 70% within +-67.5 deg of 135/315 deg). If not, Stage B starts from a bilateral mirror genome.
(b) Stratify the v1, v2 and law-grid rows by replayed motor gain. The gain is the RNG draw just before the pulse signs, as in pilot.pulse_sign.
(c) For every new metric, compute height RMSE over t >= 2 s from env.samples. HoverEnv.metrics includes the takeoff drop that all arms share.
(d) Ask the user whether a Stage-A-only (classical) outcome is acceptable, since P(SNN/NEAT-central GO) is about 3-5%.

Step 2, upset scenario and calibration (about 5 min).
Injection:
- Wrap env.air.advance (pattern: snn_hover/environment.py advance_instrumented) to add a 20 ms torque about a horizontal heading-frame axis on base_link (sim.external_body_forces[body, 3:6]). The wrapper runs after ControlEnv.step has zeroed the forces.
- Set pulse_force = pulse_torque = 0 in the case; the RNG order is unchanged.
- Onset t0 = 2.4 s + U(0, 40 ms).
Calibration: with the base PID, calibrate pitch, roll and diagonal directions separately (6 magnitudes x 8 directions x 2 seeds). Choose 3 levels per class that give PID survival of about 80/50/20%, and report each level as the induced peak body rate.
Step 3, base PID (about 4 min): choose kp/kd from gates.GRID (25 pairs x 8 training upsets), ranked by survivals and then mean J. Every arm uses this PID instead of the fixed kp x1.5.

Step 4, Stage A classical tuning (about 50 min).
All arms use the same 8-case training sets (all 8 directions, mixed levels, half with double hits), common random numbers, IMU-only features and the same primitive library:
(a) PID + IMU pulse law: 36-point grid.
(b) Gain-scheduled PID whose D term switches to the PLL-notched gyro above a rate threshold: 2-3 parameters, CEM, 384 episodes.
(c) One-shot reflex: one saturated counter twitch plus integrator freeze, no brake: 3-4 parameters, CEM, 384 episodes.
(d) PID + a dead-zoned notched-rate term that saturates the gimbal early: 24-point grid.
(e) Designer automaton HOVER -> COUNTER -> BRAKE -> HANDBACK, with a refractory period and optional lift top-up: 10 parameters, CEM 24 x 8 iterations x 8 cases = 1536 episodes, the same budget as each NEAT arm.

Step 6, Stage B code (no simulation):
- A SpikingGraph subclass with a slow or adaptive-threshold unit class (tau 50-150 ms), or a hidden-to-hidden delay buffer of at least 150 ms.
- A DelayGenome.mutate_add_node override that splits the original edge delay (d1 + d2 = d) and gives the new node a transmitting bias.
- A sparse start with near-zero readout weights and a negative output bias, so genome 0 is silent (equal to the base PID).
- 5 spiking outputs (alpha+-, beta+-, motor-up) through a decoder with 20 ms gimbal / 6 ms motor dwell and integrator freeze.
- A mirror genome if v2 failed one direction.
Unit tests: a zero readout reproduces the base PID bitwise; a delay split preserves the spike arrival time.

Step 7, Stage B runs (about 1.5 h, plus 0.5 h for the optional PPO arm).
Budget: 1536 episodes per arm (population 24 x 16 generations x 4 cases balanced over +-pitch/+-roll, cases shared within a generation). Validate the champion on 16 cases every 4 generations.
Arms:
- B-SNN: NEAT delay-LIF with slow units.
- B-ANN-matched: the same graph class with leaky rate units, identical integer delays, two 1 ms substeps and a thresholded output, so that only threshold and reset differ.
- B-fixed: a fixed dense recurrent SNN, CMA-ES on weights and delays.
- Optional B-PPO: a GRU over the same 6 discrete primitives (start from snn_hover/ppo.py).
Test every arm on the same 96 cases, plus these probes on the SNN champion:
- hidden-to-hidden delays zeroed, and separately shuffled (input delays kept);
- hidden-to-hidden edges removed;
- sensory clamp: rate and attitude inputs frozen after the first counter twitch.

Step 8, only if Stage B passes: transplant any rule the champion uses that the automaton lacks into an automaton v2, re-tune it with the same CEM budget and re-test. Report whether the gap closes, then replicate with at least 5 seeds before any write-up.
top.pass_criterion:
Stage A GO requires all three:
- On the 96 paired test cases, the CEM-tuned automaton beats the best single-mode controller (the best of PID+pulse law, gain-scheduled PID, one-shot reflex, and dead-zone rate term). It must either survive at least 8 more cases (McNemar p<0.05), or have mean J <= 0.85x with at least 60% paired wins (sign test p<0.05).
- The gain also shows in thrust-unit/whole-body peak tilt and in recovery time, not only in base_link posture.
- The best one-shot or gain-scheduled controller captures less than 80% of the automaton's gain over the PID. Otherwise multi-phase logic has no leverage.
If Stage A fails, the topic is NO-GO and only the classical result is written up.

Stage B strong GO requires all four (parity is not a GO):
- B1: the SNN survives at least 4 more of the 96 cases than the automaton, or has J <= 0.90x the automaton's with at least 60% paired wins (p<0.05).
- B2: in at least 50% of recoveries, an opposite-sign gimbal brake fires 50-150 ms after the first counter twitch, and it persists under the sensory clamp. Zeroing or shuffling only the hidden-to-hidden delays raises J by at least 20%.
- B3: J_SNN <= 0.95x B-ANN-matched AND <= 0.95x B-fixed, at equal budget.
- B4: at least 20 correct-sign onsets for each of +-pitch and +-roll, at least 70% correct sign, and false triggers before t0 no more than the automaton's.
If Stage A passes but Stage B fails, the result is a classical recovery paper with SNN/NEAT reported as a negative control.
top.implementation_notes:
New module: /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms/spike_steer/upset.py, about 500 lines for Stage A and about 300 more for Stage B. Run it in tmux after v2 finishes. Do not edit files that the running v2 job uses.

Throughput: about 4 simulated seconds per wall second on 18 workers (v2 ran 128 x 6 s episodes per ~185 s). Episodes last t0 + 1.5 s, about 4 s. Stage A takes about 1.2 h and Stage B about 1.5 h.

Reuse (paths under /home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms/):
- robust_control/environment.py: ResearchEnv(mode='direct', task='hover').
- snn_pid_compare/environment.py, ControlEnv.step: it zeroes sim.external_body_forces, sets the v3 pulses and then calls air.advance, so an advance wrapper can add the upset torque. motor_gain is applied after the clip. The tilt > 1.4 rad termination is evaluated on base_link. The TeacherPID integral/z_integral state is where the integrator freeze goes.
- snn_hover/environment.py: copy the patterns from advance_instrumented (impulse torque, saturation counts, range-dropout fraction, peak rate) and the recovery_time_s logic in metrics. Copy rather than import, because that class subclasses the 100 Hz HoverEnv.
- topology_hover/environment.py: case() (set pulse_force/pulse_torque to 0). HoverEnv.metrics computes height RMSE over the whole episode, so recompute it over t >= 2 s.
- topology_hover/sensors.py, HeightSensor: there are no range samples when cos(tilt) <= 0.7, and range is converted to height with the lagged AHRS. Take the altitude term from truth.
- spike_steer/pilot.py: the per-tick loop (cmd = env.teacher_command(); override; env.step((clip(cmd)-CENTER)/HALF)), the PID retune pattern, SpikingGraph, export, make_config with neat_template.ini, pool, summarize. Write your own run/task: pilot.run hard-codes cmd[2]=HIGH and logs only the first firing output.
- neuro_gates/gates.py: GRID, Oracle ('derocked', 'thrust_derocked'), HANDOVER_T, paired.
- neuro_gates/timing.py: run/measure, PULSE_PHASE.
- wingbeat_feasibility/preliminary.py: WingbeatPhase (crank(), slow) and com_velocity, which calls mj_subtreeVel.
- wingbeat_snn/plant.py: PHASE_OFFSET.
- wingbeat_snn/networks.py: Graph has MAX_DELAY=20 and no refractory period, and ann_step ignores delays and leak. So the matched rate arm must be new code.
- wingbeat_snn/evolve.py: DelayGenome. DelayConnectionGene initialises delay at 0 (stdev 0), so override mutate_add_node.
- Tools: cmaes 0.11.1 for CEM/CMA; snn_hover/ppo.py for the optional PPO arm.

Known pitfalls:
- The PLL may slip when body rate dominates the pitch gyro, so log its phase error against the true crank.
- The wrong-way base_link response to gimbal twitches inflates base_link tilt; this is why Step 1 is required.

top.title: Evolve the timing, differentiate the gain: Lamarckian NEAT with plant-kernel surrogate gradients for spike-timed wingbeat steering
top.why:
Ranked second for two reasons:
- Its first decision point is cheap (about 0.4 h) and genuinely uncertain: do identified, phase-indexed twitch kernels give valid per-spike credit on the non-differentiable plant?
- It attacks NEAT's measured weakness, fine weight tuning, with a tool any later spike-steering study could reuse.

The critics' fixes are adopted:
- Every arm and the classical law get the PID-margin input, because the J headroom sits in the low-headroom cases.
- Credit uses a midpoint finite difference instead of the first-order derivative, which over-prices fired spikes.
- Kernels are identified in gust windows and conditioned on margin.
- An SPSA closed-loop gradient check is added.
- CMA-ES on the same champion weights is the P1 comparator.
- A margin-aware CMA-tuned law is the P2 bar.
- Training sets are fixed, with paired accept/revert.
- P3 tests structure at an equal gradient budget.

Weak spots remain (critics 3/2.5): the novelty is SVG/IFT-like, parity with a GRU is expected, and the v2 champion is structurally the dense initializer, so P3 will very likely fail.

Most likely result: P0 and P1 pass and P2 fails, giving a methods note in which SNN/NEAT are incidental. P(NEAT-central GO) is about 3-5%.
gate_steps:
Step 0, shared prerequisites (about 15 min after v2):
- Do Step 0(a-c) of the upset plan.
- Build the margin-aware IMU law D0. Start from the pilot law. Raise its threshold as the PID's low-passed motor margin m = cmd_PID[2] - LOW[2] falls: u0_eff = u0 + c*max(0, m1 - m), or veto firing when m < m0. Feed it a lag-inverted AHRS pitch, theta_hat = theta_AHRS + sensor_tau*d(theta_AHRS)/dt; this uses only the sensor specification.
- Grid D0 over 24 points on pilot.balanced_cases('train', 16, 6., offset=900_000). The first 8 of these are v2's tune_law cases.
- Report D0 on the 32-case test split per motor-gain stratum.

Step 2, P0 validity (about 15 min):
(a) Leave-one-case-out prediction of single-twitch delta-J using the midpoint finite-difference credit J(e0 + h_hat) - J(e0).
(b) Open-loop replay of the twitch trains recorded from the v2 champion and from the tuned law onto 8 held-out PID-only flights. Report the R^2 of predicted against actual change in pitch and in height, per gain stratum.
(c) SPSA check: closed-loop finite-difference gradients of J on the v2 champion along 8 random weight directions (+-delta, common random numbers), compared with the KCSG gradient.

Step 3, torch twin (code and test, no simulation):
- A float64 re-simulation of SpikingGraph with per-edge integer delays, two 1 ms substeps, ORed spiking outputs, and twitch-occupancy and handover masks.
- A bitwise spike-equality test against numpy on recorded inputs, with nonzero delays.
- Add a 13th input for every learned arm: the PID margin m/63, clipped to [0, 2].

Step 4, P1/P2 arms (about 1.2 h), 720 episodes each.
Training protocol:
- A fixed 18-case training set covering the 4 pulse-sign combinations x 3 motor-gain terciles, reused every iteration (ILC-style).
- 8 separate validation cases every 10 iterations, with paired accept/revert and learning-rate halving.
Arms:
- A: the v2 champion with structure and delays frozen, zero-weight candidate edges completing input->hidden->output, and the margin input; trained by KCSG (Adam on weights and biases).
- A_ES: CMA-ES on the same champion's weights and biases.
- D_CMA: CMA-ES on D0's parameters (k_theta, k_q, u0, width, psi, c, m1), starting from its grid best.
Test the PID, the grid-tuned law, D0, D_CMA, the v2 champion, A and A_ES on pilot.cases('test', 32, 8.).

Step 5, P3 arms (about 1.5 h; run only if P2 passes), 720 episodes each, same 32-case test:
- A_reinit: the champion's topology and delays with re-initialized weights, trained by KCSG.
- B: a dense 13-6-2 random-delay SNN (pilot.initialize), trained by KCSG.
- C: a GRU-16 with straight-through Heaviside outputs, trained by KCSG.

Step 6, only if P0-P3 all pass: run the title method itself, Lamarckian NEAT+KCSG.
- Each genome's evaluation rollouts are reused as one KCSG step, written back before reproduction.
- Start from a sparse genome.
- Compare against dense+KCSG at equal total episodes, with at least 3 seeds.
top.pass_criterion:
P0 (stop on any failure):
- With the midpoint credit, single-twitch delta-J sign agreement >= 75% and Spearman >= 0.6.
- Replay R^2 >= 0.6 for pitch and >= 0.5 for height, in BOTH motor-gain strata.
- Mean cosine between the KCSG and SPSA gradients >= 0.3.

P1: J_A <= 0.95x the v2 champion's, AND J_A below J_A_ES by at least 2 paired SEM on the 32 cases. That is, KCSG must beat black-box tuning of the same weights at equal budget.

P2:
- A flies 32/32.
- J_A <= 0.95x min(J_D0, J_D_CMA), with at least 22/32 paired wins (sign test p<0.05).
- A is non-inferior in each gain stratum.
- Both directions are learned: at least 20 onsets per need sign, at least 70% of them within +-67.5 deg of the scan-measured optima.

P3 (NEAT-central): J_A_reinit <= 0.95x J_B with at least 22/32 wins, at equal gradient budget. If C comes within 5% of A, no SNN-specific claim is made.

Reading the outcomes:
- P0 fails: stop after about 0.4 h.
- P1 fails: KCSG adds nothing over CMA-ES.
- P2 fails: the margin-aware classical law suffices; at most a methods note.
- P3 fails (expected, since the v2 champion is 8 nodes/83 edges, i.e. the dense initializer plus noise): the gradient, not NEAT, does the work.

synth.notes:
Bottom line: no topic is strong. All twelve critiques score 2-3/10. For every topic, P(SNN/NEAT-central GO) is about 5% or less. Both plans are built to fail fast and still leave a usable classical result. Before spending Stage B or P3 compute, ask the user whether a classical-only or negative outcome is acceptable (CLAUDE.md: the user makes such decisions).

Checked by replaying the case RNG and reading JSON only (no simulation):

1) The motor-gain floor causes the height cost. motor_gain (1 +- 1.5%) multiplies the speed command after the [LOW, HIGH] clip (/home/robot/FlapSim-repo/FlapSim/experiments/algorithms/snn_pid_compare/environment.py, lines 97-100). Per-case downward headroom is therefore about 3178/g - 3115 = 16-108 rad/s. On the 16 v1 test cases:

| Cases | Controller | J | Pitch RMS | Height RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 with g <= 1.008 | retuned PID | 9.22 | 7.30 deg | 6.40 cm |
| 10 with g <= 1.008 | law_strong | 4.91 | 2.95 deg | 6.52 cm |
| 6 with g > 1.008 (16-36 rad/s) | retuned PID | 10.61 | 7.44 deg | 10.58 cm |
| 6 with g > 1.008 (16-36 rad/s) | law_strong | 8.58 | 3.15 deg | 18.10 cm |

So the pulse law's 'height cost' is LOW-floor saturation in about a third of the cases, not a general lift-steering trade-off. This removes the premises of the temporal, event and science topics.

2) The oracle-vs-IMU comparison is also confounded. On the 5 high-headroom tuning cases the oracle law reaches 2.39 deg against 2.97 deg at equal height, but it fires at twice the duty (1.97% vs 0.93%). Most of that apparent information gain is aggressiveness, which a margin-aware IMU law can also buy.

3) The v1 SNN worked in one direction only: 3.1-4.1 deg pitch in the 8 cases with x-sign -1, and 5.5-6.4 deg in the 8 with +1.

4) v2 status at about 02:08 JST:
- It was at generation 21 of 25.
- Validation J (8 balanced cases) has been flat at 8.59 since generation 3.
- The champion has 8 nodes and 83 edges, i.e. the dense initializer plus weight and delay noise.
- It will very likely fail J <= 1.05x the law. Check the both-direction onset counts in artifacts/spike_steer/v2/test.json.
- runs/run_steer_v2.sh then runs tune_law (8 cases) and test, so the machine frees at about 02:45.

5) HoverEnv.metrics computes height RMSE over the whole episode, including the takeoff drop that all arms share (topology_hover/environment.py, metrics). New gates should use t >= 2 s.

Required shared Step 0 for any further spike-steer work (about 15 min; included in both plans):
- stratify every result by motor gain;
- add a margin-aware IMU law (threshold or veto on the PID's own m_PID - LOW) with a lag-inverted AHRS pitch;
- compute height RMSE over t >= 2 s.
Firing more where headroom exists and less where it does not may plausibly move the classical J from 6.29 toward about 5.5. That raises the bar for every learner.

Recommended order after v2:
1. Step 0.
2. Upset Stage A (about 1.2 h) and KCSG P0 (about 0.4 h).
3. Report to the user.
4. Run Stage B or P1-P3 only with the user's approval.

Do not run the temporal, plasticity, science or event gates. Two optional side measurements are worth keeping as robustness notes:
- A 1-tick phase-response curve (temporal G1a), redesigned: a once-per-cycle trigger, 0.3-0.5 s bursts, regression over whole cycles, at least 8 cases.
- A PLL-referenced twitch-phase scan under plant changes (plasticity S1a).

Strategic point for the user. Across v3, P1, H5, the phase-estimation work, and spike_steer v1 and v2, every learned controller inside this interface has matched a retuned classical law rather than beaten it. The binding limits belong to the interface itself:
- about 63 rad/s of nominal downward margin;
- 2 ms ticks with 8.2 ms smoothing;
- the two-body inverse response.
If the goal is a paper where SNN/NEAT is central, there are two realistic options, and choosing between them is the user's decision:
- (a) accept a classical or negative-result paper inside v3;
- (b) revisit the interface constraint the user set.

One direction not among the six is suggested by point 2: a sensing check. Feed the margin-aware law a better de-rocked pitch and phase estimate, comparing a complementary filter, a gradient SNN and a GRU. The wingbeat line's data (phase error: GRU 0.8 deg, gradient SNN 2.4 deg, NEAT 9.3 deg; GRU equal to SNN in closed loop) predict SNN about equal to GRU, so this would not make SNN/NEAT central either.
